382	
383	erated plans, and (2) the end-to-end task execution suc-
384	cess rate. For the former, we use our newly constructed
385	ComplexTool-Plan benchmark. For the latter, we evaluate
386	our system on the established StableToolBench benchmark.
387	ComplexTool-Plan Benchmark
388	We evaluate our Plan-
389	ner on ComplexTool-Plan, our benchmark constructed from
390	a comprehensive library of 4,535 tool APIs sourced from
391	ModelScope (Li et al. 2023a). The benchmark features three
392	difficulty levels (Easy, Medium, and Hard) and provides a
393	curated SFT dataset of 3,000 instances. For RL training, the
394	dataset is filtered to comprise 787 instances, which are sub-
395	sequently divided into training and test sets using an 8:2 ra-
396	tio. Further details are available in Fig. 3.
397	End-to-End Execution Benchmark
398	To evaluate the prac-
399	tical effectiveness of our framework, we use StableTool-
400	Bench (Guo et al. 2024) for end-to-end evaluation. Stable-
401	ToolBench is an enhanced version of the test set from Tool-
402	Bench (Qin et al. 2023), specifically designed to mitigate ex-
403	ecution instability via a caching system and API simulators.
404	It categorizes test cases across two axes: tool generalization
405	and scenario complexity.
406	• Tool Generalization: Inst. (unseen instructions for seen
407	tools), Tool (unseen tools in seen categories), and Cat.
408	(unseen tool categories).
409	• Scenario Complexity: I1 (single-tool), I2 (multi-tool in-
410	category), and I3 (multi-tool in-collection).
411	Task difficulty escalates from I1-Inst. to I3-Cat., providing a
412	comprehensive testbed for agentic capabilities.
413	In our end-to-end evaluation on StableToolBench, we pair
414	our Planner with GPT-4o as the executor.
415	Baselines
416	To ensure a comprehensive evaluation, we benchmark our
417	framework against two categories of state-of-the-art base-
418	lines:
419	• Proprietary Planners: For direct planning evaluation
420	on our ComplexTool-Plan benchmark, we compare
421	against powerful proprietary models prompted to gener-
422	ate DAG plans directly. These include GPT-4o, Claude-
423	3.7, DeepSeek-V3, and Ernie-X1, which serve as a prac-
424	tical upper bound for the task.
425	• Open-Source Frameworks: For end-to-end evaluation
426	on StableToolBench (Guo et al. 2024), we compare
427	against established methods applied to the ToolLLaMA
428	model (Qin et al. 2023). This includes the reactive frame-
429	work ReAct, the planning-based method DFSDT, and
430	a highly relevant concurrent work, LLMCompiler (Kim
431	et al. 2024).
432	Evaluation Metrics
433	Planning Quality Metrics
434	To comprehensively evaluate
435	planning quality, we assess three key aspects: the correctness
436	of tool selection (node-level), the accuracy of inferred de-
437	pendencies (edge-level), and the holistic accuracy of the en-
438	tire plan. Our evaluation is conducted on a test set compris-
439	ing 500 samples from the Easy split and 500 from the Hard
440	split. For each generated Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), we
441	compute the following metrics against the ground-truth plan,
442	with all final scores macro-averaged.
443	Let Spred be the set of predicted items (nodes or edges)
444	and Strue be the set of ground-truth items.
445	• Node-level Performance (P/R/F1): Measures the accu-
446	racy of tool selection. We compute Precision, Recall, and
447	F1-score between the set of predicted nodes (Npred) and
448	ground-truth nodes (Ntrue).
449	– Precision (P): Measures fidelity by calculating the
450	fraction of predicted tools that are correct.
451	P = |Npred ∩Ntrue|
452	|Npred|
453	– Recall (R): Measures completeness by calculating the
454	fraction of required tools that were identified.
455	R = |Npred ∩Ntrue|
456	|Ntrue|
457	– F1-Score: The harmonic mean of Precision and Re-
458	call.
459	F1 = 2 · P · R
460	P + R
461	• Edge-level Performance (P/R/F1): Measures the struc-
462	tural correctness of the plan. We apply the same P/R/F1
463	metrics to compare the set of predicted edges (Epred)
464	against the ground-truth edges (Etrue). This assesses the
465	model’s ability to infer the correct execution flow.
466	• DAG Exact Match (EM): Our most stringent metric,
467	measuring the holistic correctness of the plan. A plan re-
468	ceives a score of 1 if and only if both its node set and edge
469	set perfectly match the ground truth (Npred = Ntrue and
470	Epred = Etrue), and 0 otherwise.
471	End-to-End Evaluation Metrics
472	To evaluate the end-to-
473	end task-solving capabilities of our framework, we adopt
474	the two primary metrics established by the StableToolBench
475	benchmark. The first, Solvable Pass Rate (SoPR), serves as
476	the primary measure of absolute capability and is defined as
477	the percentage of tasks that an agent successfully completes
478	according to the benchmark’s ground-truth criteria. The sec-
479	ond, Solvable Win Rate (SoWR), is a comparative met-
480	ric that evaluates performance relative to a strong baseline.
481	Specifically, it measures the win rate of our agent against the
482	benchmark’s provided GPT-3.5 (ReAct) baseline, offering a
483	clear signal of relative improvement. To ensure statistical ro-
484	bustness and mitigate performance fluctuations, all reported
485	scores are the average of three independent runs for each
486	experimental setting.

233	Methodology
234	Our method trains a language model to plan complex multi-
235	tool tasks, as shown in Fig. 2. The framework includes:
236	a formal Problem Formulation, our ComplexTool-Plan
237	data generation pipeline, and a Model Training process us-
238	ing both Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement
239	Learning (RL).
240	Problem Formulation
241	We formalize multi-tool task planning as a structured pre-
242	diction task of learning a policy π : Q × T →G. Given a
243	natural language query Q and a toolset T, the policy gener-
244	ates an execution plan as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG),
245	G = (V, E), where vertices V ⊆T are tools and edges E
246	represent data dependencies. The goal is to train a model Mθ
247	to find the optimal policy π∗that maximizes the expected
248	plan utility U(G):
249	θ∗= arg max
250	θ
251	E(Q,T )∼p(Q,T )[U(Mθ(Q, T))]
252	(1)
253	The utility U(·) is realized through a reward function.
254	ComplexTool-Plan
255	To overcome data scarcity, we developed ComplexTool-
256	Plan, a three-stage automated pipeline to generate our train-
257	ing dataset, Dtrain.
258	• Workflow Generation: We initiate the process by lever-
259	aging a powerful LLM-DeepSeek-V3, to author a large
260	set of workflows. For each workflow, the model is pro-
261	vided with a subset of tools from our predefined li-
262	brary T and prompted to generate a structurally com-
263	plex and logically consistent execution plan in the form
264	
265	============================================================
266	=== PAGE 4 ===
267	============================================================
268	
269	of a DAG, Gorig. This LLM-driven approach produces
270	the diverse, high-quality ground-truth solutions for our
271	planning tasks.
272	• Query Reverse-Engineering: Next, we employ a pow-
273	erful teacher LLM (Mteacher)-DeepSeek-V3 to reverse-
274	engineer a natural language query Q for each generated
275	workflow Gorig. The model’s objective is to capture the
276	user’s intent behind the workflow, effectively transform-
277	ing the difficult problem of plan generation into a more
278	manageable text-to-text task.
279	• Intent Analysis and Re-planning: The final stage acts
280	as a crucial quality filter. The reverse-engineered query
281	Q might be ambiguous or fail to fully capture the intent
282	of the original plan Gorig. Therefore, we use the same
283	teacher model Mteacher, now acting as an expert planner,
284	to re-solve the problem based solely on Q. This ensures
285	that the final DAG plan, Gfinal, is a faithful and optimal
286	solution derivable from the query, thus guaranteeing the
287	high fidelity of our resulting (Q, Gfinal) training pairs in
288	Dtrain.
289	Model Training
290	Our training process commences with Supervised Fine-
291	Tuning (SFT) on a suite of Qwen3 models—specifically,
292	the 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, and 8B variants. This initial SFT phase
293	serves to provide an effective initialization (i.e., a cold start),
294	which is subsequently followed by a GRPO training phase
295	for further policy refinement.
296	Base Models and Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
297	We
298	first perform Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on our dataset
299	Dtrain to initialize the model. The objective is to learn to gen-
300	erate the ground-truth plan Ggt by minimizing the Negative
301	Log-Likelihood (NLL) loss:
302	LSFT(θ) = −E(Q,Ggt)∼Dtrain[log P(Ggt|Q, T; θ)]
303	(2)
304	RL Training Set Curation
305	To ensure a stable and effi-
306	cient RL phase, we curate the training data to focus on
307	problems at the frontier of the model’s current capabilities
308	(Chen et al. 2024). We use the SFT-trained model as a filter:
309	tasks that the model already consistently solves (offering no
310	learning signal) or consistently fails (intractably hard) are
311	excluded from the RL training set. This curation of high-
312	variance instances, where the outcome is uncertain, concen-
313	trates the training on the most informative samples, prevent-
314	ing policy degradation and fostering robust optimization.
315	Reinforcement Learning with Hierarchical Rewards
316	To move beyond SFT’s limitations, we use Reinforcement
317	Learning (RL). This, however, requires a nuanced reward
318	signal to properly evaluate complex DAGs, distinguishing
319	structural from strategic errors. We address this by introduc-
320	ing a Hierarchical Reward Function R(y). To optimize this
321	complex, multi-dimensional reward, we utilize the Group
322	Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm (Shao et al.
323	2024), which is specifically designed for such scenarios and
324	ensures robust policy improvement.
325	Our reward function, R(y), where y represents the gen-
326	erated plan, evaluates plan quality through a fail-fast hierar-
327	chical process. It prioritizes structural correctness, with crit-
328	ical errors incurring large negative penalties and terminating
329	evaluation.
330	• Level 1 and 2: Structural and Semantic Penalties.
331	We first apply penalties for critical errors that render a
332	plan invalid. This includes ill-formed syntax (e.g., non-
333	JSON) or the presence of a cycle, both resulting in a large
334	penalty (-10.0). A less severe penalty (-2.0) is given for
335	a lack of connectivity (e.g., isolated nodes), which indi-
336	cates a semantic flaw.
337	• Level 3: Planning Fidelity Rewards. If a plan passes
338	all structural checks, it receives a positive reward based
339	on its quality. This reward consists of two parts: (i) an
340	Edge F1 Score Reward (RF 1), calculated as 5 times
341	the edge-level F1 score against the ground truth to re-
342	ward partial structural correctness, and (ii) a large Per-
343	fect Match Bonus (Rbonus) of +5.0 if the plan is identi-
344	cal to the ground truth, incentivizing perfect solutions.
345	The final reward, R(y), is computed based on these com-
346	ponents. If any penalty is applied, the reward is the value
347	of that penalty, checked in a specific order of precedence.
348	Otherwise, it is the sum of the fidelity rewards:
349	R(y) =
350	
351	
352	
353	
354	
355	
356	
357	Psyntax(y)
358	if invalid syntax
359	Pcycle(y)
360	else if has cycle
361	Pconnectivity(y)
362	else if disconnected
363	RF 1(y) + Rbonus(y)
364	otherwise
365	(3)
366	The domain of this reward function, [−10.0, 10.0], provides
367	a rich, multi-faceted learning signal that guides the model
368	not only on whether its plan is correct, but also on the nature
369	and severity of its errors.

371	Medium, and Hard. Harder tasks have more available tools
372	to choose from (blue) and also require more tools to be used

19	ABSTRACT
20	To improve task performance while encouraging desirable response properties,
21	LLM post-training often combines a primary reward (e.g., correctness) with aux-
22	iliary rewards (e.g., brevity or efficiency). However, how these rewards are aggre-
23	gated can critically affect training outcomes. We show that symmetric aggrega-
24	tion, which treats reward channels equally, can induce a failure where aggregate
25	reward improves while primary-task performance degrades, even when individual
26	rewards are meaningful. We investigate this aggregation-induced failure through
27	a one-step multi-reward decision formulation, characterizing when it constitutes
28	multi-reward hacking. We prove that, under symmetric aggregation, deterministic
29	conditional-mean GRPO converges to auxiliary-favoring behavior when auxiliary
30	rewards are more reliably obtained, regardless of initialization. We propose Trust-
31	Anchored Gating (TAG), which first elects an anchor channel based on the policy
32	drift induced by optimizing each channel alone, then gates auxiliary credit on an-
33	chor satisfaction. Unlike calibration-sensitive static reweighting, TAG structurally
34	eliminates credit for auxiliary-only outcomes while preserving additional credit
35	for joint success. In the same analytical setting, TAG provably reverses this se-
36	lection, converging to the primary-favoring action from any initialization when
37	the primary channel is anchored. Experiments across Qwen and Llama mod-
38	els on mathematics and program synthesis reveal substantial degradation under
39	symmetric, constrained, and normalized aggregation, whereas TAG mitigates this
40	failure. On Qwen3-4B with a brevity reward, TAG achieves 0.581 pass@4 ver-
41	sus 0.220 for additive aggregation, while shortening responses by 44% relative to
42	correctness-only training.

95	Preprint
96	focus on how to combine reward signals, leaving open when and why aggregation systematically
97	favors auxiliary behaviors over the primary objective. This paper asks the question that this practice
98	leaves open: Can reward aggregation itself undermine a primary objective, even when that objective
99	is explicitly rewarded?
100	It can, and the failure has a characteristic shape (Figure 1). Across models, tasks and aggregation
101	rules the auxiliary rate climbs toward one, so the aggregated objective keeps rising, while task cor-
102	rectness collapses (Figures 1 and 5). In most of these runs the policy stops solving the task and locks
103	onto a single behavior that games the auxiliary signal (Tables 1–2; Appendix C.5): it negates its final
104	answer to pass a sign check, shrinks its solution to a bare few-token guess to earn a brevity reward,
105	and emits programs that exit at once and solve nothing to earn a latency reward. Length exploitation
106	of this kind is documented in RLHF (Singhal et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024), and reasoning models
107	learn to exploit unit tests in agentic coding (Baker et al., 2025). We call this failure multi-reward
108	hacking (Definition 2), an instance of reward hacking (Amodei et al., 2016; Skalse et al., 2022b) with
109	a distinctive origin: unlike failures of misspecified or incomplete proxies (Pan et al., 2022; Zhuang
110	& Hadfield-Menell, 2020), it occurs with legitimate channels as well as flawed ones; aggregation
111	itself induces it. Existing reward hacking studies largely focus on imperfect proxies (Gao et al.,
112	2023; Karwowski et al., 2024), while detection methods typically assess individual reward signals
113	or behaviors. Neither fully explains how combining rewards can systematically favor an auxiliary
114	objective over a primary one. Recent multi-reward methods that rebalance the channels within each
115	group, such as MO-GRPO (Ichihara et al., 2026) and PG-OT (Ba et al., 2026), remain symmetric in
116	the channels and, as we show, collapse in the same way (Section 6).
117	We first establish a fundamental failure mode of symmetric reward aggregation, where no reward
118	channel is given priority over another. Such rules assign equal credit to primary-only and auxiliary-
119	only success, despite differences in how easily these rewards can be obtained. We formalize this
120	in a stochastic decision model that captures a common feature of real-world post-training: primary
121	rewards are often harder to obtain than auxiliary rewards. For example, solving a math problem or
122	passing unit tests requires successful reasoning, whereas producing a short response or a program
123	that exits immediately is comparatively easy. We prove that, under this imbalance, every symmetric
124	rule that rewards single-channel success drives the conditional-mean GRPO dynamics toward the
125	auxiliary-favoring behavior, regardless of initialization, even when the policy initially favors the
126	primary objective. This result reveals that symmetric aggregation can systematically favor an easier
127	auxiliary objective at the expense of the primary one.
128	The failure motivates breaking the symmetry in reward aggregation. While the analysis assumes a
129	designated primary channel, identifying which reward to prioritize in practice is not always straight-
130	forward. This raises two questions: which channel should receive priority, and how should that
131	priority be enforced? We propose Trust-Anchored Gating (TAG), which first elects an anchor by
132	briefly optimizing each channel in isolation and selecting the one that induces the least policy drift.
133	The intuition is that exploitable channels may induce large policy shifts toward shortcut behaviors,
134	making isolated drift a useful signal for anchor selection. Our experiments show that lowering the
135	auxiliary weight delays the collapse without preventing it, and that a weight which is safe at one
136	model scale fails at another (§6.2). Rather than relying on static reweighting, TAG enforces priority
137	through a structural gate: auxiliary-only success earns no more credit than failure on both channels,
138	while joint success remains more rewarding than primary-only success. We prove that, with the
139	primary channel as the anchor, TAG drives the conditional-mean GRPO dynamics to the primary-
140	favoring action from any initialization, for any positive gating weight, whenever primary success
141	remains possible.
142	We validate these findings on Qwen and Llama models (1.7B–30B), on mathematics and program
143	synthesis, with compatible and incompatible auxiliary rewards. In nearly every setting, previous
144	aggregation trades task correctness for the auxiliary reward, whereas TAG substantially mitigates
145	this degradation while retaining auxiliary benefits. On Qwen3-4B, for instance, TAG reaches 0.581
146	pass@4 under a brevity reward (0.220 for additive aggregation) with responses 44% shorter than
147	correctness-only training. Our contributions are:
148	• A provable failure of symmetric aggregation. We formalize multi-reward hacking and prove that,
149	when auxiliary rewards are more reliably obtained, symmetric aggregation drives the conditional-
150	mean GRPO dynamics toward auxiliary-favoring behavior from any initialization. We further char-
151	acterize when this selection constitutes reward hacking under the unknown true reward.

158	Preprint
159	• Trust-anchored aggregation with convergence guarantees. We propose TAG, which elects an
160	anchor by isolated policy drift and structurally conditions auxiliary credit on its satisfaction. With
161	the primary channel as anchor, TAG provably reverses the selection, converging to the primary-
162	favoring behavior from any initialization for any positive gating weight, while still rewarding joint
163	success, so that the auxiliary objective is pursued where it is compatible with the primary one.
164	• Empirical evidence in LLM post-training. Across Qwen and Llama models, mathematics and
165	program synthesis, we demonstrate severe correctness degradation under conventional reward ag-
166	gregation, including additive, normalized, and constrained methods. In all evaluated settings, anchor
167	election identifies correctness without prior knowledge of channel roles, and TAG substantially mit-
168	igates this degradation while retaining the benefits of auxiliary rewards.

561	EXPERIMENTS
562	6.1
563	SETUP
564	Reward channels.
565	We test the failure of §4 and the defense of §5 in RL post-training with two
566	reward channels whose compatibility is known by construction. The primary channel RP is always
567	correctness, a gold-answer check in mathematics and unit tests in program synthesis; the auxiliary
568	channel RA is a synthetic signal. In compatible settings some correct responses show the auxiliary
569	behavior (η > 0 in §3.3); in incompatible settings none does (η = 0) and the auxiliary credit is
570	a grader loophole in the sense of Wang et al. (2026). Settings are named by the pair of rewarded
571	behaviors: Correct & brief and Correct & negative on mathematics (§6.2), Correct & fast and Correct
572	& no-op on program synthesis (§6.3), with RA defined in those sections.
573	Models.
574	The main grid trains Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (Qwen3-4B below)
575	(Yang et al., 2025); §6.5 adds Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) and Qwen3-
576	30B-A3B.
577	Data and evaluation.
578	Mathematics arms train on the Big-Math hard split (Albalak et al., 2025;
579	Wang et al., 2026); program-synthesis arms train on DeepCoder-RT, a runtime-filtered pool built
580	from DeepCoder (Luo et al., 2025) (§6.3, Appendix C.4). We report held-out pass@4 and the rate
581	of the auxiliary behavior at the end of training and for the base model. An arm has collapsed when
582	the auxiliary behavior takes over and its held-out correctness falls far below the RP-only reference;
583	shaded table cells mark pass@4 below the base model. Appendix C (Table 6) lists the configuration.
584	Baselines.
585	All arms start from the same base model with the same data and training budget and
586	differ only in how the two channels enter training. Training on RP alone is the reference. Reward-
587	level rules shape a scalar reward and train it with standard GRPO: the additive rule (RP+RA)/2
588	(labeled RP+RA in the figures; the scale is immaterial under the group z-score), the weighted sum
589	0.9RP+0.1RA, the AND rule min(RP, RA), a Lagrangian port of Moskovitz et al. (2024) and a
590	reward-level port of PG-OT (Ba et al., 2026). Advantage-level estimators keep the additive reward
591	and change the advantage: MO-GRPO (Ichihara et al., 2026) sums per-channel group z-scores, and
592	Dr.GRPO (Liu et al., 2025) drops the group-standard-deviation of the GRPO loss. TAG uses Eq. (6)
593	with λ = 1 and the anchor elected by the probes of §5.1.
594	6.2
595	AGGREGATION-INDUCED DEGRADATION AND TAG
596	Settings. RP = 1 iff the final answer matches the gold answer. Correct & brief: RA = 1[ |y| <
597	200 tokens ], a length target a practitioner may add; short correct solutions exist (η > 0). Correct
598	& negative: RA = 1[final answer < 0], the grader flaw of Wang et al. (2026); gold answers are
599	negative on about 5% of problems (η ≈0).
600	Compatible channels: compatibility does not prevent collapse. Theorem 1 predicts that symmet-
601	ric aggregation selects the auxiliary behavior even when joint success is reachable. Correct & brief
602	bears this out: although short, correct solutions exist, conventional aggregation methods converge to
603	a bare answer template (Figure 1) that earns the brevity reward without solving the task, so pass@4

925	CONCLUSION
926	Combining individually meaningful rewards can undermine LLM post-training: the aggregate ob-
927	jective may improve even as primary-task performance deteriorates. We identify a fundamental
928	mechanism behind this failure: in a stochastic decision model, symmetric aggregation that rewards
929	single-channel success drives GRPO toward auxiliary-favoring behavior when auxiliary rewards are
930	easier to obtain, regardless of initialization. To address this, we propose Trust-Anchored Gating
931	(TAG), which elects an anchor through isolated policy drift and structurally conditions auxiliary
932	credit on anchor satisfaction. When the primary channel is anchored, TAG provably reverses this
933	selection while preserving incentives for joint success. Experiments across mathematics and pro-
934	gram synthesis demonstrate that aggregation-induced failures extend beyond symmetric rules, while
935	TAG substantially mitigates these failures and retains the benefits of compatible auxiliary rewards.
936	Limitations.
937	TAG assumes that one reward channel is the primary objective and the others are
938	auxiliary, so that a single anchor can be elected; handling several primary channels, or none that
939	deserves priority, is a direction for future work. Anchor election relies on short, channel-isolated
940	probes, which introduce additional computational cost, and low policy drift does not guarantee
941	alignment with the unknown true reward. Finally, our theoretical guarantees are established in a
942	simplified two-channel, binary-reward model. Extending the analysis to more general reward set-
943	tings and scaling anchor election to larger reward sets are further directions.
944	ETHICS STATEMENT
945	This work studies reward hacking in order to prevent it. All auxiliary channels in our experiments
946	are synthetic and injected into controlled training runs; no deployed system was attacked, and no
947	human subjects were involved. The collapse mechanisms we characterize are already documented
948	in the public literature we cite; our contribution is defensive.
949	AI USE STATEMENT
950	Generative AI tools were used to improve the clarity and readability of the manuscript and to assist
951	with editing software code. All AI-assisted text and code were reviewed and verified by the authors,
952	who take full responsibility for the final content.

954	Alon Albalak, Duy Phung, Nathan Lile, Rafael Rafailov, Kanishk Gandhi, Louis Castricato, Anikait
955	Singh, Chase Blagden, Violet Xiang, Dakota Mahan, and Nick Haber.

11	Abstract
12	Agents acting on our behalf in the real world—placing phone calls, resolving support
13	tickets—must learn online from costly, often irreversible interactions rather than cheap
14	simulator steps. Two things follow. First, deployability depends on the path, not only
15	the outcome. An agent must respect outcome-neutral constraints such as not repeat-
16	edly calling an unresponsive user, respecting business hours, or completing required
17	authentication—constraints that outcome-based rewards cannot express, since violat-
18	ing them frequently improves apparent success. Second, because each interaction is
19	expensive, the agent must learn efficiently from very few examples.
20	Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) is blind to both challenges:
21	it optimizes solely on the outcome and wastes expensive rollouts on all-fail groups
22	where group-relative advantage collapses to zero. Attempts to densify supervision by
23	rewarding progress target the hard-to-verify direction. In contrast, real agentic environ-
24	ments can cheaply detect bad moves. Since group-relative advantage is equivalent to
25	within-group variance, a dense signal helps only when it supplies variance the outcome
26	lacks. A verifiable penalty on the path meets this condition reliably, while a progress
27	potential helps only where partial progress is reachable. The resulting recipe—penalize
28	the path, reward the outcome—achieves high task success with near-zero violations,
29	where outcome-only training violates constraints on nearly every episode. We provide
30	four design rules for effective penalties, including avoidance of the inaction trap that
31	arises when a penalty is used in isolation.

86	RLVP: Penalize the Path, Reward the Outcome
87	2
88	1 Introduction
89	Consider an agent that acts on behalf of a person in the real world: it calls a bank, navigates
90	through the automatic voice menu, waits when put on hold, and eventually speaks with a
91	representative to resolve a billing dispute. Every action is a real, often irreversible interaction—
92	a genuine call rather than a resettable simulator step that can be replayed millions of times. A
93	rapidly growing class of deployed agents operate in this high-stakes regime [Pine AI, 2026a].
94	Unlike the reversible, self-contained environments of math problems, coding benchmarks, and
95	simulated games that shaped today’s foundation models, these agents must contend with
96	partial observability, irreversible consequences, long feedback delays, and genuine uncertainty
97	about the state of the external world. This regime differs from the reversible, high-throughput
98	environments used to train today’s models in two fundamental ways.
99	First, deployability depends on the path the agent takes, not the outcome alone. A successful
100	resolution is necessary but insufficient. An agent that reaches the right outcome by calling
101	a user who has explicitly declined contact, phoning outside business hours, or bypassing a
102	bank’s required authentication steps is not deployable—no matter how favorable the final
103	result. Outcome-based rewards cannot express these constraints: violating them often increases
104	the apparent success rate, because shortcuts and rule-breaking tend to accelerate resolutions in
105	the short term. A deployable agent must therefore satisfy both outcome and path constraints
106	simultaneously.
107	Second, these agents must learn online from their own live interactions, and they must do
108	so from very few examples. In math and code benchmarks, cheap simulators allow policies
109	to generate millions of rollouts, making sample efficiency secondary—slow learning can be
110	compensated by simply running more trials. In the real world, a phone call cannot be replayed.
111	An agent that learns from a single interaction that a particular bank requires a customer’s
112	date of birth and the last four digits of their account number must generalize that knowledge
113	immediately to the next user. Here, sample efficiency is not merely an optimization concern; it
114	is the difference between a system that meaningfully improves over time and one that cannot
115	be deployed at all.
116	Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) [DeepSeek-AI, 2025, Lambert et al.,
117	2024] is fundamentally blind to both challenges. It optimizes solely on the one signal the
118	environment can evaluate cheaply—the final outcome—rendering the path invisible. This
119	method also wastes its most expensive interactions on all-fail trajectories where group-relative
120	advantage is zero and no learning occurs. The natural response is to seek denser rewards by
121	crediting progress [Lightman et al., 2024, Wang et al., 2024, Setlur et al., 2025, Yu et al., 2024,
122	Feng et al., 2025]. Yet in agentic settings, judging progress is precisely the hard problem the
123	agent must solve. This leads either to a learned critic that the policy eventually fools [Cheng
124	et al., 2025, Kazemnejad et al., 2024, Gao et al., 2023] or to brittle, hand-crafted proxies.
125	Real agentic environments are asymmetric verifiers: they can cheaply and reliably detect bad
126	moves (e.g., calling before preconditions are met or acting outside business hours), but cannot
127	certify that an agent is making meaningful progress. The reliable dense signal they provide is
128	therefore a penalty on the path, not a reward for progress. Contrary to folklore, penalties are not
129	inherently problematic; the common collapse into inaction is a wiring error, not an inevitability.
130	A penalty in isolation indeed fails—its optimal policy is to do nothing, falling into an inaction
131	trap. However, when paired with an outcome reward—reward the desired result, penalize
132	forbidden paths—the penalty effectively teaches precisely the outcome-neutral constraints

866	Limitations.
867	Our strongest real-task harm reduction result was obtained in a regime where

26	Abstract
27	Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) remains the dominant critic-free
28	approach for fine-tuning LLMs and VLMs, but its compatibility with constrained
29	policy optimization (e.g. for safety-critical domains) has not been carefully exam-
30	ined. In this work, we introduce Constrained GRPO, a Lagrangian-based extension
31	of GRPO for constrained policy optimization. We show that the standard practice of
32	scalarizing rewards before normalization introduces a critical Lagrangian-specific
33	failure mode: GRPO’s within-group normalization makes constrained optimization
34	highly sensitive to how multi-component learning signals are aggregated. We
35	show that scalarizing rewards before normalization introduces shared-denominator
36	coupling, so that changing one multiplier alters not only the emphasis on its cor-
37	responding constraint, but also the relative weighting of the reward and other
38	constraints. We address this with a simple but crucial modification: scalarizing
39	standardized advantages rather than rewards. This yields a better-conditioned
40	update by addressing the coupling induced by reward scalarization, resulting in
41	better-behaved multiplier dynamics and more stable constraint enforcement in prac-
42	tice. Empirically, across a controlled gridworld, a real-world autonomous driving
43	benchmark, and a mathematical reasoning task, Constrained GRPO consistently
44	achieves better adherence to specified constraints while maintaining or improving
45	task performance.
46	1
47	Introduction
48	Recent progress in reinforcement learning (RL) has shown that large multimodal models can be
49	optimized with outcome-based signals. This has enabled the finetuning of models on mathematical
50	reasoning tasks [1–3], embodied decision making [4], among other domains where success can be
51	evaluated with programmatic or learned rewards. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [5]
52	removes the reliance on a critic for advantage estimation by a within-group normalization of the
53	rewards obtained over multiple sampled outputs for the same query. The critic-free structure of GRPO
54	is appealing when using a value function during training is challenging / computationally expensive.
55	∗Equal contribution. Primary contact: roger.girgis@gmail.com
56	Preprint.
57	arXiv:2602.05863v4  [cs.LG]  2 Sep 2026
58	
59	============================================================
60	=== PAGE 2 ===
61	============================================================
62	
63	Figure 1: Overview of our proposed approach. We extend GRPO to constrained policy optimization by enforcing user-specified
64	behavioral constraints with thresholds (left). Naively scalarizing reward distorts reward–constraint trade-offs, producing
65	inconsistent effective weights (middle; e.g., red/green swap). Scalarized advantages maintains the relative multiplier weighting
66	between advantage components, yielding more stable learning and effective constraint enforcement (right).
67	Existing GRPO-based methods have largely approached multi-objective optimization through manu-
68	ally weighting the importance of different reward terms [6–8]. In contrast, the constrained policy
69	optimization literature offers a principled framework, namely Constrained Markov Decision Processes
70	(CMDPs), for enforcing behavioural preferences and constraints by explicitly defining thresholds on
71	behaviours rather than employing fixed weights. However, GRPO has not yet been integrated into a
72	constrained optimization framework. In this work, we propose Constrained GRPO, a constrained
73	policy optimization framework employing GRPO as the policy optimization algorithm. Within our
74	framework, we specify desirable behaviours with indicator cost functions [9] and enforce target
75	behaviour rates (in percentage) using a Lagrangian relaxation with learned multipliers.
76	A central challenge arises from the interaction between Lagrangian methods and GRPO’s advantage
77	estimation through within-group standardization. A simple approach is to first scalarize rewards,
78	i.e., combine reward and cost terms into a single scalar value using the current multipliers, and then
79	apply the within-group standardization. However, we show that this seemingly innocuous choice
80	introduces an additional source of coupling in the constrained update: because the scalarized signal is
81	normalized by a shared, multiplier-dependent denominator, changing one multiplier can affect not
82	only its corresponding objective term, but also the relative contribution of of other components to
83	the policy update. We provide a formal analysis of the gradient estimator sensitivity to changes in
84	the multipliers, as well as an intuitive framing of how multiplier distortion occurs (e.g. Figure 1).
85	Motivated by this analysis, Constrained GRPO employs scalarizing advantages, i.e., standardize each
86	component within group first, and then combine the standardized components using the Lagrangian
87	multipliers. This design yields better-conditioning and well-behaved multiplier dynamics by removing
88	the shared-denominator coupling that is induced by reward scalarization. Importantly, this does not
89	imply exact preservation of the original unnormalized Lagrangian objective; rather, it produces a
90	more stable learning signal in the normalized component basis, which we validate empirically.
91	Prior and concurrent work has also found advantage scalarization beneficial in the realm of multi-
92	objective GRPO [6, 7]; our contribution places this observation in the context of constrained opti-
93	mization, showing why it is essential for effective Lagrangian constraint enforcement under GRPO.
94	Our main contributions are: (1) We introduce Constrained GRPO, a constrained policy optimization
95	framework built on GRPO, using indicator cost functions, Lagrangian relaxation and scalarizing
96	advantages to effectively enforce behaviour rates without manually tuning reward weights. (2) We
97	analyze the common approach of scalarizing rewards before normalizing, and formally characterize
98	the local response of the primal update to changes in the dual variables in Theorem 4.1. (3) We study
99	the alternative approach of scalarizing advantages and empirically demonstrate improved stability and
100	faithfulness of the behaviour specification in a gridworld environment, a realistic simulation-based
101	autonomous driving setting, and a mathematical reasoning task.

105	haviours through a single reward function. This challenge has inspired several alternative approaches

465	Experiments
466	5.1
467	Illustrative Environment
468	We begin with an illustrative example in a simple gridworld. An agent is randomly initialized in
469	a 10 × 10 grid and must navigate to a randomly sampled goal location, receiving a sparse scalar
470	reward upon reaching it. Each episode contains 20% lava tiles; stepping onto lava incurs a penalty
471	(i.e., a cost). In addition, the agent has a battery that depletes at every timestep and incurs a penalty
472	whenever its battery level falls below 10%. The action space consists of five discrete actions: moving
473	in the four cardinal directions or staying in place to recharge. This simple environment provides a
474	controlled testbed for isolating the differences between scalarized rewards and scalarized advantages
475	in constrained GRPO. Additional setup details and more experiments are provided in Appendix C.
476	We enforce constraint thresholds ˜dlava = ˜dbattery = 0.01 and train for 512k episodes. Figure 2
477	compares Constrained GRPO with scalarized advantages (ours) against a scalarized rewards baseline.
478	We see that scalarized advantages yields more stable learning across seeds (5 seeds), as reflected by
479	the narrower shaded region throughout training (column 1). Moreover, scalarized advantages leads to
480	richer behavior-rate dynamics (column 2, bottom row): the Lagrangian multipliers (column 3, bottom
481	row) adapt to allow the constraint rates to increase toward the threshold, effectively encouraging
482	the policy to use its available cost budget. On the other hand, scalarized rewards rapidly drives
483	both constraint rates close to zero early in training (column 2, top row), and keeps them near-zero
484	thereafter, even as the learned multipliers (columb 3, top row) remain small.
485	This behavior can be understood through the implicit reweighting predicted by Theorem A.3. Observe
486	that despite the small learned multipliers λlava and λbattery, the induced effective weights are larger and
487	significantly noisier due to within-group variance and covariance effects (row 4, left column). This is
488	especially problematic when the ordering of importance changes, as observed around 150K steps for
489	the goal and lava weights (red/green swap). Overall, these results support scalarized advantages as a
490	more reliable advantage construction for Constrained GRPO, as it preserves the intended role of the
491	Lagrangian multipliers in enforcing behavior specifications.
492	6
493	
494	============================================================
495	=== PAGE 7 ===
496	============================================================
497	
498	Figure 2: Gridworld under Constrained GRPO, comparing scalarized rewards (top) with scalarized advantages (bottom).
499	Scalarized advantages yields more stable training and uses the available cost budget, with behavior rates adapting toward the
500	specified thresholds as the Lagrangian multipliers adjust. In contrast, scalarized rewards collapses constraint rates toward
501	near-zero early in training with the effective weights remaining larger and noisier despite small learned multipliers.
502	5.2
503	NAVSIM Experiments
504	Benchmark Details.
505	Our next experiments are on the NAVSIM-v2 driving benchmark [40, 41], which contains 103k
506	training scenarios (Navtrain) and 12k testing scenarios (Navtest) curated from OpenScene [42, 43].
507	NAVSIM-v2 evaluates planning using explicit behavioural safety constraints alongside task-level
508	objectives such as progress and comfort, enabling targeted analysis of behaviour specification. We
509	do our evaluations on the Navhard split containing more challenging driving scenarios and planners
510	are evaluated using a two-stage pseudo-simulation protocol: Stage 1 evaluates the policy’s ability
511	to drive in unseen nominal driving scenarios while stage 2 evaluates the policy’s ability to produce
512	corrective behaviors. More details are in Appendix D.
513	The primary evaluation metric is Extended PDM Score (EPDMS ∈[0, 1]) which aggregates multiple
514	subscores via a product of hard penalty terms and a weighted average of auxiliary terms (Eq. 22 in
515	Appendix D). The penalty terms, each taking values in {0, 1}, include: (1) no at-fault collisions (NC),
516	(2) drivable area compliance (DAC), (3) driving direction compliance (DDC), and (4) traffic light
517	compliance (TLC). Since these penalties are combined multiplicatively, violating any one of them
518	sets EPDMS= 0 for that scene. The weighted average terms consist of: (1) ego progress (EP) along
519	the route, (2) time-to-collision (TTC), (3) history comfort (HC), (4) extended comfort (EC), and (5)
520	lane keeping (LK). We also report the 4-second Average Displacement Error (ADE@4s) on Stage 1
521	scenes, computed with respect to the human trajectory.
522	Although the penalty terms are designed as hard constraints at evaluation time, directly optimizing
523	a multiplicative hard-gated objective can lead to sparse learning signals and unstable optimization,
524	as we show. We therefore treat penalty terms as soft behavioural constraints, targeting near-perfect
525	satisfaction (0.99) while preserving informative gradients throughout training.
526	Model Baselines.
527	We initialize all experiments with the Qwen2.5-VL 3B Instruct model [44],
528	which we pre-train following the Poutine supervised finetuning (SFT) recipe [45]. We then perform
529	additional SFT on the NAVSIM training set [40, 41] (see Appendix D), reserving ≈11k scenes as a
530	held-out split for RL finetuning (RLFT). Our baselines are as follows:3
531	(1) GRPO with EPDMS: optimize EPDMS as the reward, in the spirit of CaRL [46] (which optimizes
532	a similar objective with PPO). Because EPDMS is multiplicative, any NC/DAC/DDC/TLC violation
533	collapses the reward to zero, acting as a hard constraint.
534	(2–5) Linear scalarization: a weighted sum of constraints and the weighted-average terms (WAT):

905	Lagrangian weights exert their intended influence on the learning dynamics. Finally, around ∼2500
906	steps, the NC multiplier increases sharply as DAC becomes satisfactory but collision compliance
907	degrades, showing that the optimizer adaptively reallocates emphasis across constraints.
908	Hard constraints lead to suboptimal learning dynamics. Finally, observe that directly optimizing
909	EPDMS as a reward (i.e., GRPO with EPDMS) underperforms the soft-constraint formulations,
910	yielding lower overall EPDMS on both Stage 1 and Stage 2. Intuitively, EPDMS couples constraints
911	through a multiplicative structure, collapsing the learning signal whenever any penalty term is violated.
912	This removes the ability to trade off and prioritize objectives smoothly during training, and prevents
913	variance-aware balancing of component signals. In contrast, our soft-constraint formulation retains
914	informative gradients even when constraints are partially violated, enabling more stable optimization
915	and ultimately improved behavior specification.
916	5.3
917	GSM8K Experiments
918	Benchmark Details.
919	We further evaluate our approach in a language reasoning setting using the
920	GSM8K dataset, which consists of grade-school math word problems requiring multi-step reasoning.
921	For each completion, we consider four signals: correctness, format adherence, integer validity, and
922	length (which favors shorter reasoning chains).
923	Model Baselines.
924	We initialize all experiments from Qwen2.5-Instruct models at three scales:
925	1.5B, 3B, and 7B parameters. For the baselines, we compare to GDPO and PPO-Lagrangian.
926	GDPO [8] is a prior advantage-scalarization baseline designed for multi-objective GRPO training.
927	PPO-Lagrangian uses a learned value function and enforces constraints through the standard primal-
928	dual PPO formulation. For our constrained formulation, we treat correctness, format adherence, and
929	integer validity as constraints, and optimize the length objective as the primary reward. Our goal
930	is not to claim that correctness is only required up to a threshold; rather, the thresholds serve as
931	optimization targets that prevent the policy from trivially improving length by sacrificing correctness
932	or output validity.
933	Results.
934	Tables 2 reports our GSM8K results. Across all three model scales, constrained
935	GRPO achieves higher correctness than GDPO while maintaining strong performance on format
936	adherence and integer validity. The gains are most pronounced at larger scale: at 3B, constrained
937	GRPO improves correctness from 0.770 to 0.802, and at 7B from 0.768 to 0.887. These results
938	suggest that explicitly enforcing correctness as a constraint prevents the model from over-optimizing
939	easier auxiliary objectives such as reducing output length. We observe that GDPO often produces
940	substantially shorter generations, especially at the 7B scale, where it reduces length to 127.49 tokens
941	on average but at the expense of correctness. Compared to PPO-Lagrangian, constrained GRPO
942	achieves comparable or better performance on all four metrics at the 1.5B and 3B scales. At 7B,

949	PPO-Lagrangian attains slightly higher correctness (0.891 vs. 0.887), but constrained GRPO remains

951	6
952	Conclusion
953	We introduced Constrained GRPO, a Lagrangian extension of GRPO that enforces user-specified
954	constraints via indicator costs and learned multipliers. We showed that scalarizing rewards before
955	normalization introduces shared-denominator coupling, so that changing one multiplier can affect
956	not only its corresponding constraint term, but also the relative contribution of the other terms to
957	the policy update. By instead scalarizing standardized advantages, Constrained GRPO yields a
958	better-conditioned update and more stable multiplier dynamics in practice.

14	Abstract
15	Deep research tasks require agents to navigate large knowledge spaces, synthe-
16	size evidence across many sources, and adapt their plans as intermediate findings
17	emerge. Directed acyclic graph (DAG)-based multi-agent systems are well suited
18	to this setting because they support parallel execution and isolate each sub-task
19	within a focused dependency context. Yet existing DAG-based agents typically
20	instantiate a task-level plan before execution and then repair the graph only after
21	failures or missing evidence are observed. This Plan-then-Patch strategy is brittle
22	for deep research: the system commits most strongly when its evidence is weakest,
23	and later revisions often waste computation on branches that should not have been
24	planned in the first place. To address this brittleness, we propose DAGent, a DAG-
25	based multi-agent framework that introduces Evaluate-then-Grow incremental
26	planning. Instead of committing to a full DAG upfront, an Orchestrator grows the
27	task graph one batch at a time, conditioning each new expansion on confidence and
28	uncertainty signals from completed nodes. To support long-horizon evidence use
29	without overloading each sub-task, DAGent maintains a hierarchical context layer
30	that propagates compact QueryDocs by default while preserving full execution
31	traces for on-demand recall. The cleanly recorded DAG topology in turn admits
32	structural RL signals that an outcome-only recipe cannot define; we instantiate this
33	with DAGRPO, a GRPO adaptation that injects topology-conditioned credit on
34	Executor rollouts and a structural compliance regularization on Orchestrator plans.
35	Across BrowseComp-Plus, GAIA, and xbench-DeepSearch, DAGent surpasses the
36	strongest open-source baseline by 5.3 / 5.8 / 2.0 points at the Qwen3-235B-A22B
37	scale, with the lead replicating across four open-source backbones from four ven-
38	dors and extending to GPT-5 at 327K context. At the Qwen3-8B scale, DAGRPO
39	further improves over a same-budget outcome-only GRPO baseline by 3.0 average
40	Pass@1 points. A same-architecture comparison further shows that incremental,
41	evidence-conditioned planning reaches higher accuracy at lower per-task token,
42	tool-call, and step footprints than its Plan-then-Patch counterpart, so the gains come
43	from more targeted evidence expansion rather than additional computation. Code
44	is available at https://github.com/hanwenliu6825/DAGent.
45	1
46	Introduction
47	The rapid advancement of large language models has given rise to a new class of information-intensive
48	tasks broadly referred to as deep research: tasks that require an AI system to autonomously navigate
49	large knowledge spaces, synthesize information across dozens or hundreds of sources, and resolve
50	complex queries through extensive multi-step reasoning. A growing body of work has established that
51	∗Corresponding author.
52	40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026).
53	arXiv:2609.39154v1  [cs.CL]  30 Sep 2026

55	============================================================
56	=== PAGE 2 ===
57	============================================================
58	
59	DAG-based multi-agent systems are an effective architectural foundation for such tasks, decomposing
60	a query into a directed acyclic graph of sub-tasks so that independent branches execute in parallel
61	and each agent operates within a focused context window informed only by its dependencies rather
62	than the full upstream history. The paradigm has been applied to parallel function calling [17], web
63	search [6], multi-hop retrieval [39, 5] and long-horizon task decomposition [19].
64	Deep research, however, places greater demands on the planning mechanism than traditional informa-
65	tion search: intermediate findings can redirect subsequent investigation and invalidate assumptions
66	that looked reasonable at the outset, making static or semi-static planning a poor fit. Recent DAG-
67	based deep research systems acknowledge this through execution-time editing. Flash-Searcher [33]
68	produces its complete plan in a single decomposition call and then periodically updates it, and
69	FlowSearch [14] initializes its knowledge-flow graph over several planner iterations, all of which
70	precede execution, and then lets a separate refiner rewrite the graph through six edit operations. In
71	both systems a plan that covers the whole task is committed before any node has executed, and later
72	edits patch that standing plan. We term this paradigm Plan-then-Patch: it makes its largest planning
73	commitment at precisely the moment when the system’s understanding of the problem is shallowest,
74	and the resulting trajectories mix plan commitment with plan revision, degrading answer accuracy
75	and wasting compute as task complexity grows.
76	Therefore, we argue that benefiting fully from DAG-based decomposition in deep research requires
77	both the planning paradigm and the reinforcement learning (RL) objective to reflect the fact that
78	the DAG is built incrementally.

1731	B
1732	Design Decisions
1733	This appendix explains the main design decisions of DAGent and DAGRPO and relates DAGRPO to
1734	concurrent credit-assignment methods.
1735	B.1
1736	Evaluate-then-Grow versus Plan-then-Patch
1737	The Plan-then-Patch label refers to when a planning decision is made and how much the system
1738	knows at that moment, not to how many nodes one call produces. Flash-Searcher [33] produces its
1739	entire plan in one decomposition call before execution and then periodically updates it, removing

505	the G sampled trajectories, while the Executor group contains all retained Executor rollouts spawned
506	by them. Here, α ∈[0, 1] controls the attenuation of off-chain Executor credit, S(τ) denotes the
507	answer-inclusive closure, and rproc(τ) ≤0 is the structural compliance regularization, both detailed
508	below. We also include a small KL-to-reference loss outside Eq. (5) to stabilize long-horizon agent
509	training. Additional details and the reasons behind these choices are given in Appendix B.
510	Topology-Conditioned Credit.
511	Let tanswer denote the answer-type node scheduled in the terminating
512	iteration. We define the answer-inclusive closure S(τ) as tanswer together with all of its ancestors in G:
513	the set of ReAct Executor rollouts whose outputs directly or transitively fed the final synthesis. ReAct
514	Executors in S(τ) retain the full R(τ) while those outside are attenuated by α. When τ contains
515	no answer-type node, we set α = 1 as a fallback and recover the outcome-only GRPO behavior.
516	The closure is a structural proxy for contribution rather than a causal attribution: it is read off the
517	recorded graph without re-execution, and Appendix B explains why it cannot be exploited by inflating
518	dependency edges during training.
519	Structural Compliance Regularization.
520	Evaluate-then-Grow imposes structural constraints on
521	Orchestrator decisions, requiring each plan to be both syntactically valid and consistent with the
522	incremental execution loop. Specifically, the Orchestrator must assign every node in the previous
523	batch an explicit Success, Uncertain, or Not Found status; expand each refinable Uncertain or Not
524	Found node with a refine node within the three-attempt budget; schedule the answer-type node as a
525	singleton batch so final synthesis can access all upstream evidence; avoid duplicate sub-task prompts;
526	and output parseable JSON with valid dependency references. Let N(τ) denote the number of
527	Orchestrator turns in τ that violate these constraints. We define rproc(τ) = −λproc min(N(τ), Kproc),
528	where λproc ∈(0, 1] controls the regularization scale and Kproc caps its magnitude. This term is added
529	to the trajectory-level Orchestrator reward to penalize structurally invalid planning decisions.
530	Remark.
531	DAGent rests on a single structural fact: incremental planning produces a DAG whose
532	growth history is recorded turn by turn, and that recorded structure is what the rest of the method
533	exploits. The hierarchical context layer uses it to bound each node’s per-sub-task footprint by graph
534	topology rather than total trajectory length; DAGRPO uses it to define credit-assignment signals that
535	an outcome-only recipe cannot express. Both rest on the incremental loop of §3.1, and removing it
536	weakens both. The complete DAGent workflow is summarized in Algorithm 1 in Appendix A.
537	4
538	Experiments
539	We organize the experiments around four research questions (RQs). RQ1: How does DAGent compare
540	with deep research baselines on representative benchmarks in both training-free and training-based
541	settings? RQ2: Does the lead replicate across backbone scales, vendors, and a frontier closed-source
542	backbone? RQ3: Which planning and DAGRPO structural components drive the gains of DAGent?
543	RQ4: How efficient is DAGent compared with the Plan-then-Patch alternative?
544	6

548	============================================================

550	4.1
551	Experimental Setup
552	Benchmarks.
553	We evaluate on three deep research benchmarks, each with a fixed retrieval backend
554	that every method shares. BrowseComp-Plus [7] pairs the original BrowseComp queries [40] with
555	a verified corpus; retrieval is local dense retrieval over this corpus with Qwen3-Embedding-8B,
556	and we adopt the 680/150 train/evaluation split of Sun et al. [38], balanced across easy, medium,
557	and hard difficulty. GAIA [26], a benchmark for evaluating complex task-solving capabilities, is
558	evaluated primarily on its 103-task text-only validation subset with live Google search through
559	Serper and page extraction through Jina; the full 165-task validation set is used only for the GPT-5
560	327K comparison in Figure 4, for comparability with prior work, with image, document, and audio
561	inspector tools added to handle multi-modal questions as detailed in Appendix D.1. The 2505 release
562	of xbench-DeepSearch [4, 45] contains 100 Chinese-language tasks and uses the same Serper and
563	Jina stack as GAIA. Checkpoints trained on BrowseComp-Plus transfer zero-shot to the other two
564	benchmarks, following the standard practice of agent RL [38].
565	Baselines.
566	We compare against five agent families under the same backbone and tool stack: (1)
567	ReAct Agent [47] at 32K and 109K context with a pre-overflow warning as a termination control;
568	(2) Summary Agent [13, 44, 16, 22], which invokes a summary on overflow with up to 10 sessions;
569	(3) Fold Agent [38, 48, 35], representative of context-folding methods; (4) Flash-Searcher [33], a
570	Plan-then-Patch DAG agent reproduced from the authors’ release with summary interval 4 to fit the
571	32K-per-sub-task budget; and (5) FlowSearch [14], a Plan-then-Patch DAG agent evaluated with the
572	authors’ released implementation with its Coordinator (the execution-conditioned refiner) enabled,
573	at Qwen3-32B only, because its code was released after our initial submission (configuration in
574	Appendix C.3). At Qwen3-8B we additionally report the three trainable baselines under outcome-only
575	GRPO, and DAGent under both outcome-only GRPO with α = 1.0 and no structural regularization
576	(denoted GRPO-DAGent) and DAGRPO (denoted DAGRPO-DAGent); the GRPO variant is the same-
577	budget direct baseline for DAGRPO.
578	Implementation.
579	Backbones are Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B, and Qwen3-235B-A22B [46] for
580	training-free evaluation and Qwen3-8B for RL training, all with thinking disabled and, per sub-
581	task, a 32K-token response budget on top of an 8K-token prompt (Appendix C.2). RL is trained on
582	BrowseComp-Plus with the DAPO asymmetric clip [49], off-chain credit α = 0.5, and the structural
583	compliance regularization. Inference uses greedy decoding; Pass@1 is scored by a human-calibrated
584	LLM judge, with details in Appendix C.
585	4.2
586	Main Results (RQ1, RQ2)

19	ABSTRACT
20	Ambiguous or incomplete task specifications complicate both execution and clar-
21	ification for language-model agents. Yet agents’ responses to these information
22	gaps remain poorly characterized across models and execution harnesses. We
23	present AM-BENCH, a benchmark built from 48 tasks adapted from Terminal-
24	Bench 2.0 and Harness-Bench. Each task includes a fully specified reference
25	and six variants spanning ambiguous or missing goals, context, and constraints.
26	We evaluate every pairing of five models and four harnesses over 20,160 runs.
27	Our results reveal distinct execution deficits: goal gaps hinder completion, con-
28	text gaps increase token use, and constraint gaps weaken compliance without
29	necessarily preventing completion. Missingness lowers success more than am-
30	biguity in all three domains. These effects also reshape system comparisons:
31	advantages under complete information need not persist, and rankings depend
32	on model × harness pairings and the evaluation criterion—completion, success,
33	or repeat consistency.
34	Estimates based on observed clarification requests and
35	matched fully specified runs further suggest that clarification could recover un-
36	finished work while leaving most constraint violations unresolved.
37	Together,
38	these findings motivate joint model–harness evaluation across information con-
39	ditions and targeted clarification of unresolved requirements before dependent
40	actions.
41	To support future research on agents under task underspecification,
42	we provide the AM-BENCH project repository at https://github.com/
43	s4-lab-cuhksz/AM-Bench.git.
44	1
45	INTRODUCTION
46	Language-model agents execute user tasks as multi-step workflows across web interfaces, applica-
47	tions, and command-line tools. Benchmarks such as WebArena, AppWorld, τ-bench, and Terminal-
48	Bench assess their ability to complete these workflows (Zhou et al., 2024; Trivedi et al., 2024; Yao
49	et al., 2025; Merrill et al., 2026). Executing these workflows requires understanding the intended
50	goal, identifying relevant context, and respecting constraints on permitted actions. In practice, users
51	may lack the time or domain knowledge to specify all three. The requested deliverable may admit
52	several interpretations, necessary inputs may be unspecified, or an operational restriction may be
53	omitted. Under such task underspecification, an agent must decide whether to seek information,
54	request clarification, or proceed with an interpretation that may not match the intended task.
55	These decisions depend on both the model and its execution harness. The model interprets available
56	information and proposes actions, while the harness assembles context and manages the tool-use
57	loop. Evaluating their combined behavior also requires distinguishing task completion from adher-
58	ence to the intended constraints: an agent may finish the work while violating those constraints, or
59	appropriately request clarification while leaving the task incomplete. Existing benchmarks examine
60	complementary aspects of this problem. Harness-Bench compares models and harnesses on shared
61	tasks without systematically varying task information (Yao et al., 2026). ToolEmu studies execu-

70	Figure 1: Benchmark pipeline. Each task yields a Full condition and six Goal/Context/Constraint
71	variants. Isolated model × harness executions interact with case-local tools; traces, artifacts, and

73	tion risks arising from underspecification, while LHAW and UnderSpecBench examine responses
74	to changes in task information (Ruan et al., 2024; Pu et al., 2026; Ji et al., 2026). ClarifyBench
75	and AppWorld-UL focus on clarification and other forms of user interaction (Suri et al., 2026; Chen
76	et al., 2026). What remains unclear is how different information gaps affect execution and clarifi-
77	cation across model × harness configurations, and whether performance advantages persist across
78	information conditions and component pairings.
79	We investigate these relationships through three connected questions: RQ1: How do different un-
80	derspecified conditions affect task execution? RQ2: How do models and harnesses jointly shape
81	execution performance? RQ3: When do agents request clarification, and how much could those re-
82	quests help? These questions motivate a benchmark that groups information conditions of the same
83	task, provides portable environments for model × harness comparisons, and measures execution and
84	clarification on a common basis.
85	We introduce AM-BENCH, named for Ambiguity and Missingness, to address these questions. The
86	benchmark adapts 48 tasks from Terminal-Bench 2.0 and Harness-Bench into executable tool envi-
87	ronments (Figure 1). Each task pairs a fully specified reference (Full) with six variants spanning am-
88	biguous or missing goals, context, and constraints. The intended task remains the evaluation refer-
89	ence across all seven conditions. Task-specific evaluators assess Completion and Compliance sepa-
90	rately; Success requires both. We evaluate every pairing of five models and four harnesses, with three
91	runs per setting, yielding 20,160 runs. Grouped task conditions and the complete model × harness
92	grid support comparisons of absolute performance and relative rankings, using each configuration’s
93	Full performance as its complete-information reference. For clarification, we combine observed
94	requests with matched Full runs to estimate potential improvements under a common complete-
95	information reference, without introducing differences in user-response completeness or interaction
96	strategies into the system comparison.
97	Our experiments yield three connected findings. First, information gaps produce distinct execution
98	deficits (RQ1). Unclear goals impede Completion, unclear context incurs the highest token use,
99	and unclear constraints weaken Compliance while largely preserving Completion. Averaged across
100	configurations, missingness yields lower Success than ambiguity in all three domains, even when
101	it increases Completion or reduces token use. Second, these effects change which systems perform
102	better (RQ2). Advantages under Full need not persist under underspecification. Rankings also
103	depend on the evaluation criterion: higher Completion need not imply higher Success, and higher
104	Success need not imply greater repeat consistency. Model × harness pairings matter as well, since
105	the same harness change can improve one model’s Success while reducing another’s. Third, existing

113	clarification requests offer uneven opportunities to address these deficits (RQ3). The Full-reference
114	estimates primarily indicate potential recovery of unfinished work, with limited relief for constraint
115	violations. Larger estimated gains under missingness narrow its Success disadvantage for context
116	and reverse it for goals, while leaving the constraint gap largely unchanged. These opportunities
117	also differ across configurations: within the evaluated grid, request rates and estimated gains vary
118	more across harnesses than models.
119	These findings suggest complementary priorities for users and developers. Users should make con-
120	straints and goals explicit and supply the context needed for execution. Model developers should
121	evaluate Completion, Success, and repeat consistency across Full and underspecified conditions;
122	harness developers should support targeted clarification before actions that depend on unresolved
123	requirements and test this behavior across supported models.

276	BENCHMARK CONSTRUCTION
277	We implement the design through executable task environments, grouped information conditions,
278	and common evaluation records (Figure 1).
279	Task selection and adaptation.
280	AM-BENCH adapts 48 base tasks:
281	28 from Terminal-
282	Bench 2.0 (Merrill et al., 2026) and 20 from Harness-Bench (Yao et al., 2026). We select practical
283	workflows with checkable outcomes that can be executed through external tools, including direc-
284	tory permissions, audio transcription, and access-log reports. Task sources and workflow coverage
285	appear in Appendix B.1.
286	Using source task objectives and workflows, we construct case-local environments with specified
287	inputs, required artifacts, workflow checks, and access rules. Each case combines a request, initial
288	workspace, task-specific Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, and evaluator. We implement task
289	operations as core MCP tools, alongside distractor tools offering alternative goals, objects, or sources
290	and restricted tools accessing protected information or acting outside task constraints. Figure 2
291	illustrates a directory-permission task using access control lists (ACLs), which define permitted file
292	or directory access, together with representative tools and evaluation evidence.
293	Construction of task conditions. Starting from the source task materials, we specify the intended
294	goal, context, and constraints σ⋆
295	i for each adapted task i and construct Full. We then create six
296	underspecified variants according to Table 1. GPT-5.6-Sol assisted in drafting the variants using a
297	construction skill, and the authors reviewed them. This yields 48 Full references and 288 underspec-
298	ified instances, or 336 executable task–condition instances.
299	The changes cover information in requests, execution guidance, tool descriptions, and tool returns.
300	Each variant primarily targets one information domain. The intended outcome and execution con-
301	straints in σ⋆
302	i remain the evaluation reference across all seven conditions of task i. The construction
303	skill calls for comparing Full and each variant across requests and tool names, descriptions, schemas,
304	returns, and errors to check what information remains available. Per-variant change notes record ed-
305	its to the request, task configuration, tool information, and workspace and stay outside the agent’s
306	workspace.
307	For example, a file-counting task changes a precise line-count request into a request for a suitable
308	summary (GA), or identifies the input file without specifying a deliverable (GM). A sales-report task
309	replaces its authoritative-source instruction with a reference to available sources (CA), then omits
310	the source guidance and submission interface (CM). In a scheduling task, KA prohibits clearly secret
311	material but describes profile tools as submission resources; KM removes the request-level access
312	prohibition. These examples illustrate changes to both requests and tool-provided information. The
313	construction skill and the three Full/A/M comparisons appear in Appendix B.
314	Execution interface and records. Harnesses manage model context and tool use through a com-
315	mon interface to each case’s MCP server and workspace, allowing model × harness configurations
316	to execute the same cases. For each run, the runner starts the case’s MCP service, supplies its end-

324	point to the harness, and invokes the evaluator after execution. The harness runs inside an isolated

327	that produced them.
328	Evaluation and annotation. Task evaluators check artifacts, state, and required actions for Com-
329	pletion, and action logs for Compliance. In the ACL task, producing acl_state.json alone is

339	5.1
340	EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
341	To make task-condition effects and component differences comparable, we evaluate the same tasks
342	and conditions across a crossed model–harness grid, using repeated runs to distinguish consistent
343	outcomes from isolated successes.
344	Models and harnesses.
345	We evaluate DS-Flash (deepseek-v4-flash-0731), DS-Pro
346	(deepseek-v4-pro-0813), GPT-Luna (gpt-5.6-luna), GPT-Sol (gpt-5.6-sol), and
347	GLM-5.3 (glm-5.3) with each of Codex, NanoBot, NullClaw, and OpenClaw, yielding 20 config-
348	urations. The DeepSeek and GPT pairs support within-family comparisons. We use a 300-second
349	timeout and three runs per task, condition, and configuration: 48 × 7 × 20 × 3 = 20,160 records, or
350	2,880 per condition.
351	Measurement and aggregation. Clarification requests receive no additional user reply; execution
352	metrics describe the resulting runs. Rates include timeouts; token means exclude zero or missing
353	totals. Token changes use a matched Full-run cost reference. Comparisons with Full match task,
354	model, and harness. Model and harness means equally weight their partner components; overall
355	means equally weight all 20 configurations. In the model and harness figures, Mean equally averages
356	the six underspecified conditions in K \ {Full}. Repeated-success comparisons use k = 3. We
357	compare component variation using the population SD of model or harness means. Runtime settings
358	and analysis details appear in Appendix C.
359	5.2
360	RQ1: EFFECTS OF TASK UNDERSPECIFICATION
361	To identify which parts of a task users should make explicit before execution, we distinguish failure
362	to complete, constraint violations, and additional cost. We first compare the three information do-
363	mains using Completion, Compliance, Success, and tokens, then compare missing and ambiguous
364	conditions within each domain.
365	Goal underspecification impedes completion, context underspecification increases cost, and
366	constraint underspecification weakens compliance. Using the observed outcomes in Table 2, we
367	compare the three information domains by averaging their ambiguous and missing forms. Goal
368	underspecification has the lowest Completion, 57.2 pp below Full. Most runs remain compliant,
369	but many do not complete the task, including those that pause to request information needed to
370	proceed. Context underspecification instead uses the most tokens, averaging 66.6k more than Full
371	without improving Success. Locating and comparing candidate data sources is one plausible source
372	of this overhead. Constraint underspecification largely preserves Completion (2.1 pp below Full) but
373	reduces Compliance by 73.0 pp. Further analyses compare all three domains within each execution
374	metric, combining outcome decompositions, token distributions, and recorded actions to explain the
375	execution patterns behind these aggregate contrasts (Appendix D.1).
376	Missingness reduces success more than ambiguity, but can raise completion or reduce token
377	use. Within each domain, the observed outcomes in Table 2 show lower Success under missingness

778	CONCLUSION AND DISCUSSION
779	AM-Bench shows that execution advantages under complete information need not persist un-
780	der underspecification.
781	Information gaps change execution outcomes and comparisons across
782	model × harness configurations, while estimated clarification gains address only part of these
783	deficits. These findings call for clearer task requirements, evaluation across information conditions,
784	and clarification support during execution; practical recommendations are detailed in Appendix G.
785	Users should prioritize constraints and goals, then provide inputs: state permitted operations
786	and data access first, since agents rarely seek clarification when constraints are unclear, then specify
787	the required result and identify the inputs needed to support completion and reduce search.
788	Model developers should compare models on the same tasks and harnesses across information
789	conditions: test Full, ambiguous, and missing conditions using Completion, Success, and repeat
790	consistency, because advantages in one condition or metric need not extend to others.
791	Harness developers should preserve requirements and support clarification before dependent
792	actions: keep requirements available when assembling model context, enable questions about spe-

36	Abstract
37	Agentic software-engineering and industrial systems increasingly
38	operate through executable workflows rather than code genera-
39	tion alone: they search artifacts, invoke tools, inspect structured
40	observations, and query databases. Training these agents requires
41	supervision data that captures valid tool interactions and executable
42	workflows. However, traditional query-first data synthesis can fail
43	because plausible user requests may not correspond to valid tool
44	sequences, compatible parameters, or available data. To address this
45	limitation, we propose SyntheticAgentTraceQA, an execution-
46	first framework for generating scalable supervision data for tool-
47	augmented agents. Our framework first constructs high-level work-
48	flow structures, maps them to available tools through dependency-
49	aware assignment, executes and validates the resulting traces in con-
50	trolled environments, and only then synthesizes natural-language
51	user tasks, teacher-generated reasoning annotations, and reference
52	answers. We evaluate the framework across four tool ecosystems
53	and use the resulting data to fine-tune and evaluate Qwen model
54	variants. The results show that execution-grounded supervision
55	improves tool execution behavior, reference-trace agreement, and
56	answer-generation performance on the evaluated tasks. Further
57	analysis reveals a supervision trade-off: masked supervision, which
58	excludes reasoning annotations from the training objective, im-
59	proves final-answer metrics, whereas full supervision, computing
60	loss over the complete assistant output including reasoning tokens,
61	underperforms on answer quality and does not consistently im-
62	prove reference-trace agreement, particularly at the 9B scale. These
63	findings highlight the importance of designing synthetic supervi-
64	sion according to the desired capabilities of tool-augmented agents.

67	bugging; • Computing methodologies →Natural language
