82	Introduction
83	Large language models (LLMs) have enabled a new generation of
84	autonomous agents capable of interpreting complex user requests
85	and interacting with external environments. A particularly effec-
86	tive paradigm is that of tool-augmented agents, which extend
87	the capabilities of LLMs by invoking external tools such as APIs,
88	data-analysis engines, search systems, and other specialized ser-
89	vices [27, 48]. By integrating these resources, LLM-based agents
90	move beyond next-token prediction toward dynamic, interactive
91	problem solving [33, 38].
92	Despite these advances, these agents can still fail in complex,
93	multi-step technical workflows. Common failure modes include
94	selecting inappropriate tools [21, 46], generating invalid tool ar-
95	guments (e.g., incorrect parameter names or data types), failing
96	to incorporate intermediate execution results into subsequent rea-
97	soning, and producing responses that are not fully supported by
98	the evidence gathered during execution [5, 21, 30]. These failures
99	become particularly consequential in software engineering tasks in-
100	volving artifact retrieval, programmatic tool execution, structured
101	data access, and the orchestration of multiple API calls, where cor-
102	rectness depends on accurate tool use and faithful reasoning over
103	intermediate observations [15, 21, 26, 43]. They also compound
104	broader usability and oversight challenges in deployed agent sys-
105	tems [29].
106	This paper focuses on a specific aspect of agent performance
107	rather than general coding ability. Specifically, we study whether
108	agents can construct and execute multi-step tool workflows whose
109	correctness can be objectively verified through tool outputs and
110	environment states. Across all tasks, the central capability under

540	Multi-Domain Extensions & Tool Sets
541	SyntheticAgentTraceQA is designed to be domain-agnostic: the
542	same execution-first pipeline operates across environments with
543	different schemas and tool sets without modifying the generation
544	process. We evaluate the framework on four domains spanning
545	enterprise analytics and an external benchmark (Table 1). Three
546	domains (finance, research portfolio, and supply chain) represent
547	structured enterprise workflows over financial assets, internal R&D
548	projects, and supply chain entities. The fourth domain is the ge-
549	nius_song_lyrics tool group from ToolBench, which provides an
550	external API-based environment for music search and metadata
551	retrieval with a distinct entity model and tool ecosystem derived
552	from the ToolBench benchmark [9, 24].
553	Shared operational abstraction. All domains share the operational
554	taxonomy introduced in Section 4.1. During profiling, each tool is
555	assigned to an operational class and its parameters are annotated
556	according to their functional roles. The resulting metadata are con-
557	sumed by the same template generation, instantiation, execution,
558	validation, and task-synthesis stages, independent of the underlying
559	application domain.
560	External benchmark integration. To evaluate portability beyond
561	our enterprise domains, we incorporated the genius_song_lyrics
562	tool group from ToolBench. Integration required only lightweight
563	interface wrappers that normalize entity identifiers and parameter
564	formats before profiling. No modifications were made to template
565	generation, trace instantiation, execution, or validation, demon-
566	strating that the framework transfers to external tool ecosystems
567	through interface adaptation alone.
568	6
569	Experiments
570	We investigate whether execution-grounded synthetic traces im-
571	prove tool-augmented agents under realistic settings involving
572	multi-domain tool use, execution feedback, and varying task diffi-
573	culty.
574	6.1
575	Hypotheses and Ablation Axes
576	Our experimental design is structured around four hypotheses:
577	• H1 (Data utility): Supervised fine-tuning on execution-
578	validated traces improves tool-use reliability, Reference-Trace
579	Agreement, and final-answer quality relative to the corre-
580	sponding base models.
581	• H2 (Reasoning initialization): At a fixed model size, Think-
582	ing base models outperform their No-Thinking counterparts
583	on execution-grounded reasoning tasks.
584	• H3 (Process vs. outcome supervision): For Thinking mod-
585	els, Masked supervision, which excludes <think> tokens
586	from the training loss, leads to different performance than
587	Full supervision, which computes the training loss over the
588	complete assistant output.
589	• H4 (Scale interaction): Model size interacts with execution-
590	grounded supervision, with larger models benefiting differ-
591	ently across evaluation metrics.
592	Our study considers the 4B and 9B variants of Qwen3.5. We first
593	benchmark the pretrained checkpoints with and without Think-
594	ing enabled. We then fine-tune the models using two supervision
595	strategies:
596	• Masked: Excludes tokens within <think> blocks from the
597	training loss while retaining supervision over executable
598	tool calls and final-answer tokens.
599	• Full: Computes the training loss over both the reasoning
600	trace and the final answer.
601	6.2
602	Dataset Construction and Splits
603	Generation protocol. Tool metadata (Profiler) were generated
604	using Claude Sonnet 4.6. Abstract templates were generated with
605	eight LLMs: Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Amazon Nova
606	Pro, Amazon Nova Lite, Qwen3-235B-A22B, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude
607	Opus 4.1, and GPT-5.5. For each domain, templates were generated
608	in batches of up to 30 instances (10 per difficulty level) with a
609	temperature of 0.7. Generating templates independently for each
610	domain reduces cross-domain contamination. The same LLM that
611	generates a template is subsequently used for trace validation and
612	task synthesis.
613	Grounded depth-first search (DFS) expanded 676 abstract tem-
614	plates (287 easy, 282 medium, and 107 hard) into 2,587 valid execu-
615	tion traces and 616 invalid traces, corresponding to a valid-trace
616	rate of 80.8%.
617	Task synthesis. Each validated trace is converted into three natural-
618	language tasks (Basic, Intermediate, and Challenging), yielding
619	7,761 samples evenly distributed across difficulty levels. To pre-
620	serve stylistic diversity, each task is generated by the same LLM
621	that produced its source template, while the use of multiple gen-
622	erators prevents any single model from dominating the linguistic
623	distribution. The annotator also generates a textual rationale de-
624	scribing how the recorded tool calls contribute to solving the task
625	and producing the reference answer.
626	Dataset splits. For computational efficiency, we fine-tune on a
627	subset of the generated corpus. The data are partitioned at the
628	execution-trace level using a fixed random seed and stratified by
629	trace complexity (easy, medium, and hard). All questions derived
630	from the same validated execution trace are assigned to the same
631	split, preventing data leakage. Because each execution trace gen-
632	erates one question at each difficulty level, stratifying by trace
633	complexity while keeping traces intact also preserves a balanced
634	distribution of question difficulties across the training, validation,
635	and test sets. All reported results are evaluated on the held-out test
636	set (𝑛= 200) and reported as mean ± standard error (SE) across
637	tasks.
638	6.3
639	Training Protocol
640	To assess the quality and usefulness of the generated synthetic
641	traces, we fine-tuned the target models on the training split of our
642	dataset and evaluated their performance on the held-out test set.

8	TRAINING INSTRUCTION FOLLOWING
9	Eran Goldstein∗
10	Yuval Belfer
11	Yonatan Belinkov
12	Daniel Gissin
13	AI21 Labs
14	ABSTRACT
15	Common instruction following (IF) benchmarks, such as IFEval, evaluate the abil-
16	ity of language models (LMs) to follow simple constraints that can easily be veri-
17	fied programmatically. These same constraints, in turn, are used as reward signals
18	for reinforcement learning. This design may lead to reward hacking of constraints,
19	pushing models away from the main task. Recent attempts to address this resulted
20	in benchmarks with richer constraints, but required expert labor, remained closed-
21	access, and cannot be easily extended. We present LIFT-Bench, an IF bench-
22	mark that asks a model to draft a document given a topic and a structured outline.
23	Constraints are scoped to certain document sections, providing finer control over
24	constraint density. LIFT-Bench includes both verifiable and judged constraints, as
25	well as a training counterpart, LIFT-Train. Importantly, LIFT-Bench provides both
26	main task and instruction-following constraints, mitigating shallow reward hack-
27	ing. On experiments with multiple models, we find that frontier models struggle
28	with the harder subsets of our benchmark and analyze model performance along
29	multiple axes. We also find that training on LIFT-Train is much less susceptible
30	to reward hacking than training on the common IFTrain. LIFT-Bench and LIFT-
31	Train are publicly available, as well as the data generating pipeline.
32	Code: https://github.com/AI21Labs/lift-bench
33	Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/ai21labs/LIFTBench
34	1
35	INTRODUCTION
36	Instruction following (IF) is the ability to satisfy explicit constraints on a response while still per-
37	forming the task for which the response is intended. It is typically measured by benchmarks that
38	programmatically check constraint satisfaction in the language model (LM) response (Zhou et al.,
39	2023; Pyatkin et al., 2025). Early work trained for IF with supervised fine-tuning (Wei et al., 2022;
40	Sanh et al., 2022; Mishra et al., 2022) or reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF;
41	Ouyang et al., 2022). More recent efforts train LMs to follow instructions by reusing the same
42	programmatic checkers as RL rewards (Pyatkin et al., 2025), a kind of reinforcement learning from
43	verifiable rewards (RLVR; Lambert et al., 2025).
44	We highlight four shortcomings of existing IF benchmarks. First, the specified constraints, and their
45	checkers, are independent of the main task, leading to potential reward hacking (Amodei et al.,
46	2016; Singhal et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026). Second, constraint diversity in dominant benchmarks
47	is low, largely consisting of lexical and formatting constraints (Zhou et al., 2023; Pyatkin et al.,
48	2025). Third, constraints in many benchmarks are written by humans (Zhou et al., 2023; Wen et al.,
49	2024; He et al., 2026), which limits size, reproducibility, and adaptation to new domains. In addition,
50	the richest sets are also eval-only or closed (Wen et al., 2024; He et al., 2026). Fourth, difficulty is
51	assessed by total constraint count, ignoring the spread or density of constraints along the response.
52	We introduce Localized Instruction-Following Tasks (LIFT-Bench), a benchmark of synthetic
53	document-drafting tasks that aims to mitigate these shortcomings. Each LIFT-Bench task provides
54	a topic and an outline—a nested tree of headers whose leaves hold paragraphs, code blocks, tables,
55	and lists—and attaches constraints to individual elements. Each constraint is scoped: it is evaluated
56	only against the element it is attached to, not against the whole document. This distinguishes “a para-
57	graph in French somewhere” from “section 2.1 in French”. Scoping allows us to define density, how
58	∗Corresponding author: erango@ai21.com
59	1
60	arXiv:2610.28819v1  [cs.CL]  20 Oct 2026
61	
62	============================================================
63	=== PAGE 2 ===
64	============================================================
65	
66	Preprint. Under review.
67	many constraints attach to each section. This structured design also renders evaluation more feasible
68	compared to verifying each constraint against the entire document, as in existing benchmarks.
69	Constraints in LIFT-Bench are either verifiable, using deterministic checkers, or judged, scored by
70	an LM judge against generated criteria; the latter cover the content a section must contain. Together
71	with scoping, this addresses the above shortcomings: judged content constraints put main-task ad-
72	herence inside the reward and extend the vocabulary past lexical and formatting checks; synthesis
73	removes the annotator ceiling on size and domain; and density becomes a generation parameter
74	rather than a property the benchmark cannot express.
75	LIFT-Bench contains 784 examples organized along 10 splits factored by document size, constraint
76	density, and scoping. We also release LIFT-Train, a corresponding dataset for IF training, consisting
77	of 34,258 examples. We evaluated a range of frontier and open models on LIFT-Bench, reveal-
78	ing that models are distinguished by how sharply their scores degrade with increasing density of
79	constraints. The globally-scoped constraints used by current IF benchmark is the hardest regime
80	of all, despite carrying an order of magnitude fewer constraints. On the training side, training on
81	LIFT-Train leads to large improvements on LIFT-Bench, as expected, while training on the common
82	IFTrain (Pyatkin et al., 2025) barely improves on our benchmark and often leads to reward hacking.
83	At the same time, training on LIFT-Train does not degrade on a more challenging out-of-distribution
84	benchmark, AdvancedIF (He et al., 2026), unlike IFTrain.
85	To summarize, our contributions are:
86	• LIFT-Bench: a synthetic IF benchmark of document-drafting tasks with scoped constraints,
87	combining verifiable and judged scoring in a single weighted metric.
88	• LIFT-Train: the training-side release, which is more robust to reward hacking found when
89	training on lexical-only IF rewards.
90	• An open-source pipeline for synthesizing drafting tasks in verifiers-compatible format
91	(PrimeIntellect, 2025), ready for IF-RLVR training and evaluation.
92	• Analyses that our factored design makes possible: analyses of failures by per-section density
93	and scoping, which require scoped constraints, alongside constraint load, type, and scoring
94	mechanism.

278	SYNTHESIS PIPELINE
279	Figure 2: Synthesis pipeline overview.
280	The pipeline is a sequence of atomic stages, outlined in Fig. 2:2
281	1. Topic seeding: sample seed topics from Wikipedia.
282	2. Outline construction: (a) outline templating, where we generate structural document skeletons.;
283	and (b) outline expansion, where an LM fills each skeleton into a concrete, topic-specific outline.
284	3. Constraint generation: parallel per-type generators propose candidate constraints over the out-
285	line, one block per constraint type, covering both mechanisms.
286	4. Task configuration
287	2Appendix A gives the full description, including prompts, models, and parameters for each released split.

295	(a) Constraint sampling: draw the task’s constraints from the candidate pool, with knobs for
296	setting how many constraints each section carries, how many sections carry constraints at
297	all, and which constraint types appear.
298	(b) Reward shaping: set the structure/content budget split for the task.
299	5. Task Scoping: render the task as a prompt (Fig. 1). Scoping can be structured, the outline with
300	its per-header constraints, or flat, an IFEval-style prompt in which the same constraints are stated
301	as applying to the entire output. The flat form allows us to compare scoped and globally-scoped
302	prompting directly, holding topic, outline, and constraint content fixed (§4).
303	3.4
304	THE RELEASED SPLITS
305	Ten splits come from three generation runs: short outlines, long outlines, and flat (no outline).
306	Within each run, every split shares the same topics and outlines; only the number of constraints
307	attached to them changes. Appendix D provides descriptive statistics.
308	Splits are comparable only if they share the same scoping (flat or structured). A flat split labelled
309	many carries far fewer constraints in absolute terms than a structured split with the same label,
310	because a flat task has no sections across which to distribute them—every constraint lands in a
311	single scope. The ten splits are therefore not a monotonic difficulty scale.

816	CONCLUSION
817	Instruction-following is measured by checking constraints and trained by rewarding the same
818	checks, and both halves of that arrangement are blind to whether the requested task was performed.
819	LIFT-Bench closes the blindspot by scoping constraints to individual sections and scoring content
820	requirements alongside formatting ones, which makes constraint density a controlled variable and
821	main-task adherence part of the reward rather than an assumption about it. Our experiments with
822	various closed frontier models and leading open models demonstrate that LIFT-Bench is a useful
823	benchmark for evaluating instruction following. Its modular composition exposes weaknesses of
824	different models along constraint density, mechanism, and type. In addition, the released training
825	counterpart, LIFT-Train, is less susceptible to reward hacking than the common IFTrain, thanks to
826	the content-adhering part of its reward.
827	There are a few possible extensions for LIFT-Bench to pursue. A finetuned rubric judge and a learned
828	rubric generator, in the style of AdvancedIF’s verifier (He et al., 2026), would harden the scoring
829	stage that the benchmark and the reward both rely on, and can be easily added to the pipeline. The
830	task distribution can grow along further axes: richer constraint compositions, adding the conditional
831	and chained dependencies of ComplexBench (Wen et al., 2024) to our conjunctive ones, and multi-
832	turn splits, where an editorial follow-up tests ongoing edits rather than drafting alone.
833	LIFT-Bench, LIFT-Train and the synthesis pipeline are available at https://github.com/
834	AI21Labs/lift-bench, and the datasets at https://huggingface.co/datasets/
835	ai21labs/LIFTBench.

6	Evaluating Implicit Regulatory Compliance in LLM Tool Invocation via
7	Logic-Guided Synthesis
8	Da Song1,2, Yuheng Huang3*, Boqi Chen4, Tianshuo Cong1,2,
9	Randy Goebel5, Lei Ma3,5, Foutse Khomh6
10	Abstract
11	The integration of large language models
12	(LLMs) into autonomous agents has enabled
13	complex tool use, yet in high-stakes domains,
14	these systems must strictly adhere to regulatory
15	standards beyond simple functional correctness.
16	However, existing benchmarks often overlook
17	implicit regulatory compliance, thus failing to
18	evaluate whether LLMs can autonomously en-
19	force mandatory safety constraints. To fill this
20	gap, we introduce LOGISAFETYGEN, a frame-
21	work that converts unstructured regulations into
22	Linear Temporal Logic oracles and employs
23	logic-guided fuzzing to synthesize valid, safety-
24	critical traces. Building on this framework, we
25	construct LOGISAFETYBENCH, a benchmark
26	comprising 240 human-verified tasks that re-
27	quire LLMs to generate Python programs that
28	satisfy both functional objectives and latent
29	compliance rules. Evaluations of 13 state-of-
30	the-art (SOTA) LLMs reveal that larger mod-
31	els, despite achieving better functional correct-
32	ness, frequently prioritize task completion over
33	safety, which results in non-compliant behav-
34	ior.
35	1
36	Introduction
37	Recent advances in large language models (LLMs)
38	have enabled the emergence of LLM-based agents
39	that can interpret complex user instructions, invoke
40	* Corresponding Author
41	1School of Cryptologic Science and Engineering, Shandong
42	University, Jinan, Shandong, China
43	2Shandong Key Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence Security,
44	Shandong University, Jinan, Shandong, China
45	3The University of Tokyo, Tokyo, Japan
46	4McGill University, Montreal, Canada
47	5University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB, Canada
48	6Polytechnique Montreal, Montreal, Canada
49	Emails:
50	{song_da,
51	tianshuo.cong}@sdu.edu.cn,
52	yuhenghuang42@g.ecc.u-tokyo.ac.jp,
53	boqi.chen@mail.mcgill.ca,
54	rgoebel@ualberta.ca,
55	ma.lei@acm.org, foutse.khomh@polymtl.ca
56	external tools, and interact with the physical or dig-
57	ital world to achieve multi-step goals (Qin et al.,
58	2024). While this capability extends far beyond
59	that of traditional chatbots, it also introduces sub-
60	stantially higher safety and regulatory risks. In
61	high-stakes domains such as financial services, le-
62	gal reasoning, healthcare, and smart home control,
63	functional task completion alone is insufficient;
64	LLMs must consistently satisfy safety and regu-
65	latory constraints throughout the entire decision-
66	making and execution process. Violations may
67	result in severe consequences (Ye et al., 2024; Ra-
68	dosevich and Halloran, 2025), including physical
69	harm and regulatory non-compliance.
70	To mitigate such risks, systematic evaluation
71	and pre-deployment testing are essential for under-
72	standing an LLM’s capability boundaries and for
73	building trust among developers, regulators, and
74	end-users. In particular, evaluation must jointly as-
75	sess whether an LLM can (1) achieve the intended
76	functional goal and also (2) adhere to mandatory
77	safety constraints under realistic interaction sce-
78	narios. However, existing evaluation practices fall
79	short of this requirement.
80	On the one hand, current benchmarks largely
81	rely on static test sets derived from manual cura-
82	tion or web scraping. These datasets are expen-
83	sive to scale (Zhang et al., 2024a), difficult to vali-
84	date (Huang et al., 2025), and prone to data satura-
85	tion (Chen et al., 2025a). More critically, they pri-
86	marily evaluate functional correctness, while treat-
87	ing safety or regulatory compliance as secondary
88	or implicit. On the other hand, real-world safety
89	constraints are often specified in lengthy natural
90	language policy documents, such as regulatory acts
91	(e.g., EU AI Act (EU, 2024)) or internal compli-
92	ance manuals, making it prohibitively costly to
93	involve domain experts in mapping relevant rules
94	to possible user instructions or execution traces.
95	To address these limitations, we propose LO-
96	GISAFETYGEN, an automated framework for syn-
97	1
98	arXiv:2601.08196v1  [cs.CL]  13 Jan 2026
99	
100	============================================================
101	=== PAGE 2 ===
102	============================================================
103	
104	thesizing high-quality test cases for safety-critical
105	LLMs. LOGISAFETYGEN takes tool specifications
106	and regulation documents as input and automati-
107	cally generates test scenarios with explicit, verifi-
108	able safety constraints. The framework consists of
109	three stages. (1) Automated Oracle Construction,
110	which translates unstructured policy documents
111	into deterministic Linear Temporal Logic (LTL)
112	over finite traces, establishing a formal “gold stan-
113	dard” for compliance. (2) Logic-Guided Trace Gen-
114	eration, which leverages a fuzzing engine to syn-
115	thesize executable ground-truth traces that are com-
116	pliant with both tool semantics and temporal safety
117	constraints by construction. (3) Safety Masking,
118	which converts these traces into natural language
119	instructions that omit mandatory safety steps, forc-
120	ing LLMs to infer implicit constraints from context
121	that closely reflect real-world user interactions.
122	We instantiate LOGISAFETYGEN in three repre-
123	sentative high-stakes domains—Financial Services,
124	Tele-Healthcare, and Smart Home IoT—and con-
125	struct LOGISAFETYBENCH, a benchmark of 240
126	manually verified test cases. Each requires LLMs
127	to interleave task-oriented reasoning with manda-
128	tory safety operations under temporal constraints.
129	Our contributions are summarized as follows:
130	• We introduce LOGISAFETYGEN, an automated
131	benchmark generation framework that integrates
132	LTL-based formal verification with logic-guided
133	fuzzing to produce safety-critical test cases.
134	• We propose a Dual-Oracle Evaluation protocol
135	that jointly verifies functional correctness and
136	strict temporal safety compliance, thus enabling
137	precise measurement of the Inference Gap be-
138	tween task success and rule adherence.
139	• We release LOGISAFETYBENCH, a challenging,
140	human-verified benchmark spanning three high-
141	stakes domains, which require LLMs to satisfy
142	implicit regulatory constraints during execution.
143	• We conduct a systematic evaluation of SOTA
144	LLMs, showing that although scaling improves
145	general reasoning ability, it does not resolve fail-
146	ures in implicit regulatory compliance.
147	2
148	Related Work
149	Trustworthiness Evaluation of LLM. A grow-
150	ing body of work aims to provide benchmarks
151	on the safety, security, and regulatory compliance
152	of LLM-based systems, which is crucial for their
153	trustworthy deployment in real-world (Moham-
154	madi et al., 2025). Early work, such as Agen-
155	tHarm (Andriushchenko et al., 2025; Mazeika et al.,
156	2024), analyzes LLM behavior under malicious
157	user requests. While important, these scenarios
158	differ from evaluating rule adherence under be-
159	nign conditions and mainly focus on question-
160	answering tasks.
161	More recent frameworks, in-
162	cluding ToolEmu (Ruan et al., 2024), Agent-
163	SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2024b), and Agent-
164	Bench (Liu et al., 2024), examine general tool-use
165	safety beyond simple QA. However, in these set-
166	tings, safety largely means correct tool manipula-
167	tion rather than interpreting regulations in text and
168	following specific rules.
169	In a related but distinct direction, researchers be-
170	gin to anchor evaluation in explicit regulatory con-
171	texts. EU-Agent-Bench (Lichkovski et al., 2025)
172	and HSE-Bench (Wang et al., 2025a) introduce
173	evaluation scenarios derived from concrete policies
174	and standards, while RuleArena (Zhou et al., 2025)
175	and CNFinBench (Ding et al., 2025) move closer
176	to structured rule reasoning by embedding real-
177	world regulations into their tasks. These bench-
178	marks test agents’ ability to interpret and reason
179	about regulatory constraints expressed in natural
180	language, but they do not require LLMs to generate
181	executable tool-call scripts that satisfy formal com-
182	pliance rules, which can be essential in real-world
183	LLM-based agent deployment.
184	Benchmark Construction Methods. One ma-
185	jor approach to benchmark construction is to col-
186	lect high-quality data with human effort.
187	Hu-
188	manEval (Chen et al., 2021) is one of the classic ex-
189	amples in this category. Some benchmarks also ex-
190	pand their coverage by using web crawlers and then
191	applying manual annotation. In tool-use evaluation,
192	BFCL (Patil et al., 2025) is a representative exam-
193	ple that relies on crawling large-scale repositories.
194	However, since manual benchmarks are both costly
195	and potentially contaminated (Zhu et al., 2024),
196	researchers have explored LLM-in-the-loop bench-
197	mark generation as a more scalable alternative.
198	In these approaches, models help synthesize test
199	instances automatically (Ghazaryan et al., 2025).
200	Notable examples include AutoCodeBench (Chou
201	et al., 2025), which generates code-centric tasks,
202	and MCPBench (Wang et al., 2025c), which pro-
203	duces tool-use test cases with LLM assistance. Al-
204	though these methods reduce annotation effort and
205	broaden evaluation scope, the stochastic nature of
206	LLM generation makes it hard to guarantee strict

393	Automated Safety Oracle Construction
394	Establishing a gold standard for compliance from
395	massive, unstructured regulatory texts is non-trivial.
396	Unlike robotics approaches restricted to closed vo-

407	Rule Extraction. We first leverage LLMs to distill
408	regulations into atomic constraints, applying Scope
409	Alignment and Constraint Deduplication to retain
410	only relevant policies. Furthermore, rather than al-
411	lowing unconstrained free-form logical translation
412	with LLMs, we restrict all extracted constraints
413	to two LTL templates that capture the dominant
414	forms of compliance logic in business, as observed
415	in prior work (Chen et al., 2025b). Specifically,
416	we adopt a dual-template formulation comprising:

418	tive action P2 until a check P1 holds, formalized

420	quires that a trigger P1 implies a future outcome

438	Logic-Guided Trace Generation
439	With the formal Safety Oracles (Φ) established, our
440	next goal is to synthesize concrete execution traces
441	(τ). These ordered tool invocation sequences serve
442	as the ground-truth solutions for our benchmark,
443	providing the “gold standard” behavior for how an
444	ideal LLM can interleave functional reasoning with
445	mandatory safety checks to satisfy the constraints

448	on direct LLM prompting is insufficient, as proba-

450	cutability, and frequently hallucinate inappropriate
451	parameters or violate temporal dependencies.
452	To bridge this gap, we adopt Fuzzing (Zhu et al.,
453	2022), a dynamic testing paradigm that discovers
454	valid execution paths by systematically exploring
455	the state space under strict constraints. Unlike stan-
456	dard text generation, our fuzzer treats trace con-
457	struction as a bounded search problem: it itera-
458	tively proposes candidate actions and rejects any
459	that fail to meet formal specifications. We imple-
460	ment a safety-constrained fuzzer (with ≈3600 lines
461	of code) that constructs traces τ = [a1, a2, ..., ak]
462	incrementally. The core of the fuzzer is a Dual-
463	Constraint Pruning Mechanism. At each step t,
464	given the current environment state St, the fuzzer
465	samples a potential action at+1 and validates it
466	against two strict boundaries.
467	Precondition Satisfaction (Vschema): The action
468	must be executable in the current state St. This
469	ensures that the trace is functionally sound.
470	Safety Satisfaction (Vsafe): The updated trace τt+1
471	must satisfy the LTL Safety Oracles. We verify
472	this using a runtime LTL monitor: Vsafe(τt+1) =
473	True ⇐⇒∀ϕ ∈Φ, τt+1 |= ϕ.
474	To operationalize these checks efficiently, we
475	employ a Bottom-Up Depth-First Search strategy
476	Traditional top-down planning requires pre-solving
477	constraints for the entire API call graph, but with
478	complex LTL rules, this becomes computationally
479	intractable. In contrast, our bottom-up approach
480	enables Lazy Evaluation. We compute the valid
481	search space and check compliance only for the
482	immediate next step (St →St+1). If a candidate
483	action violates either the schema or the safety con-
484	straint, the branch is immediately pruned.
485	When the fuzzer attempts a business action that
486	violates a safety constraint (LTL), the LTL mon-
487	itor triggers a violation (Vsafe = False), pruning
488	that path. The search is then forced to backtrack
489	and explore alternative branches until it selects the
490	mandatory safety operation. By iterating this pro-
491	cess until the target trace length is reached, the
492	fuzzer produces a ground truth trace τ ∗where ev-
493	ery user action is wrapped in the necessary safety
494	checks, guaranteeing that the test case is solvable,
495	executable, and strictly compliant by construction.

667	We instantiate LOGISAFETYGEN across three high-

671	anchored in authoritative international regulations:
672	Financial Services. Based on the European Union
673	Payment Services Directive 2 (EU, 2015), this do-
674	main tests whether an LLM can enforce safety con-
675	straints during online banking services.
676	Tele-Healthcare. Based on the USA HIPAA Secu-
677	rity Rule (HHS, 1996), a widely accepted standard
678	for protecting health information, LLMs must com-
679	ply with safety constraints while handling patients’
680	sensitive records.
681	Smart Home IoT. Based on the European Telecom-
682	munications Standards Institute EN 303 645 stan-
683	dard (ETSI, 2024), a leading international policy
684	for consumer IoT security, it tests LLMs’ ability to
685	reason about physical safety risks like door locks.

693	test cases derived from it.

702	high consistency confirms that our Automated Or-
703	acle Construction pipeline can effectively distill

ToolPrivacyBench: Benchmarking Purpose-Bound Privacy in Tool-Using LLM Agents⋆
Shijing Hua, Liang Liub, Zhu Menga,∗, Zhicheng Zhaoa,∗
aBeijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing, 100876, China
bBeijing Academy of Blockchain and Edge Computing, Beijing, 100085, China
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) have increasingly moved from standalone text generation systems to agents that invoke external
tools, access environments, and execute multi-step tasks. However, conventional function-calling benchmarks mainly evaluate task
completion and API correctness, while privacy evaluation benchmarks typically focus on final responses or privacy judgments.
Neither perspective captures purpose-bound information flow across an executed multi-tool trajectory. Motivated by this limi-
tation in current agent evaluation, ToolPrivacyBench audits whether task-private atoms are routed only to authorized tools and
downstream sinks, thereby evaluating both task completion and privacy over-disclosure during tool use. The benchmark contains
2,150 cases, including 1,150 fully synthetic privacy-sensitive business workflows and 1,000 cases adapted from existing multi-tool
and function-calling benchmarks. Each case is represented by a policy knowledge base. After an agent executes against mock
business backends, the evaluator compares recorded tool arguments and backend audit logs with this policy knowledge base. The
evaluation covers nine widely used agents to characterize purpose-bound privacy over-disclosure. The results show that successful
tool execution does not imply appropriate privacy disclosure: an agent may complete a task while transmitting unnecessary private
information through intermediate tool calls. ToolPrivacyBench therefore formalizes a need-to-know disclosure boundary, under
which each tool should receive only the information necessary for its stated purpose, and uses trajectory-level auditing to identify
privacy over-disclosure in multi-tool workflows.
Keywords: tool-using LLM agents, purpose-bound privacy, policy knowledge base, knowledge-based auditing, benchmark
1. Introduction
As large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used
to call external tools and execute multi-step tasks, their task-
execution capability has become a central evaluation target. Ex-
isting agent benchmarks provide an important basis for measur-
ing tool use and task completion across multi-turn, interactive,
and executable settings [1–3]. Beyond task completion, how-
ever, it is also necessary to evaluate how agents handle and dis-
close private information during execution.
Privacy evaluation for LLMs provides a starting point, but
existing work mainly studies memorization, training-data ex-
traction, contextual privacy judgment, and privacy disclosure in
generated text [4, 5]. It provides limited systematic evidence
about how LLM agents handle and transmit private informa-
tion during tool invocation. In a multi-tool workflow, a private
field may be necessary for one tool but should not be passed
to another. It is therefore necessary to evaluate whether agents
respect need-to-know disclosure boundaries during tool use.
To fill this evaluation gap, ToolPrivacyBench is introduced
as a purpose-bound privacy auditing benchmark for multi-tool

Future Blockchain and Privacy Computing (GJJ-25-009).

workflows. The benchmark asks a central question: when com-
pleting a task, does an LLM agent transmit private infor-
mation only to the tools that actually need it? Unlike simply
removing all sensitive information, purpose-bound privacy re-
quires the evaluator to determine whether each private field is
necessary at the current workflow stage and to compare that
judgment with the tool arguments actually received by backend
systems. ToolPrivacyBench therefore models privacy disclo-
sure as a knowledge-based auditing problem. It records private
atoms, tool purposes, sink types, allowed and forbidden field-
tool relations, free-text slots, and backend audit evidence in an
explicit policy knowledge base.
Evaluating purpose-bound privacy risk in multi-tool agents
requires more than a small set of isolated tasks or a single ap-
plication domain. LLM agents are being used across business
processes such as healthcare, finance, insurance, tax, recruiting,
education, IT operations, and software security, where private
information types, tool purposes, and sink boundaries differ.
ToolPrivacyBench therefore constructs 2,150 multi-tool cases
across these domains. The benchmark includes 1,150 fully syn-
thetic privacy-sensitive business workflows and 1,000 public-
derived cases adapted from existing multi-tool and function-
calling benchmarks. This design covers high-risk privacy sce-
narios while retaining workflow structures from realistic tool-
use tasks, so the evaluation is not restricted to a single task
family or privacy-field type.
Moreover, a multi-domain task collection alone is insufficient

SiLR: Structure-Preserving Admission and Process Reward for LLM Tool Agents
Chenyu Zhou1∗, Qiliang Jiang2∗, Shuning Wu3, Xu Zhou3
1School of Engineering, Institute of Science Tokyo, Japan
2College of Control Science and Engineering, Zhejiang University, China
3Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, National University of Singapore, Singapore
zhou.c.76d6@m.isct.ac.jp, zhouxu_nus@u.nus.edu
Abstract
A runtime gate for an LLM tool agent is usually cast as a filter.
In a ReAct loop, however, a rejected proposal is followed by
another at the same state: the gate is a search operator over
the proposal stream, and its admission criterion shapes which
trajectories are reachable. We study post-violation recovery
admission, where progress must be admitted while the system
is still in violation, and identify the scalar projection trap: an
aggregate-score gate can accept a locally improving proposal
and commit the trajectory to a residual plateau. SiLR instead
shadow-executes each proposal and admits it under a product
order over the branch-level violation state (overloaded-branch
support and per-branch severity). We prove that no scalar
surrogate is sound for this order, so the failure is a represen-
tational impossibility rather than a matter of threshold tun-
ing. On mined Gym-ANM scenarios, SiLR recovers 21/21
multi-action episodes, against 0/21 for terminal admission
and 9/21 for the best scalar gate, an advantage significant
across the full 24-scenario benchmark. The terminal-versus-
structured dichotomy holds across three model families and
in CityLearn. Because admission rests on deterministic simu-
lation, the LLM lies outside the trust boundary and admission
authority resides in the verifier: a magnitude-redistribution
attack that defeats both scalar and support-only baselines is
contained only by the full per-branch predicate. With two con-
straint families active, every tested scalar projection admits
physically unsafe actions, and the support-only gate admits
the largest fraction (63.2% of 42,410 unsafe actions; product
order 0). In the hardest dual-family traces, scalar gates recover
only through that unsafe class. Reused as a GRPO process re-
ward, the same signal outperforms its count projection in every
mined scenario and is the only tested reward under which the
ungated policy exceeds the untrained base (0.844 vs. 0.778).
Scalar projection loses the violation geometry at both design
points; only the full product order is structurally sufficient.
Introduction
Critical-infrastructure operations—power dispatch, datacen-
ter scheduling, financial settlement—increasingly rely on
tool-using large language model (LLM) agents (Zhang
2025). Recent runtime-enforcement systems (SARC (Be-
sanson 2026), AgentSpec (Wang, Poskitt, and Sun 2026),
GuardAgent (Xiang et al. 2025), ShieldAgent (Chen, Kang,
and Li 2025), VeriGuard (Miculicich et al. 2025)) advance
∗These authors contributed equally.
the runtime governance of these agents. They share an im-
plicit premise: the system starts inside the safe set, and the
gate’s job is to keep it there. Infrastructure under autonomous
control, however, will sometimes start outside it, already in
violation and needing several actions to recover. The enforce-
ment question then inverts: the gate must decide whether an
action that still leaves the system unsafe nonetheless makes
admissible progress toward recovery. This post-violation re-
covery admission problem differs structurally from runtime
prevention, and prior runtime governance for LLM tool
agents does not address it. Runtime mediation intercepts un-
safe actions, yet it rarely enables recovery after blocking an
unsafe proposal (Sah et al. 2026): enforcement is not recov-
ery.
We frame the problem around admission semantics: the
formal criterion by which a runtime gate decides to apply
or reject an LLM-proposed action. Our thesis is that this
choice—not the gate’s strictness—has first-order effects on
whether multi-step recovery is possible. A terminal gate (ad-
mit only fully-recovered post-states) is safe but admits no
intermediate step, deadlocking every multi-action episode
on our mined Gym-ANM (Henry and Ernst 2021) bench-
mark. The natural relaxation is a scalar admission gate, ad-
mitting any proposal whose aggregate violation penalty is
non-increasing within a small slack. It is representationally
insufficient: relaxing the slack does not close the recovery
gap.
The reason is the scalar projection trap, an admission-
level instance of proxy gaming (Skalse et al. 2022; Krakovna
et al. 2020). In a ReAct loop (Yao et al. 2023) a rejected
proposal is followed by another at the same state, so the
gate is not a filter but a search operator over the agent’s
proposal stream. Admitting on an aggregate score collapses
the multi-component violation geometry and can commit
the trajectory to a residual plateau. A gate that preserves
the per-branch geometry instead rejects a scalar-improving
proposal that violates the product order and keeps the search
alive. The gap is representational, which we make precise
as an impossibility result and confirm empirically: 21/21
structured vs. 9/21 best scalar and 0/21 terminal, significant
across the full 24-scenario benchmark.
Contributions.
Our unifying claim concerns one object: a
product order over the branch-level violation state. It is the

PeakBench: Benchmarking Resource-Aware
Tool Invocation in LLM Agents
Zhi-Kai Chen1,2, Xu-Xiang Zhong1,2, Song-Yan Li3, De-Chuan Zhan1,2, Han-Jia Ye1,2∗
1School of Artificial Intelligence, Nanjing University, China
2National Key Laboratory for Novel Software Technology, Nanjing University, China
3Nanjing University, China
Abstract
LLM agents increasingly solve tasks by invoking multiple
tools, where parallel execution is essential for low latency but
difficult to manage safely. Existing agent benchmarks primar-
ily evaluate tool selection, argument generation, and end-to-
end success under mostly serial execution, largely overlook-
ing valid parallelization and resource-constrained scheduling.
This missing scheduling dimension creates a practical fail-
ure mode: serial execution is safe but slow, while resource-
agnostic parallel execution is fast but prone to avoidable re-
source overflows. To address this gap, we introduce Peak-
Bench, a benchmark of executable multi-tool workflows with
execution-grounded dependency annotations and measured
resource profiles. A central challenge in evaluating such work-
flows is attribution: failures and inefficiencies may arise from
incorrect dependency planning, poor resource-constrained
scheduling, or both. PeakBench addresses this challenge with
a two-part evaluation framework that disentangles logical
planning from physical scheduling, with dedicated metrics for
each dimension. Using this framework, we show that strong
logical planning does not reliably translate into safe or efficient
execution under resource constraints. We further show that ex-
posing resource information can reduce avoidable overflows
and improve resource utilization, making PeakBench a useful
testbed for diagnosing resource-aware agent behavior. Code is
available at https://github.com/Czzzk/Staggering-the-Peaks.
Introduction
Large Language Models (LLMs) have undergone a paradigm
shift, transitioning from passive conversationalists to au-
tonomous “task-solvers” capable of interacting with the phys-
ical and digital worlds (Wang et al. 2024; Park et al. 2023;
Xi et al. 2025). At the heart of this evolution lies the mecha-
nism of tool invocation, which enables agents to extend their
reasoning capabilities through external APIs, databases, and
computational engines. (Schick et al. 2023; Patil et al. 2024;
Yao et al. 2022) As agents are increasingly deployed in com-
plex, real-world workflows—ranging from automated soft-
ware engineering (Jimenez et al. 2024) to open-ended em-
bodied or environment-interactive tasks (Wang et al. 2023)—
the ability to interact with tools has become the definitive
characteristic of “agentic” intelligence.
As task complexity escalates, modern agentic workflows
demand concurrent execution to overcome the latency bot-
tlenecks of sequential (step-by-step) models (Wei et al. 2022;

Ning et al. 2023). Safe concurrency first requires understand-
ing step-level prerequisite and concurrency relations: which
tool calls must wait for prior outputs, and which calls can run
independently (Besta et al. 2024; Liu et al. 2023). Current
agents may hallucinate false dependencies (needlessly serial-
izing tasks and degrading throughput) or miss critical prereq-
uisites (leading to execution-blocking errors) (Valmeekam
et al. 2023, 2022). Yet these logical relations only define
what may run in parallel; they do not determine whether
those parallel calls can safely share finite infrastructure.
Furthermore, even when agents identify or are given valid
dependency and concurrency structure, a critical systemic
vulnerability emerges. Current frameworks conflate “logi-
cal independence” with “execution readiness.” Because they
are fundamentally resource-agnostic, they operate under the
naive assumption of infinite infrastructure capacity (Kwon
et al. 2023; Yu et al. 2022; Aminabadi et al. 2022; Mei
et al. 2024). Once independent tasks are identified, agents
greedily dispatch all parallelizable tool invocations simulta-
neously without any physical scheduling awareness. As de-
picted in Figure 1, this unmanaged translation from logical
parallelism to physical execution triggers massive “Resource
Bursts.” Heavy, resource-intensive tools compete for finite
hardware, leading to sharp spikes in infrastructure strain (Li

8	6:ATLAS: Constraints-Aware Multi-Agent
9	7:Collaboration for Real-World Travel Planning
10	8:Jihye Choi1 2 *, Jinsung Yoon1, Jiefeng Chen1, Somesh Jha2 and Tomas Pfister1
11	9:1Google Cloud, 2University of Wisconsin-Madison
12	10:While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable advancements in reasoning and tool use,
13	11:they often fail to generate optimal, grounded solutions under complex constraints. Real-world travel
14	12:planning exemplifies these challenges, evaluating agents’ abilities to handle constraints that are explicit,
15	13:implicit, and even evolving based on interactions with dynamic environments and user needs. In this
16	14:paper, we present ATLAS, a general multi-agent framework designed to effectively handle such complex
17	15:nature of constraints awareness in real-world travel planning tasks. ATLAS introduces a principled
18	16:approach to address the fundamental challenges of constraint-aware planning through dedicated
19	17:mechanisms for dynamic constraint management, iterative plan critique, and adaptive interleaved
20	18:search. ATLAS demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on the TravelPlanner benchmark, improving
21	19:the final pass rate from 23.3% to 44.4% over its best alternative. More importantly, our work is the
22	20:first to demonstrate quantitative effectiveness on real-world travel planning tasks with live information
23	21:search and multi-turn feedback. In this realistic setting, ATLAS showcases its superior overall planning
24	22:performance, achieving an 84% final pass rate which significantly outperforms baselines including ReAct
25	23:(59%) and a monolithic agent (27%).
26	24:1. Introduction
27	25:Constraint awareness and compliance is a fundamental aspect of intelligence, crucial for reasoning
28	26:and problem-solving (Dechter, 2003; Holyoak and Simon, 1999). Solving real-world problems under
29	27:constraints requires a delicate interplay of understanding requirements, searching for information,
30	28:and synthesizing a solution that respects all rules. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have
31	29:made rapid advancements in reasoning and tool use (Nakano et al., 2021; Schick et al., 2023),
32	30:their reliability is still limited in practical tasks with complex, multifaceted constraints. Despite
33	31:their capabilities, they often produce plans that are incoherent or invalid, a critical shortcoming for
34	32:real-world deployment (Kambhampati et al., 2024; Valmeekam et al., 2023).
35	33:Existing research often sidesteps the core challenge. Some methods focus on constraint compliance
36	34:but assume all necessary information is provided upfront (Lee et al., 2025; Parmar et al., 2025),

80	--ABSTRACT--
81	15:Abstract
82	16:While large language models (LLMs) can generate multi-step plans, they frequently
83	17:produce steps that violate high-level intent or domain constraints. We introduce
84	18:Constraints-of-Thought (Const-o-T), a structured intermediate representation that
85	19:converts each reasoning step into an 〈intent, constraint〉pair, where the constraint
86	20:is an executable predicate evaluated by a domain validator. These constraints
87	21:restrict the feasible action space at each state and transform free-form reasoning
88	22:traces into controllers that actively shape search. The primary contribution of this
89	23:work is the executable intent–constraint representation, which converts reasoning
90	24:steps into constraints that directly restrict the planner’s feasible action space. We
91	25:demonstrate the utility of this representation by integrating it with Monte Carlo
92	26:Tree Search (MCTS), where extracted constraints restrict the planner’s admissible
93	27:actions during search. This yields both improved task accuracy and reduced search
94	28:complexity, reflected in lower branching factors and faster convergence. Across
95	29:four domains representing distinct reasoning settings including planning, code
96	30:synthesis, symbolic reasoning, and scientific knowledge, Const-o-T consistently
97	31:outperforms prompting-only and search-based baselines. Each reasoning step
98	32:produces an executable constraint κt that induces a restricted action set Aκt(s) ⊆
99	33:A(s), which is enforced prior to node expansion during search.The key intellectual
100	34:contribution is demonstrating that executable intent–constraint representations can
101	35:serve as a general, domain-agnostic prior that converts language model reasoning
102	36:from descriptive rationales into verifiable search controllers.
103	37:1
104	38:Introduction
105	39:Large language models (LLMs) can generate multi-step reasoning traces, but these traces often violate
106	40:domain constraints and fail to align with user intent. While approaches such as Chain-of-Thought
107	41:(CoT) reasoning [1] appear to “think through” the space of possible plans, they produce free-form
108	42:reasoning without an executable mechanism to enforce feasibility during planning. As a result,
109	43:generated actions frequently violate domain constraints or logical consistency across a range of tasks,
110	44:including combinatorial planning (e.g., strategy games and program synthesis [2, 3, 4]) and symbolic
111	45:reasoning (e.g., arithmetic [5]). Prior work typically uses reasoning traces as guidance or post-hoc
112	46:verification, but does not modify the planner’s feasible action space, leading to exploration of invalid
113	47:or misaligned actions during search [6].
114	48:We propose Constraints-of-Thought (Const-o-T), a framework that converts reasoning steps into
115	--INTRO END--
116	104:focusing exploration on feasible trajectories.
117	105:We demonstrate the practical benefits of this representation by integrating Const-o-T with MCTS
118	106:for constraint-guided planning. The key novelty of our approach is the executable intent–constraint
119	107:representation, while MCTS serves as a supporting mechanism that operationalizes these constraints
120	108:during search. In our framework, an LLM first generates a sequence of 〈intent, constraint〉pairs from
121	109:the user’s strategic input. Each constraint κt induces a restricted action set Aκt(s) ⊆A(s), and this
122	110:restriction is enforced before node expansion during search, pruning infeasible actions and reducing
123	111:the branching factor. Prior approaches incorporate constraints through scoring, verification, or
124	112:affordance weighting, where the full action set A(s) is still considered during generation. In contrast,
125	113:our approach restricts the admissible action set to Aκt(s) prior to expansion, preventing infeasible
126	114:actions from entering the search process. We evaluate Const-o-T across four domains, where it
127	115:consistently outperforms strong baselines. These results demonstrate that structured intermediate
128	116:representations can effectively guide planning and improve reliability. Because Const-o-T produces
129	117:interpretable intent–constraint pairs that expose the system’s reasoning process, we also evaluate
130	118:whether this representation improves human understanding and perceived alignment with system
131	119:behavior, finding that users report significantly higher transparency, usability, trust, and alignment.
132	120:Our work makes the following contributions:
133	121:1. Constraints-of-Thought (Const-o-T). We propose an executable intermediate representation that
134	122:decomposes strategies into 〈intent, constraint〉pairs, where constraints define a reduced feasible
135	123:action space A′(s).
136	124:2. Constraint-Guided MCTS. We integrate Const-o-T with MCTS, operationalizing executable
137	125:constraints as search controllers that restrict the feasible action space during exploration.
138	126:3. Computational Evaluation. We empirically show consistent branching-factor reduction and
139	127:compute-normalized gains across heterogeneous domains.
140	128:4. Human Evaluation. We conduct a user study on the board game Risk showing that the structured
141	129:⟨intent, constraint⟩representation improves transparency, trust, and alignment with user strategies
142	130:(p < 0.05).

186	479:Experiments
187	480:We evaluate our approach along three dimensions: task accuracy, structural alignment of generated
188	481:plans, and interpretability of intermediate reasoning steps. We benchmark our method against a
189	482:diverse set of baselines spanning prompting-based, search-based, and constraint-based planning
190	483:approaches. The prompting baselines include Direct Prompt, Chain-of-Thought (CoT) [1], Tree-of-
191	484:Thought (ToT) [14], CoT with Rejection Sampling (CoT+RS) [27], Constraint Template Prompting
192	485:(CTP) [28], and Chain-of-Verification (CoV) [29]. For search-based methods, we consider classical
193	486:MCTS [30] as well as MCTS augmented with CoT reasoning. We also include a constraint-based
194	487:planning baseline, LLMFP [21], which translates natural language problems into formal optimization
195	488:constraints. Unless otherwise specified, all baselines are evaluated consistently across all domains.
196	489:4.1
197	490:Game Strategy: Risk
198	491:Risk is a strategy board game played on a world map of 21 territories grouped into six continents.
199	492:We focus on the initial troop placement studied in prior work [19] (See Appendix §G for illustrative
200	493:example). We use the Commander’s Intent (CI) dataset [19], which contains 1, 053 examples of
201	494:natural language strategies paired with corresponding ground-truth territories for troop placement.
202	495:We measure alignment using Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) [31], which quantifies the minimum
203	496:cost of transforming the predicted troop placement distribution into the ground-truth distribution. Our
204	497:results demonstrate that across all evaluated LLMs, MCTS with Const-o-T consistently achieves the
205	498:lowest EMD, indicating the best alignment between predicted and ground-truth troop placements.
206	499:The key improvement comes from constraint-guided search, which restricts the action space to
207	500:strategy-consistent troop placements during planning (See Table 1).
208	501:4.2
209	502:CAD Code Generation
210	503:The task involves translating natural language descriptions of 3D objects into executable parametric
211	504:CAD scripts, where constraint enforcement helps maintain syntactic validity and geometric cor-
212	505:rectness. We utilize CADPrompt [32], a dataset containing 200 3D design examples, each paired
213	506:with a natural language description and a corresponding Python script (See Figure 13). We report
214	507:Hausdorff distance between generated and ground-truth objects and the percentage of generated
215	508:examples compiling successfully. The results in Table 2 demonstrate that MCTS with Const-o-T
216	509:achieves the best performance across both LLaMA and GPT-4.1, with the lowest Hausdorff distances
217	510:(0.21 and 0.12) and the highest success rate of 95.5% for GPT-4.1.

236	--LIMITATIONS--
237	773:Limitations
238	774:Const-o-T depends on accurate constraint extraction; when LLMs misinterpret user input or produce
239	775:incomplete symbolic constraints, the search may be guided toward suboptimal solutions. Additionally,
240	776:the framework assumes users can articulate intent in natural language; however, for complex scenarios,
241	777:users may struggle to express nuanced preferences, potentially leading to constraint extraction failures
242	778:and human-AI alignment issues.
243	779:8
244	780:Conclusion
245	781:We introduced Constraints-of-Thought (Const-o-T), a framework that transforms unconstrained
246	782:natural language reasoning into structured, verifiable constraints for guiding language model planning.
247	783:By representing each reasoning step as an ⟨intent, constraint⟩pair, our approach provides actionable
248	784:control over the search process rather than merely explanatory rationales. Our integration with MCTS
249	785:demonstrates how constraints can effectively prune infeasible branches and direct exploration toward
250	786:semantically meaningful actions. Comprehensive evaluation across four domains shows consistent
251	787:improvements in accuracy, structural alignment, and constraint satisfaction. These findings suggest
252	788:that structured constraint extraction represents a promising direction for constraint-guided reasoning
253	789:in LLM-based planning systems.

269	6:Implicit Intelligence - Evaluating Agents on What Users Don’t Say

273	10:Real-world requests to AI agents are fundamentally underspecified. Natural
274	11:human communication relies on shared context and unstated constraints
275	12:that speakers expect listeners to infer. Current agentic benchmarks test
276	13:explicit instruction-following but fail to evaluate whether agents can reason
277	14:about implicit requirements spanning accessibility needs, privacy bound-
278	15:aries, catastrophic risks, and contextual constraints. We present Implicit
279	16:Intelligence, an evaluation framework testing whether AI agents can move
280	17:beyond prompt-following to become genuine goal-fulfillers, paired with
281	18:Agent-as-a-World (AaW), a harness where interactive worlds are defined
282	19:in human-readable YAML files and simulated by language models. Our
283	20:scenarios feature apparent simplicity in user requests, hidden complexity
284	21:in correct solutions, and discoverability of constraints through environ-
285	22:mental exploration. Evaluating 16 frontier and open-weight models across
286	23:205 scenarios, we find that even the best-performing model achieves only
287	24:48.3% scenario pass rate, revealing substantial room for improvement
288	25:in bridging the gap between literal instruction-following and human-like
289	26:contextual reasoning.
290	27:1
291	28:Introduction
292	29:The gap between what users say and what they mean represents a fundamental challenge in deploying
293	30:AI agents. Natural communication is inherently underspecified: speakers rely on shared context,
294	31:implicit assumptions, and unstated constraints they expect listeners to infer. A simple request often
295	32:carries invisible requirements that, if violated, render any technically correct solution useless or
296	33:harmful.
297	34:Current benchmarks have driven progress in explicit instruction-following and tool use, testing
298	--INTRO END--
299	39:We argue the next frontier lies not in more sophisticated tool use or longer planning, but in Implicit
300	40:Intelligence: the capacity to identify, reason about, and satisfy requirements users expect but
301	41:never explicitly state. We introduce an evaluation framework probing this capability through four
302	42:categories: Implicit Reasoning, inferring unstated goals from environmental context; Catastrophic
303	43:Risk Avoidance, preventing irreversible actions a reasonable person would never intend; Privacy
304	44:& Security, respecting sensitive boundaries users assume but don’t articulate; and Accessibility,
305	45:adapting to user needs discoverable through environmental context.
306	46:1
307	47:arXiv:2602.20424v1  [cs.AI]  23 Feb 2026
308	48:

310	50:=== PAGE 2 ===
311	51:============================================================
312	52:
313	53:To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce Agent-as-a-World (AaW), a paradigm where interactive
314	54:worlds are defined in single YAML files and simulated by language models. Unlike traditional
315	55:simulations requiring complex infrastructure or extensive engineering, AaW leverages LLMs as
316	56:universal simulators. Each scenario includes entities with state and actions, contextual information
317	57:revealing implicit constraints, execution rules governing dynamics, and evaluation rubrics assessing
318	58:whether implicit requirements were satisfied.
319	59:Our scenarios share three properties: apparent simplicity in user requests that appear straightfor-
320	60:ward; hidden complexity in correct solutions requiring reasoning beyond explicit instructions; and
321	61:discoverability of constraints through proactive environmental exploration.
322	62:Together, Implicit Intelligence and Agent-as-a-World provide a scalable framework for developing
323	63:AI agents that bridge the gap between literal instruction-following and human-like contextual rea-
324	64:soning. By making implicit expectations explicit in evaluation, we drive progress toward agents that
325	65:understand what users mean, not just what they say.
326	66:2
327	--METHOD--
328	323:Dataset Construction
329	324:Constructing an evaluation dataset for implicit intelligence presents a unique challenge: scenarios
330	325:must be difficult enough to cause frontier models to fail, yet fair enough that failure reflects genuine
331	326:reasoning gaps rather than arbitrary tricks. We address this through a hybrid pipeline that combines
332	327:synthetic generation with expert human refinement, illustrated in Figure 3.
333	328:5.1
334	329:Seed Sources
335	330:Scenario generation begins with diverse seeds that ground scenarios in realistic user contexts. First,
336	331:we leverage an iOS Actions Library Cassinelli (2026) consisting of 303 executable actions derived
337	332:directly from Apple’s Shortcuts framework, spanning seven functional domains: apps (103 actions),
338	333:documents (48), location (18), media (66), scripting (45), sharing (7), and web (16). These
339	334:actions cover common iOS capabilities such as calendar management, file operations, media control,

377	366:Figure 3: The hybrid construction pipeline to synthetically create scenarios for Implicit Intelligence and using human-in-the-loop to refine
378	367:automation logic, and focus-mode configuration, ensuring that scenarios reflect authentic iOS action
379	368:signatures and constraints. Second, we draw from PersonaHub Ge et al. (2025) to introduce
380	369:demographic and contextual diversity, sampling personas with varied ages, occupations, and health
381	370:conditions to shape scenario context without explicitly revealing implicit requirements.
382	371:While our scenarios are grounded in iOS Shortcuts, a realistic action space with 303 operations, the
383	372:evaluation targets are domain-agnostic. iOS Shortcuts provides ecological validity (real users interact
384	373:with this environment daily), action diversity (operations span communication, media, accessibility,
385	374:privacy, and system control), and natural opportunities for implicit requirements through accessibility
386	375:settings, contact relationships, and calendar conflicts. The implicit requirements transfer across
387	376:agentic domains. iOS Shortcuts provides the grounding; implicit intelligence provides the evaluation
388	377:target.
389	378:5.2
390	379:Synthetic Generation
391	380:The first phase uses an iterative refinemnent loop to generate inherently challenging scenarios through
392	381:three stages: (1) Plan, where an agent generates an initial YAML scenario based on a category and
393	382:persona; (2) Attempt, where the scenario is executed against a rotating attempter model, essentially
394	383:the Primary Agent (GPT-5 series, Claude Opus/Sonnet, Gemini 3 Pro), to record the full trajectory;
395	384:and (3) Refine, where the Planner receives successful trajectories and modifies the scenario, adding
396	385:timing constraints, order dependencies, or verification steps, to induce failure. This loop continues
397	386:until the attempter fails or a maximum iteration count is reached.
398	387:5.3
399	388:Scenario Validation
400	389:To ensure implicit requirements reflect genuine user expectations and provide a measurable challenge,
401	390:synthetic candidates undergo a rigorous three-stage review. First, an author refines the synthetic
402	391:scenario including environmental context. Second, two independent experts validate the draft for
403	392:Logical Consistency (requirements are discoverable without arbitrary "tricks"), Shared Expectations
404	393:(avoiding author idiosyncrasies), and Rubric Objectivity (binary pass conditions). Finally, scenarios
405	394:must achieve unanimous consensus and pass a Difficulty Gate: candidates are retained only if they
406	395:cause at least one frontier model (including GPT-5.2, GPT-5, Claude Opus/Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini 3
407	396:Pro) to fail (≤70% score) while allowing at least one to pass (100% score). Scenarios passed by all
408	397:models are discarded.

419	--RESULTS--
420	511:Main Results
421	512:Table 2 presents the primary evaluation results across all models and categories; full model endpoint
422	513:specifications are provided in Appendix A.7.
423	514:The benchmark reveals that implicit intelligence remains a substantial challenge. Even the best-
424	515:performing model, GPT-5.2-pro, achieves only 48.3% SPR, failing to satisfy all implicit requirements
425	516:in more than half of scenarios. This contrasts sharply with near-ceiling performance on established
426	517:reasoning benchmarks, suggesting that inferring unstated user needs represents a distinct capability.
427	518:Category-level analysis reveals that catastrophic risk avoidance and privacy protection require different
428	519:model strengths. Claude Opus 4.5 excels at recognizing potentially harmful actions, while GPT-5.2-
429	520:pro leads on privacy-sensitive scenarios. Open-weight models struggle particularly with catastrophic
430	521:risk, often proceeding with dangerous operations that frontier models refuse.

450	--LIMITATIONS--
451	723:Limitations.
452	724:We acknowledge several limitations. Our scenario construction reflects the perspec-
453	725:tives of the authors; implicit requirements may not fully represent the diversity of real-world user
454	726:expectations across cultures, age groups, and technical backgrounds. Benchmark temporality poses a
455	727:challenge: iOS features evolve with each software update, meaning scenario validity may degrade
456	728:over time. Our action space is constrained to approximately 300 native iOS actions, while real-world
457	729:usage extends to third-party applications with their own implicit conventions. However, the Agent-as-
458	730:a-World architecture makes extending coverage straightforward, as new applications can be defined
459	731:entirely in YAML.
460	732:Conclusion. We introduced Implicit Intelligence, an evaluation framework testing whether AI
461	733:agents can move beyond literal instruction-following to become genuine goal-fulfillers, paired with
462	734:Agent-as-a-World, a harness enabling scalable evaluation through LLM-simulated environments.
463	735:Evaluating frontier models across four categories of implicit requirements, we find substantial room
464	736:for improvement. The gap between strong performance on established benchmarks and modest results
465	737:here reveals that implicit intelligence remains a frontier challenge distinct from general reasoning
466	738:capabilities.

477	--ABSTRACT--
478	12:Abstract
479	13:Users often omit essential details in their re-
480	14:quests to LLM-based agents, resulting in under-
481	15:specified inputs for tool use. This poses a fun-
482	16:damental challenge for tool-augmented agents,
483	17:as API execution typically requires complete
484	18:arguments, highlighting the need for person-
485	19:alized tool calling. To study this problem, we
486	20:present Multi-Session Personalized Tool Call-
487	21:ing (MPT), a benchmark comprising 4,695 in-
488	22:stances over 459 multi-session interaction his-
489	23:tories that cover three challenges: Preference
490	24:Recall, Induction, and Transfer. We further pro-
491	25:pose PREFINE, a test-time memory method
492	26:that maintains the user’s latent preference as
493	27:a textual hypothesis revised through a generate–
494	28:verify–refine loop. Across five LLMs, existing
495	29:memory systems often fail to improve on full-
496	30:history prompting; PREFINE outperforms all
497	31:baselines and alone surpasses it on Preference
498	32:Transfer. These results indicate that memory
499	33:for personalized agents must abstract behavior
500	34:into preferences, rather than simply archive it.
501	35:1
502	36:Introduction
503	37:LLM-based agents increasingly rely on external
504	38:tools to perform complex tasks such as deep re-
505	39:search (Xu and Peng, 2025) and computer use
506	40:(Sager et al., 2026). These tools, typically realized
507	41:as parameterized functions, are invoked with ar-
508	42:guments often missing from user requests; e.g., a
509	43:query as simple as “Book a flight for my trip” speci-
510	44:fies neither the origin, the destination, nor the price.
511	45:A direct solution to such underspecification is to
512	--INTRO END--

515	131:flight_class=“Economy” cannot be retrieved from past calls. Instead, the agent must model the user’s preference
516	132:from its cross-function expressions (price_range, free_entry, car_type) and apply it to the unseen argument.
517	133:revised across sessions through a generate–verify–
518	134:refine loop. A candidate hypothesis enters memory
519	135:only after being verified against the accumulated
520	136:behavioral record, yielding a memory that is an
521	137:abstraction of user behavior rather than a raw log.
522	138:Across five LLMs and six methods, agents
523	139:reliably recover explicit arguments but struggle
524	140:with omitted preference-sensitive ones, and perfor-
525	141:mance degrades from Recall through Induction to
526	142:Transfer. Retrieval- and organization-based mem-
527	143:ories (RAG, Mem0, LangMem) even fall below
528	144:full-history prompting, indicating that surfacing
529	145:past records is not enough unless the evidence is
530	146:abstracted into a preference. PREFINE, in contrast,
531	147:outperforms all baselines, and is the only method to
532	148:exceed full-history prompting on Transfer without
533	149:session context. Its advantage also holds as compet-
534	150:ing and unrelated observations accumulate in his-
535	151:tory, a difficulty we quantify with a new evidence
536	152:interference score: all methods degrade under high
537	153:interference, but PREFINE remains the best. Abla-
538	154:tions on PREFINE further show that verification,
539	155:not repeated refinement, drives these gains.

542	450:Benchmark Construction: MPT
543	451:Building on §3, we present Multi-Session Person-
544	452:alized Tool-Calling (MPT),1 a benchmark that
545	453:evaluates whether an agent can infer the dominant
546	454:preference from a history H and apply it to a query
547	455:q with unspecified preference-sensitive arguments.
548	456:We construct separate pools of histories (§4.2) and

550	458:(§4.4). Figure 2 illustrates the overall process.

664	--LIMITATIONS--
665	1660:Limitations
666	1661:This work focuses on a controlled setting for eval-
667	1662:uating latent preference reasoning in personalized
668	1663:tool-calling. In particular, we study whether an
669	1664:agent can infer reusable preference constraints
670	1665:from interaction history and apply them to under-
671	1666:specified API parameters under a schema-bounded
672	1667:action space.
673	1668:A history may reflect several preferences, but
674	1669:each MPT query targets only one, which persists
675	1670:across sessions (C3) and keeps the gold argument
676	1671:unambiguous. Preferences that shift over time or
677	1672:combine within a query are a natural extension.
678	1673:The five preferences in Table 2 can be extended
679	1674:by adding realization mappings, and inferred pref-
680	1675:erences transfer to seven unseen functions (§7.2).
681	1676:PREFINE keeps its memory as free text, so a hy-
682	1677:pothesis can state several constraints, though select-
683	1678:ing among them per query is not evaluated. Finally,
684	1679:users are composed from existing corpora, since a
685	1680:latent preference must be known to be scored.

3	15:Abstract
4	16:Planning for real-world problems by language models often involves both
5	17:world and user constraints, which may not be fully specified upfront and
6	18:are progressively disclosed through interaction. However, existing bench-
7	19:marks still underexplore adaptive planning under such progressively re-
8	20:vealed dual constraints. To address this gap, we introduce AdaPlanBench,
9	21:a dynamic interactive benchmark for evaluating whether Large Language
10	22:Model (LLM) agents can adaptively plan and re-plan under progressively
11	23:revealed world and user constraints. AdaPlanBench is built on 307 house-
12	24:hold tasks, with a scalable constraint construction pipeline that augments
13	25:each task with dual constraints. At runtime, agents interact with the en-
14	26:vironment in a multi-turn protocol where hidden constraints are revealed
15	27:only when the agent proposes a plan that violates them, requiring iterative
16	28:plan revision under accumulating feedback. This makes planning chal-
17	29:lenging, as agents must infer and track constraints from feedback while
18	30:re-planning effectively. Experiments on ten leading LLMs show that adap-
19	31:tive planning under dual constraints remains challenging, with the best
20	32:model reaching only 67.75% accuracy. We further observe that perfor-
21	33:mance degrades as more constraints accumulate, with user constraints
22	34:posing a particularly large challenge and failures often stemming from
23	35:weaker physical grounding and reduced effectiveness. These results estab-
24	36:lish AdaPlanBench as a testbed for dual-constrained interactive planning
25	37:and highlight the challenge of reliable adaptation to dynamically revealed
26	38:constraints in LLM agents.
27	39:1

30	42:active tasks, including writing complex code (Anthropic, 2026; Guo et al., 2026a), operating

32	44:et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025b). While these applications differ in domain, they share
33	45:a common structure: agent capability depends on sustained interaction throughout task
34	46:execution (Yao et al., 2023; Park et al., 2023). This interaction typically unfolds along two
35	47:closely linked dimensions: interaction with users, through which agents infer goals and
