88	--RESULTS--
89	655:Results
90	656:Current LLM Agents are still far from effective under dynamic dual constraints.
91	657:The
92	658:main results indicate that planning under progressively disclosed dual constraints remains
93	659:challenging for all evaluated models. Even GPT-5, the best-performing model, reaches only
94	660:67.75% accuracy. Another strong model, Gemini-3.1-Pro, scores only around 35%, while
95	661:most models fall below 45%. Open-weight models perform particularly poorly, typically
96	662:around 30% or lower. Although most models maintain a valid-plan ratio above 70%, they
97	663:still frequently violate already disclosed constraints. Additionally, averaged across the
98	664:10 evaluated models, each query contains 0.295 repeated violations of disclosed world
99	665:constraints and 0.503 repeated violations of disclosed user constraints. As a result, 17.91%
100	666:of queries terminate early in average because the model violates disclosed constraints two
101	667:consecutive times without triggering any new constraint. Together, these results indicate
102	668:that progressively disclosed dual constraints remain a substantial challenge for current
103	669:models, affecting both consistent constraint adherence and overall plan quality.
104	670:High valid-plan rates do not necessarily translate into final task success.
105	671:A high valid
106	672:plan ratio (VPR) does not guarantee strong end-task accuracy. For example, both Gemini-3.1-
107	673:Pro and Gemini-3-Flash achieve relatively high VPRs, exceeding 90%, yet their accuracies
108	674:remain below 45%. This pattern is further supported by their relatively low AWRV and
109	675:AURV, suggesting that these models are reasonably effective at tracking disclosed constraints
110	676:and avoiding repeated violations. However, despite maintaining executable plans and
111	677:showing relatively strong constraint-tracking behavior, they still often fail to reach correct
112	678:final solutions. This pattern suggests that relatively strong constraint tracking alone is
113	679:insufficient to ensure strong final performance under progressive disclosure.

119	--LIMITATIONS--
120	1043:Limitations
121	1044:Limited Domain Coverage.
122	1045:AdaPlanBench is currently instantiated in the household
123	1046:domain, which provides a natural setting where user preferences and world constraints
124	1047:interact. This choice offers a controlled and realistic testbed for studying adaptive planning,
125	1048:but some domain specific phenomena from settings such as travel, office workflows, or
126	1049:robotics may not yet be covered. We partially mitigate this limitation by focusing on general
127	1050:benchmark properties, including dual constraints, progressive disclosure, and open ended
128	1051:evaluation, which are not unique to household tasks. Future work can instantiate the same
129	1052:framework in additional domains to test how well the findings transfer.
130	1053:Potential Bias in LLM-based Evaluation.
131	1054:Our evaluation relies on LLM judges for con-
132	1055:straint checking and rubric scoring, which may introduce model-specific preferences or
133	1056:systematic bias. Although this setup enables scalable evaluation, it is still not equivalent to
134	1057:fully manual assessment. We partially mitigate this risk in two ways: first, we use multiple
135	1058:judges and aggregate their rubric scores to reduce the bias from a certain judge model;
136	1059:second, human annotation shows high consistency with the rubric-based LLM judgments.
137	1060:Text-only Evaluation Setting
138	1061:AdaPlanBench evaluates adaptive planning in a text-only
139	1062:interaction setting, without visual perception, embodied execution, or direct contact with
140	1063:real environments. This means the benchmark does not capture the full difficulty of real-
141	1064:world agent deployment, especially when perception and action grounding are tightly
142	1065:coupled. At the same time, this is a deliberate trade-off: by removing perception errors and
143	1066:low-level control noise, the benchmark more cleanly isolates adaptive planning abilities

146	--ABSTRACT--
147	13:Abstract
148	14:Despite their strong reasoning capabilities and
149	15:extensive world knowledge, Large Language
150	16:Models (LLMs) frequently generate plans that
151	17:violate task constraints, undermining their re-
152	18:liability in real-world applications. This defi-
153	19:ciency arises from a lack of systematic mech-
154	20:anisms to incorporate constraint information
155	21:during the generation process. While existing
156	22:approaches attempt to mitigate this by rely-
157	23:ing on external tools or task decomposition,
158	24:they fail to enhance the model’s intrinsic con-
159	25:straint awareness.
160	26:To address this, we pro-
161	27:pose Constraint-Aware Reinforcement Learn-
162	28:ing (CARL), a novel RL framework designed
163	29:to strengthen LLMs’ intrinsic focus on con-
164	30:straints. CARL introduces a constraint-aware
165	31:reward by comparing the model’s output distri-
166	32:butions under constrained and unconstrained in-
167	33:puts, encouraging constraint focus and penaliz-
168	34:ing neglect. Compatible with various RL frame-
169	35:works and requiring no external solvers or top
170	36:models, CARL enables scalable, end-to-end
171	37:constraint-aware planning. Extensive experi-
172	38:ments on BlocksWorld, TravelPlanner, and T-
173	39:Eval demonstrate that CARL significantly out-
174	40:performs standard Reinforcement Fine-Tuning
175	41:(RFT) baselines and state-of-the-art reasoning
176	42:models, exhibiting a markedly increased focus
177	43:on constraints.
178	44:1
179	45:Introduction
180	46:Large Language Models (LLMs) have demon-

182	270:mance. Recent advances such as Group Relative
183	271:Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024)
184	272:and Reinforcement Learning with Online Optimiza-
185	273:tion (RLOO) (Ahmadian et al., 2024) seek to bal-
186	274:ance performance with computational efficiency.
187	275:Parallel research has attempted to enhance input
188	276:awareness through specialized rewards or prefer-
189	277:ence pairs. For example, Kiruluta et al. (2025) uti-
190	278:lize attention scores as reward signals to prioritize
191	279:crucial tokens, while Gu et al. (2024); Deng et al.
192	280:(2024) construct preference pairs from original and
193	281:noise-perturbed images to strengthen visual anchor-
194	282:ing. However, these methods are primarily limited
195	283:to simple QA or visual tasks, and their efficacy
196	284:in complex reasoning scenarios such as planning
197	285:remains unverified.
198	286:In this work, we introduce a constraint-aware
199	287:reward mechanism tailored for planning tasks.
200	288:Our key innovation lies in quantifying constraint
201	289:sensitivity through the distributional shift in log-
202	290:probabilities between constrained and uncon-
203	291:strained conditions. This formulation is natively
204	292:compatible with on-policy methods (PPO, GRPO)
205	293:and can be seamlessly adapted to off-policy frame-
206	294:works like DPO by transforming constraint signals
207	295:into preference pairs, ensuring robust constraint
208	296:compliance across training paradigms.

211	154:framework designed to explicitly strengthen LLMs’
212	155:focus on constraints. CARL introduces a novel
213	156:constraint-aware reward derived from the distri-
214	157:butional shift of the model’s outputs under con-
215	158:strained versus unconstrained inputs. By utiliz-
216	159:ing the KL divergence between log-probabilities in
217	160:these two settings as a reward signal, CARL guides
218	161:the model to integrate constraint signals more ef-
219	162:fectively. Unlike discrete task rewards, our contin-
220	163:uous constraint-aware reward provides smoother
221	164:optimization gradients and encourages meaningful
222	165:exploration during planning failures.
223	166:CARL provides a novel and effective training
224	167:framework for enhancing intrinsic planning com-
225	168:petence. As illustrated in Figure 1, models trained
226	169:with CARL exhibit significantly higher attribution
227	170:scores for constraint tokens (e.g., non-self-driving
228	171:transportation, Asian cuisine) compared to standard
229	172:RFT, leading to improved plan validity. Further-

376	##### library/01_constraint_compiler/2610.00797_Sapien/2610.00797_Sapien_fulltext.txt  (1860 lines)
377	--ABSTRACT--
378	10:Abstract
379	11:Contextual security defenses prevent AI agents from tak-
380	12:ing rogue actions by synthesizing a task-specific policy and
381	13:enforcing it on the agent’s tool calls. In multi-step tasks,
382	14:however, which actions are valid often depends on what the
383	15:agent has already done and learned. We present Sapien, a
384	16:policy engine for enforcing stateful contextual policies. A
385	17:Sapien policy specifies permitted tool-call sequences using
386	18:a regular expression extended with stateful predicates, de-
387	19:ferred policy generation, and scoped semantic checks. We
388	20:show that Sapien stays within a few percent of an uncon-
389	21:strained agent’s utility. Even if the agent is fully hijacked,
390	22:Sapien’s policies rule out 93–95% of attacks on AgentDojo
391	23:and 62–85% on Toolathlon (twice as many as tool allowlists
392	24:on long-horizon tasks).
393	25:1
394	26:Introduction
395	27:AI agents use large language models (LLMs) to autonomously
396	28:plan and carry out natural-language tasks by calling exter-
397	29:nal tools [15, 17, 39]. Unlike traditional programs governed
398	30:by hard-coded control flow, agents rely on the LLM’s rea-
399	31:soning to interpret tool outputs and dynamically plan their
400	32:next steps, allowing them to tackle complex, long-horizon
401	33:tasks. Increasingly, developers aim for general-purpose agents,
402	34:equipping AI models with a broad suite of tools to handle
403	35:open-ended tasks across domains on behalf of a user—for
404	36:example, managing online accounts, organizing meetings
405	37:and notes, or coordinating travel.
406	38:Yet delegating tool invocation to an LLM makes agents
407	39:inherently unreliable and prone to rogue actions—tool calls
408	40:that diverge from the user’s intent. As trajectories span more
409	41:steps, agents are more likely to encounter untrusted content
410	42:that hijacks them via prompt injection [19, 64], or to spon-
411	43:taneously drift from their goal, misinterpret a tool output,
412	--INTRO END--
413	133:Sapien’s policies rule out 93–95% of attacks on AgentDojo
414	134:and 62–85% on Toolathlon (doubling the defense rate of tool
415	135:allowlists for the latter).
416	136:This paper makes the following contributions:
417	137:1. A stateful policy language targeting autonomous AI
418	138:agents performing long-horizon tasks (§4);
419	139:2. Sapien, an automaton-based engine that synthesizes
420	140:policies from trusted user prompts and enforces them
421	141:over tool calls with actionable recovery feedback (§5);
422	142:and
423	143:3. An evaluation of Sapien’s effect on utility and worst-
424	144:case security, the latter using an analytical methodol-
425	145:ogy that checks whether a policy admits any attack
426	146:trajectory by a fully hijacked agent (§6).
427	147:While prior systems [9, 45, 62] also express dependencies
428	148:across tool calls, they rely on static policies derived ahead of
429	149:time (manually or with offline LLM assistance) from fixed
430	150:domain rules (§8).1 This suits single-purpose agents, but
431	151:not general-purpose agents whose appropriate actions may
432	152:vary with every user request. Beyond the design of Sapien’s
433	153:language and enforcement engine, our work suggests that
434	154:today’s LLMs can synthesize expressive, fine-grained policies
435	155:from natural language, providing strong protection across
436	156:diverse tasks without humans writing or auditing policies.
437	157:1Progent [51] generates task-specific policies with an LLM, but its policy
438	158:language only constrains individual tool calls; to adapt across steps, it feeds
439	159:tool outputs back to an LLM after every call to rewrite those rules (§8).
440	160:2
441	--EXP SETUP--
442	859:Evaluation
443	860:Our evaluation measures the advantages of Sapien’s ap-
444	861:proach to balance utility-security tradeoffs and its practi-
445	862:cality:
446	863:1. Utility: Does Sapien impact the agent’s task success rate?
447	864:2. Security: Can attackers achieve their goals (caused e.g.,
448	865:by prompt injections) in the presence of Sapien policies?
449	866:3. Efficiency: What latency and overheads does Sapien add
450	867:to agent execution, and why?
451	868:Baselines. We compare three agents that differ in what
452	869:governs their tool calls: no policy (“NoPolicy”), a Sapien
453	870:policy, and a per-task allow-list of tool names generated from
454	871:the task prompt in the style of Conseca [57] (“AllowList”).
455	872:AllowList stands in for coarse-grained, stateless contextual
456	873:policies: it allows or denies each tool for the whole task,
457	874:regardless of arguments or execution state, and is generated
458	875:in a single LLM call (without Sapien’s self-correction pass,
459	876:§5.3).
460	877:Benchmarks. We evaluate Sapien on AgentDojo [13] and
461	878:Toolathlon [31]. AgentDojo comprises 97 short tasks (most
462	879:within five turns) set in synthetic environments across four
463	880:suites—workspace, Slack, travel, and banking—each exposing
464	881:a small set of 11–28 tools. Toolathlon features 108 longer-
465	882:horizon tasks (dozens of turns) situated in a realistic en-
466	883:vironment with a local file/shell workspace and 32 soft-
467	884:ware applications—including GitHub, Notion, and Google
468	885:Workspace—that together expose over 600 tools via MCP.
469	886:To prevent Toolathlon from granting agents blanket, un-
470	887:limited capabilities via a handful of “almighty tools” like
471	888:local_python_execute, all agents upfront deny access to
472	889:local_python_execute (impacting a handful of tasks that
473	890:would otherwise use it for arbitrary computation), and we
474	891:require Sapien to specify command predicates (e.g., the com-
475	892:mand must be grep) for terminal_run_command.

493	1531:Conclusion
494	1532:General-purpose agents need task-specific policies that track
495	1533:what the agent has done and learned. Sapien provides a state-
496	1534:ful policy language and an engine that enforces such policies
497	1535:over tool calls. Our evaluation shows that Sapien preserves
498	1536:utility while tightly constraining even a fully hijacked agent,
499	1537:making stateful contextual policies a promising path toward
500	1538:safely deploying autonomous agents.

511	--ABSTRACT--
512	11:Abstract
513	12:Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) rapidly produces
514	13:high-quality solutions for problem structures encountered dur-
515	14:ing training, but operational requirements may change af-
516	15:ter deployment and be communicated in natural language.
517	16:We propose LangNCO, a framework that compiles instance-
518	17:specific requirements into structured inference-time interven-
519	18:tions for a frozen NCO solver, without changing the pre-
520	19:trained policy’s architecture, learned input representation, or
521	20:parameters. A pretrained LLM serves as a replaceable se-
522	21:mantic front end, translating each requirement into a schema-
523	22:validated domain-specific language (DSL) rule set. A deter-
524	23:ministic Rule Executor applies the rules as nonexpansive hard
525	24:action masks. Because local masking prevents immediate vi-
526	25:olations but does not ensure that a complete feasible contin-
527	26:uation remains reachable, Critical-Offset Decoding extracts
528	27:rule-referenced critical nodes and reallocates part of a fixed
529	28:rollout budget to multi-strength biased rollouts. Using con-
530	29:trolled task-specific language to isolate solver adaptation from
531	30:open-ended language robustness, we evaluate a CVRP policy
532	31:on road closures, time windows, vehicle assignments, visit-
533	32:order requirements, all pairwise combinations, and twelve
534	33:additional constraint types. LangNCO achieves 100% fea-
535	34:sibility on the four primary datasets with mean reference
536	35:gaps of 1.63–3.26%, 97.33–100% feasibility when separately
537	36:generated rules are composed for pairwise constraints, and
538	37:98.67% feasibility across the additional constraints. These re-
539	38:sults demonstrate modular post-training adaptation of a frozen
540	39:NCO solver through inspectable language-derived rules, with-
541	40:out retraining.
542	41:1
543	42:Introduction
544	43:Combinatorial optimization underlies routing, scheduling,
545	44:production planning, and robotic decision making. In these
546	--INTRO END--
547	117:needed by an assigned customer, delay a time-window cus-
548	118:tomer beyond recovery, or close a route before a prerequisite
549	119:is served. We therefore introduce Critical-Offset Decoding,
550	120:which extracts explicitly referenced critical nodes from the
551	121:generated rules and reallocates part of a fixed rollout budget
552	122:to multi-strength biased rollouts. It never revives a masked
553	123:action and balances completion-oriented exploration with the
554	124:original policy’s cost-oriented search.
555	125:Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate post-
556	126:training request adaptation of a fixed CVRP policy and intro-
557	127:duce a modular language-to-rule interface whose validated
558	128:output drives deterministic, nonexpansive action interven-
559	129:tion, without adding constraint-specific inputs to the NCO
560	130:policy or changing its architecture or weights. Second, we
561	131:propose Critical-Offset Decoding, which biases a subset of
562	132:rollouts toward rule-derived critical nodes, reducing future
563	133:deadlocks and improving solution quality without increas-
564	134:ing the rollout budget. Third, we evaluate the framework on
565	135:four primary constraint types, all pairwise combinations, and
566	136:twelve additional types. The complete method attains 100%
567	137:feasibility on all four primary datasets with mean reference
568	138:gaps of 1.63–3.26%, 97.33–100% feasibility when separately
569	139:generated rules are composed for pairwise constraints, and
570	140:98.67% feasibility across the additional constraints. These
571	141:results show that structured language-derived rules can ex-
572	142:tend a frozen NCO solver beyond its training-time problem
573	143:definition without retraining.

3	14:Abstract
4	15:Symbolic constraints (programmatic, determin-
5	16:istic checks for tool calls) enable deterministic

8	19:safety policies rather than tool dependencies
9	20:in complex tool environments. We explore
10	21:whether symbolic constraints can be mined
11	22:from environments and observations beyond
12	23:predefined policies, and whether they can im-
13	24:prove end-to-end task performance. We present
14	25:Symbolic Constraint Agents (SCA), a frame-
15	26:work that mines symbolic constraints from API
16	27:documentation, refines them against execution
17	28:traces, and checks the agent’s tool calls with
18	29:an SMT solver at runtime. A violation triggers
19	30:a natural-language warning or, when the valid
20	31:replacement is uniquely determined, an auto-

22	33:error-detection F1 from 37.0 to 58.3 on GPT-
23	34:5.5 traces and from 39.3 to 61.9 on Qwen3.5-
24	35:27B traces. At runtime, repair raises GPT-5.4-
25	36:mini’s task success by 5.4 points under a 40-call
26	37:budget and 9.8 points when environment errors
27	38:are hidden, while removing 59–87% of failed
28	39:calls across models, and transfers to τ 2-bench
29	40:with gains of up to 5.6 points. These findings
30	41:show that automatically acquired symbolic con-
31	42:straints can improve tool-calling reliability and
32	43:task completion, particularly when failures are
33	44:costly or difficult to diagnose.

49	143:We make three contributions. First, we introduce
50	144:an environment-grounded constraint mining frame-
51	145:work that mines executable tool-call rules from API
52	146:documentation and iteratively refines them against
53	147:execution traces, even without requiring manually
54	148:specified task-success criteria. Second, we develop
55	149:solver-based interventions that translate detected
56	150:violations into natural-language feedback, or au-

58	152:errors. Third, we demonstrate that symbolic con-
59	153:straints can improve end-to-end task completion
60	154:through experiments on AppWorld (Trivedi et al.,

67	534:Experimental Setup
68	535:Benchmark.
69	536:We evaluate SCA on two tool-
70	537:calling benchmarks with different error structures.
71	538:AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024): we use the
72	539:test-challenge set (417 instructions). The App-
73	540:World environment exposes 457 APIs across nine
74	541:diverse stateful applications, including email, mu-
75	542:sic, notes, and contacts. Using these tools, the
76	543:agent should complete users’ tasks such as ac-
77	544:cepting Venmo transactions and sending emails
78	545:to friends. The default environment provides an
79	546:informative error message whenever the tool call
80	547:fails due to incorrect parameter values, authentica-
81	548:tion error, etc. (Standard) However, an agent can
82	549:often recover from a rejected call by reading the er-
83	550:ror message and retrying, so a prevented error may
84	551:only save cost. We therefore introduce two chal-
85	552:lenging variants of AppWorld that make tool errors
86	553:increasingly expensive: 40-call budget, where the
87	554:agent may make at most 40 tool calls instead of the
88	555:Standard setting’s 300, so every call spent on an
89	556:error is lost to the task; and silent errors, where the
90	557:environment rejects erroneous calls with an empty
91	558:response, which are harder for agents to recover
92	559:from failures (Zhang et al., 2026). For the silent
93	560:errors setting, the constraint generation/refinement

96	563:and retail domains with 20 and 40 held-out tasks,

147	668:stance, in AppWorld, whether a file actually exists
148	--LIMITATIONS--
149	1101:Limitations
150	1102:Constraints are built once with a strong proprietary
151	1103:model (GPT-5.5) and refined on execution traces
152	1104:of training tasks, which requires access to such
153	1105:traces and incurs a one-time cost. Our constraints
154	1106:check each tool call against the call history, so they
155	1107:detect errors that are visible in that history: wrong
156	1108:or miscopied arguments, calls in the wrong state,
157	1109:missing prerequisites. They cannot detect failures
158	1110:that depend on hidden environment state (e.g., a
159	1111:credit limit the agent has not queried), and they
160	1112:cannot detect omissions, where the agent never
161	1113:makes a necessary call. This is why recall is much
162	1114:lower than precision (Table 1), and why constraints
163	1115:help little for agents whose failures are mostly of
164	1116:these kinds, such as Qwen3.5-9B.
165	1117:Improvements in task success are largest when
166	1118:tool errors are costly or invisible and when the
167	1119:agent makes many call-level errors. In the standard
168	1120:AppWorld setting, success gains are small, and a
169	1121:strong model that rarely makes these errors (Claude
170	1122:Sonnet-5) benefits little. Warnings can also mis-
171	1123:lead: a false alarm may cause an agent to retry a
172	1124:call that was valid.

255	16:Estimating whether a problem is too complex

259	20:need for new tools to aid the agent. While
260	21:existing estimators rely on the problem text,
261	22:LLM-annotated task difficulty labels, or sig-
262	23:nals obtained after a model attempts to solve
263	24:the problem, such as its hidden states, none
264	25:explicitly leverage the constraint structure in-
265	26:herent in the problem: the variables to assign
266	27:and how the constraints over them interact.
267	28:We introduce CIRCE,1 which extracts a prob-
268	29:lem’s structure by using a cheap LLM to con-
269	30:struct a Constraint Intermediate Representation
270	31:that deterministically compiles into the con-

274	35:encoder improves predictions of LLM response
275	36:correctness, reducing negative log-likelihood
276	37:from 0.465 to 0.423 and increasing AUROC

278	39:baseline for each metric.

291	117:prediction. To capture interactions beyond aggre-
292	118:gate statistics, we also use a graph neural network
293	119:(CIRCE-GNN). We compare frozen encoders with
294	120:random initialization or self-supervised pretrain-
295	121:ing on separate unlabeled problems. A lightweight,
296	122:model-specific predictor maps either representation
297	123:to the probability of a correct response.
298	124:We evaluate CIRCE against four prediction base-
299	125:lines and a constant predictor on seven reason-
300	126:ing benchmarks and four LLMs. Five-fold cross-
301	127:validation over 200 problems per benchmark fits
302	128:each predictor on approximately 160 training prob-
303	129:lems, with ten responses per problem supplying
304	130:correctness labels. Relative to the strongest base-
305	131:line overall for each metric, the pretrained variant
306	132:reduces average negative log-likelihood of response
307	133:correctness by 9.5% (0.465 to 0.421) and increases
308	134:AUROC by 3.9 percentage points (0.691 to 0.730).
309	135:Even a frozen, randomly initialized GNN encoder
310	136:outperforms every baseline on average and nearly
311	137:matches the pretrained variant. These results show
312	138:that constraint structure recovered from text is a
313	139:useful signal for predicting LLM failures before
314	140:generation. Text-to-SQL and program synthesis
315	141:are promising targets for future evaluation.

318	202:methods such as GraphMAE (Hou et al., 2022)
319	203:further enable graph representation learning with-
320	204:out problem-specific labels. However, rather than
321	205:using these representations to solve problems or
322	206:support reasoning directly, we leverage the con-
323	207:straint structure to estimate the empirical difficulty
324	208:of individual problems for a target LLM.

326	210:Method
327	211:The way constraints connect variables can affect
328	212:the reasoning required to answer a problem. We use
329	213:these relationships as a signal for complexity esti-
330	214:mation. Extracting them directly from the problem
331	215:using an LLM is challenging. CIRCE addresses

341	225:the graph.

343	227:first extract a CIR and compile it into a constraint
344	228:graph (Section 3.2). We then represent the graph

348	232:a gradient-boosted predictor maps the structural
349	233:representation to a correctness probability for the
350	234:target model (Section 3.5).

474	7:Orchestration for Cyber-Physical Systems
475	8:Muhammad Ashfaq1�

483	16:Abstract. Modern cyber-physical systems (CPS) integrate heteroge-
484	17:neous sensors, actuators, controllers, and services, composed at run-
485	18:time rather than at design time. Orchestrating such systems through
486	19:natural language (NL) is attractive, but unconstrained large language
487	20:model (LLM) tool use is risky because actions must respect device ca-
488	21:pabilities, runtime state, and safety constraints. We present SafeOrches-
489	22:trate, a reference architecture for runtime-checked, intent-driven CPS
490	23:orchestration. Given an NL intent, it derives atomic goals, generates a
491	24:runtime-checkable specification for each, grounds the specifications to
492	25:device affordances, and verifies candidate actions against runtime state
493	26:and safety constraints before execution. In a Web of Things (WoT) in-
494	27:stantiation, the architecture produces Linear Temporal Logic-style spec-
495	28:ifications from the NL intent, grounds them to Thing Description (TD)
496	29:affordances exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and
497	30:checks candidate actions against satisfiability modulo theories (SMT)-
498	31:backed guardrails. We evaluate this instantiation on simulated smart
499	32:home, greenhouse, and industrial automation tasks against a direct LLM-
500	33:to-MCP baseline. SafeOrchestrate maintains 100% required-action accu-
501	34:racy on every task and 100% MCP Execution Similarity (MCP-ES) on all
502	--INTRO END--
503	101:=== PAGE 3 ===
504	102:============================================================
505	103:
506	104:backed guardrails, orchestrating heterogeneous devices through a uniform,
507	105:runtime-checked execution interface.
508	106:We investigate the following research question (RQ): How does grounding NL-
509	107:derived specifications to MCP-exposed WoT affordances, and verifying candidate
510	108:actions against runtime state before execution, affect the correctness of LLM-
511	109:driven CPS orchestration, relative to direct LLM-to-MCP tool use? We make
512	110:the following contributions:
513	111:1. We propose SafeOrchestrate, a reference architecture for LLM-driven CPS
514	112:orchestration that integrates specification generation, role-aware grounding,
515	113:and SMT-backed runtime guardrails over MCP-exposed affordances.
516	114:2. We introduce MCP Execution Similarity (MCP-ES), an alignment metric be-
517	115:tween expected and actual MCP tool-call trajectories that penalizes missing,
518	116:extra, substituted, and mis-ordered calls.
519	117:3. We evaluate the WoT/MCP instantiation of SafeOrchestrate across smart
520	118:home, greenhouse, and industrial automation tasks, where it matches a direct
521	119:LLM-to-MCP baseline on simple tasks and substantially outperforms it on
522	120:event-triggered, ordered, and multi-device tasks.
523	121:The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews
524	122:WoT mashups, LLM-assisted workflow generation, and verified tool execution.
525	123:Section 3 presents the SafeOrchestrate architecture. Section 4 describes the
526	124:WoT/MCP implementation. Section 5 reports the evaluation, and Section 6
527	125:concludes with limitations and future work. The implementation of SafeOrches-
528	126:trate and all evaluation artifacts are publicly available in the accompanying
529	127:repository4.

615	844:This paper presents SafeOrchestrate, a runtime-checked framework for LLM-
616	845:driven CPS control that combines MCP-based tool execution with guardrails.
617	846:The results show improved reliability over purely LLM-driven orchestration, es-
618	847:pecially on event-triggered, ordered, and multi-device tasks. The evaluation exer-
619	848:cises precondition satisfaction and trigger discipline; because its tasks are largely
620	849:single-rule with an empty constraint set C, the SMT layer’s cross-rule and safety-

3	10:Abstract
4	11:Tool-integrated agents that interleave reasoning
5	12:with API calls are promising for complex tasks,
6	13:yet aligning them for high-stakes, domain-
7	14:specific deployment remains challenging: ex-
8	15:isting reinforcement learning approaches rely
9	16:on coarse binary rewards that cannot distin-
10	17:guish tool selection errors from malformed
11	18:parameters.
12	19:We present ToolRLA, a three-
13	20:stage post-training pipeline (SFT →GRPO
14	21:→DPO) for domain-specific tool agents. The
15	22:core contribution is a fine-grained reward func-
16	23:tion with multiplicative correctness decompo-
17	24:sition spanning four dimensions—format va-
18	25:lidity, tool selection, parameter accuracy, and
19	26:regulatory compliance—that encodes domain
20	27:priority orderings as inductive biases in the
21	28:reward landscape.

24	31:queries), ToolRLA achieves over three months:
25	32:a 47% improvement in task completion rate

27	34:tion errors (38%→14%), and a 93% reduction
28	35:in regulatory violations (12%→0.8%), within
29	36:sub-2-second latency. Ablation studies show
30	37:the multiplicative reward design accounts for 7

198	6:SEVerA: Verified Self-Evolving Agents with Specification
199	7:Guidance
200	8:DEBANGSHU BANERJEE∗, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, USA
201	9:CHANGMING XU∗, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, USA
202	10:EUGENE IE, Google, USA
203	11:MING ZHANG, Google, USA
204	12:DAIYI PENG, Google, USA
205	13:CHU-CHENG LIN, Google, USA
206	14:TARUN SURESH, Stanford University, USA
207	15:GAGANDEEP SINGH, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, USA
208	16:Recent advances have demonstrated the effectiveness of self-evolving LLM agents on tasks such as program
209	17:repair and scientific discovery. In this paradigm, a planner LLM continuously synthesizes agent programs that
210	18:invoke parametric components, including generative models such as LLMs, and fine-tunes them. However,
211	19:existing work has shown that self-evolving agent frameworks can exhibit undesirable behavior on unseen
212	20:inputs. Because these synthesized programs are often executed autonomously, the lack of formal guarantees
213	21:that hold for all inputs raises serious reliability and security concerns. To address this gap, we introduce
214	22:specification-driven self-evolving agent synthesis, which combines formal behavioral specifications that the
215	23:synthesized agents must satisfy on all inputs with best-effort soft objectives that capture task utility. We
216	24:propose Formally Guarded Generative Models (FGGM), which allow the planner LLM to bind each generative-
217	25:model call to a formal output contract. Each FGGM call automatically wraps the underlying parametric
218	26:generative model within a stateful rejection sampler and a verified fallback, treating model outputs as samples
219	27:from a proposal distribution. Consequently, every returned output satisfies the specified contract for any input
220	28:and any parameter setting of the underlying model. Building on FGGM, we present SEVerA (Self-Evolving
221	29:Verified Agents), a four-stage framework for specification-driven agent synthesis. In the Ideation stage, the
222	30:planner LLM proposes task-specific generative components by constructing FGGMs. In the Search stage, the
223	31:planner LLM synthesizes candidate parametric programs containing multiple FGGM components. In the
224	32:Verification stage, we prove correctness with respect to the hard constraints for all parameter values, thereby
225	33:reducing the remaining optimization problem to unconstrained learning. Finally, in the Learning stage, we
226	34:apply scalable gradient-based optimization, including GRPO-style fine-tuning for LLMs, to optimize the soft
227	--INTRO END--
228	127:local contracts on model calls using Hoare-style preconditions and postconditions defined by
229	128:trusted, user-provided oracles. FGGM operates solely on LLM output strings and is compatible with
230	129:both open-source and closed-source models. The FGGM framework provides formal guarantees on
231	130:model outputs while also enabling gradient-based parameter optimization to tune the underlying
232	131:model to conform to the specified contracts.
233	132:• We introduce SEVerA: the first self-evolving agent synthesis algorithm with verifiable guarantees.
234	133:The approach consists of four stages: (a) Ideation, where a planner LLM proposes task-specific
235	134:generative components through FGGM setup; (b) Search and (c) Verify, which together instantiate
236	135:component-based synthesis, in which the planner LLM samples parametric programs in a verifier-
237	136:aware language such as Dafny that invoke the proposed components and the language’s built-in
238	137:verifier checks that they satisfy the user-specified specification over all parameter values of the
239	138:embedded generative-model calls; and (d) Learn, where verified parametric programs reduce the
240	139:constrained learning problem to an unconstrained optimization problem over model parameters,
241	140:enabling scalable gradient-based training without sacrificing correctness.
242	141:• We prove that SEVerA is sound: any synthesized agent satisfies the behavioral specification for all
243	142:inputs and parameter values (Theorem 5.7). We further show that, under sufficient conditions,
244	143:SEVerA can construct specification-compliant agents that match or exceed the utility of the
245	144:underlying GMs, and that FGGMs preserve the expressivity of transformer-based models.
246	145:• We evaluate SEVerA on tasks spanning LLM-assisted program verification, symbolic math syn-
247	146:thesis, agentic tool use, and constrained symbolic regression. Across all benchmarks, SEVerA
248	147:achieves provably zero constraint violations while outperforming state-of-the-art agents in task
249	148:performance: 97.0% verification rate on HumanEvalDafny (vs. 86.9% for the best baseline), 66.0%
250	149:accuracy on GSM-Symbolic (vs. 44.7% for the best constrained-decoding method), and 52.6% pass
251	150:rate on 𝜏2-bench’s airline domain using Qwen3-8B. Notably, on 𝜏2-bench airline SEVerA even
252	151:beats Agent-C [22] with Claude Sonnet 4.5, a state-of-the-art constrained agent using a frontier
253	152:model. These results show that behavioral constraints do not merely enforce safety but actively
254	153:prune the search space of candidate programs and steer synthesis toward higher-quality agents.
255	154:2

298	1349:Main Results
299	1350:We begin with the central question motivating SEVerA:
300	1351:RQ1 (Safety). What goes wrong without formal constraints, and does SEVerA eliminate these failures?
301	1352:We compare unconstrained agent synthesis against SEVerA across all four tasks to show that hard
302	1353:behavioral specifications are necessary: without them, agents silently produce invalid outputs on
303	1354:unseen inputs that are undetectable by soft performance metrics.

328	--CONCLUSION--
329	1793:Conclusion
330	1794:We presented SEVerA, a framework for specification-driven synthesis of self-evolving LLM agents
331	1795:with formal behavioral guarantees. Its core abstraction, the Formally Guarded Generative Model
332	1796:(FGGM), binds each generative-model call to a Hoare-style local contract enforced by a stateful
333	1797:rejection sampler with a verified fallback. Because the fallback discharges the contract for every
334	1798:parameter value, correctness is parameter-independent and survives arbitrary fine-tuning. This
335	1799:lets SEVerA split the constrained learning problem into four stages (ideation, search, verification,
336	1800:and learning), so that scalable methods such as GRPO can optimize task reward without putting
337	1801:the specification at risk. We proved that SEVerA is sound, gave a sufficient condition under which
338	1802:a verified agent matches or exceeds the reward of the best unconstrained model, and showed
339	1803:that FGGMs retain the expressivity of the underlying transformer. Across program verification,
340	1804:symbolic math synthesis, policy-compliant tool use, and constrained symbolic regression, SEVerA
341	1805:attains zero constraint violations on held-out inputs while improving task performance over both
342	1806:unconstrained frameworks and task-specific state of the art. These results suggest that behavioral
343	1807:specifications play a dual role: certifying compliance on all inputs and, by pruning shortcut-laden
344	1808:candidates, steering evolution toward higher-utility agents.

346	##### library/02_objective_factorization/2605.08327_InteractiveCritiqueRevision/2605.08327_InteractiveCritiqueRevision_fulltext.txt  (1275 lines)
347	--ABSTRACT--
348	23:Abstract
349	24:In structured decision-making workflows such as form filling, compliance check-
350	25:ing, and maintenance reporting, LLM outputs must be locally correct, globally
351	26:consistent, and auditable against task-specific rules. Existing refinement methods
352	27:often rely on heuristic debate, self-play, or LLM-generated supervision, creating a
353	28:second-order assurance problem. We propose DPA-GRPO (Dual Paired-Action
354	29:Group-Relative Policy Optimization), a paired-action training method for a two-
355	30:player generator–verifier game with structured verifier interventions. The generator
356	31:proposes outputs and may revise them when challenged; the verifier either remains
357	32:silent or raises a safety assurance case (SAC) containing a claim, argument, and
358	33:evidence. These SAC/no-SAC and KEEP/REVISE decisions induce paired coun-
359	34:terfactual action groups, which DPA-GRPO uses for role-specific KL-regularized
360	35:GRPO updates. We analyze the unregularized game and show that positive proba-
361	36:bility on strictly lower-reward intervention or revision actions creates a profitable
362	37:unilateral deviation. Under standard stochastic-approximation assumptions, DPA-
363	38:GRPO tracks the corresponding game ODE, whose isolated asymptotically stable
364	39:limit points are stationary and candidate local equilibria under role-wise local
365	40:optimality. Experiments on TaxCalcBench TY24 show that DPA-GRPO improves
366	41:structured decision accuracy over zero-shot generation and generator-only RL
367	42:baselines across Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B. Training increases correct silent accep-
368	43:tance, reduces missed errors, and improves calibrated revision behavior, indicating
369	44:gains for both generator and verifier.
370	45:1
371	46:Introduction
372	47:Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance on open-ended generation, reason-
373	48:ing, and tool-use tasks [Brown et al., 2020, Achiam et al., 2023, Wei et al., 2022, Yao et al., 2022,
374	49:Schick et al., 2023], yet their use in complex, structured decision-making workflows remains brittle.
375	50:In domains such as form filling, compliance checking, maintenance reporting, and program-like
376	51:reasoning, LLM outputs must be plausible, locally correct, globally consistent, and auditable against
377	52:required rules and standards [Ji et al., 2023, Huang et al., 2025, Cobbe et al., 2021, Lightman et al.,
378	53:2023]. Addressing this mismatch is crucial for high-stakes structured workflows.
379	54:Preprint.
380	55:arXiv:2605.08327v1  [cs.LG]  8 May 2026
381	56:
382	--INTRO END--
383	63:to directly verify or supervise other LLMs creates a second-order verification problem in which the
384	64:verifier itself requires assessment. A verifier rewarded for finding errors may produce persuasive
385	65:objections with weak grounding [Ji et al., 2023, Huang et al., 2025, Bai et al., 2022, Madaan et al.,
386	66:2023, Shinn et al., 2023]. A generator that follows verifier feedback uncritically may over-correct
387	67:accurate outputs. A generator that discounts useful feedback may preserve unsafe errors. Second,
388	68:multi-agent debate improves reasoning by allowing model instances to challenge one another. Existing
389	69:implementations often use debate as a prompting or test-time scaling mechanism rather than as a
390	70:role-specific training paradigm [Du et al., 2024, Khan et al., 2024a], without a systematic framework
391	71:to co-train or co-adapt all agents in concert [Cobbe et al., 2021, Lightman et al., 2023, Lifshitz et al.,
392	72:2025, Jung et al., 2026, Yu et al., 2025a]. Finally, recent work on self-play and competitive evaluation
393	73:methods shows promise for learning from game outcomes and inter-model competition, and leave
394	74:open safety-case-style assurance with respect to specific requirements and auditability [Kuba et al.,
395	75:2025, Alyahya et al., 2025, Liu et al., 2025, Liao et al., 2024]. The challenges to get AI agents to
396	76:agree are highlighted in [Berdoz et al., 2026].
397	77:We propose DPA-GRPO (Dual Paired-Action Group-Relative Policy Optimization), a game-theoretic
398	78:solution for safety-case-based assurance of structured LLM outputs. Game theory provides a mathe-
399	79:matical framework for analyzing strategic interaction between learning agents, and a well-designed
400	80:equilibrium pushes them toward desired collective behaviors. We train a two-player Markov game
401	81:[Shapley, 1953] between a generator and a verifier. The generator proposes solutions (e.g., form fill-
402	82:ing or multi-step planning) and may revise them when challenged. The verifier observes the proposed
403	83:solutions and chooses whether to remain silent or raise a safety assurance case (SAC) consisting of a
404	84:claim, argument, and evidence. This idea is closely related to a long tradition of safety certification.
405	85:Safety-critical engineering has long used safety cases: structured claim-argument-evidence records
406	86:that justify why a system satisfies required properties and is sufficiently safe for deployment [Kelly
407	87:and Weaver, 2004, Denney et al., 2015a, Dezfuli et al., 2015, Lincoln, 2012]. Such records are
408	88:attractive for LLM validation because they make objections interpretable: the verifier states a claim,
409	89:supports it with an argument, and grounds the argument in evidence. This structure provides a
410	90:structured interface for verifier challenges and generator revisions. A more detailed discussion of

452	--EXP SETUP--
453	610:Experimental Setup
454	611:Benchmark and evaluation units.
455	612:TaxCalcBench TY24 provides synthetic U.S. federal tax-form
456	613:instances with ground-truth Form 1040 outputs produced by a deterministic tax engine. We use a
457	614:fixed-seed 80/20 train/test split. Although each tax return contains many form fields, our evaluation
458	615:follows the benchmark protocol and scores 19 selected Form 1040 lines per case. A decision unit
459	616:corresponds to a structured output component, such as a form field or tax-form line, that can be
460	617:checked against the ground-truth Form 1040 output. We measure accuracy as the fraction of evaluated
461	618:decision units whose submitted value exactly matches the ground-truth value.
462	619:Models and methods.
463	620:We evaluate Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B backbones [Yang et al., 2025]. The
464	621:zero-shot baselines use the generator directly without parameter updates and without the verifier loop.
465	622:The trained single-agent baselines update only the generator using GRPO-style objectives, including
466	623:GRPO [Shao et al., 2024], DAPO [Yu et al., 2025b], and GSPO [Zheng et al., 2025]. These baselines
467	624:produce a single proposal for each decision unit and are evaluated by proposal correctness.

503	--LIMITATIONS--
504	990:Limitations and Broader Impact
505	991:DPA-GRPO is evaluated on TaxCalcBench TY24, a controlled benchmark with deterministic ground-
506	992:truth Form 1040 outputs. This setting is useful for studying verifiable structured decisions, but future
507	993:work should evaluate the method on additional domains with noisier, incomplete, or partially subjec-
508	994:tive supervision. Our theoretical analysis is local and relies on standard stochastic-approximation
509	995:and game-theoretic assumptions; it does not imply global convergence or guarantee that finite-step
510	996:LLM training reaches a Nash equilibrium. Empirically, performance may depend on model capacity,
511	997:reward design, SAC quality, and the frequency of useful revision opportunities.
512	998:The method also incurs additional computational cost relative to generator-only training because it
513	999:trains both a generator and a verifier and constructs paired counterfactual action groups. While LoRA
514	1000:adapters reduce this cost, scaling to larger models and longer workflows may require more efficient
515	1001:sampling and verifier-scoring strategies. From a broader-impact perspective, SACs can improve
516	1002:auditability by exposing claim-argument-evidence records, but they should not be interpreted as
517	1003:formal guarantees of correctness or safety. In high-stakes settings, outputs should remain subject to
518	1004:expert review and independent validation.

527	1013:Algorithm 1 DPA-GRPO training for the generator–verifier game.
528	--CONCLUSION--
529	767:Conclusion
530	768:We proposed DPA-GRPO, a two-player generator-verifier framework for verifiable assurance reason-
531	769:ing in structured LLM workflows. By representing verifier feedback as safety assurance cases and
532	770:converting intervention/revision decisions into paired counterfactual actions, DPA-GRPO provides
533	771:training signals for both agents while preserving interpretability. Our analysis connects the induced
534	772:case taxonomy to local Nash equilibrium conditions and stochastic-approximation dynamics. Experi-
535	773:ments on TaxCalcBench TY24 show that DPA-GRPO improves structured decision accuracy over
536	774:zero-shot generation and generator-only RL baselines across Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B backbones.
537	775:The decision-unit taxonomy further shows that training increases correct silent acceptance, reduces
538	776:missed errors, and improves calibrated responses to verifier interventions. These results suggest that
539	777:structured verifier interventions can serve not only as explanations, but also as actionable training
540	778:signals for improving both generator and verifier behavior.

546	##### library/02_objective_factorization/2605.23382_PARPO/2605.23382_PARPO_fulltext.txt  (3597 lines)
547	--ABSTRACT--
548	18:Abstract
549	19:Agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL) has achieved strong progress in tasks
550	20:with clear success signals. However, many real-world agent applications require
551	21:user-conditioned behavior: the same query may call for different planning strategies
552	22:and tool-use decisions across users. This setting raises key challenges: generic
553	23:rewards cannot capture heterogeneous user preferences, observed behaviors are
554	24:entangled with conformity effects, and flat memories cannot support personal-
555	25:ized skill retrieval. To this end, we propose a unified personalized Agentic RL
556	26:framework that embeds personalization into training-time optimization. At its
557	27:core is Personalized Anchor Reward-Decoupled Policy Optimization (PARPO),
558	28:which decouples generic task-quality rewards from personalized preference re-
559	29:wards and uses user-specific anchors to stabilize learning under heterogeneous
560	30:reward scales. We further introduce a two-stage preference-disentangled reward
561	31:model and Preference-Aligned Skill Evolution Graph Memory (PSGM) for per-
562	32:sonalized supervision and preference-aligned skill retrieval. Together, they form a
563	33:closed loop of preference identification, policy optimization, and structured skill
564	34:accumulation. Experiments on ETAPP, ETAPP-Hard, and SJAgent show that our
565	35:framework consistently outperforms strong memory and RL baselines. Code and
566	36:data are included in the supplementary materials.
567	37:1
568	38:Introduction
569	39:Large language model (LLM)-based agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL) has emerged as
570	40:a powerful paradigm for optimizing LLM agents, achieving strong performance in code genera-
571	41:tion [Gehring et al., 2025, Le et al., 2022, Yang et al., 2024], web navigation [Nakano et al., 2021,
572	42:Qi et al., 2025], tool use [Qian et al., 2026, Feng et al., 2026a, Xia et al., 2026], and long-horizon
573	43:planning [Tang et al., 2026, Peng et al., 2026, Xi et al., 2026]. However, most of this progress
574	44:has been made in verifiable settings [Qian et al., 2026, Jin et al., 2025, Shao et al., 2024], where
575	45:policy optimization can rely on a unique ground-truth answer. In contrast, in many real-world agent
576	46:applications—such as e-commerce assistance, travel planning, and daily scheduling [Skarlinski
577	47:et al., 2024, Schmidgall et al., 2024, Ning et al., 2025, Xie et al., 2024, Lyu et al., 2026]—this
578	48:verifiability breaks down because optimal behavior is user-dependent: the same query may admit
579	49:multiple plausible trajectories, with the preferred one determined by the user’s preferences, habits,
580	50:and constraints.
581	51:Recent work has begun to extend LLM optimization beyond strictly verifiable tasks. Non-verifiable
582	--INTRO END--
583	79:the same trajectory, nor can they handle heterogeneous reward scales across users. (C2) Personalized
584	80:preference disentanglement: observed user behaviors are often shaped by both intrinsic interests
585	81:and external conformity or contextual effects, making individualized preference signals noisy and
586	82:difficult to identify accurately. (C3) User-aware memory and skill organization: existing agent
587	83:memories are often flat and query-centric, and thus cannot explicitly model or retrieve the structured
588	84:relations among users, intents, skills, tools, scenarios, and trajectories.
589	85:To bridge this gap, we propose a unified personalized Agentic RL framework that embeds personaliza-
590	86:tion into the training-time optimization loop. At its core is Personalized Anchor Reward-Decoupled
591	87:Policy Optimization (PARPO), which decouples generic task-quality rewards from personalized pref-
592	88:erence rewards and uses user-specific anchors to stabilize learning under heterogeneous reward scales.
593	89:PARPO preserves general task competence while enabling user-contingent policy improvement. To
594	90:provide cleaner personalized supervision, we develop a two-stage preference-disentangled reward
595	91:model that separates intrinsic interests from conformity and contextual effects. To support personal-
596	92:ized rollout context, we introduce Preference-Aligned Skill Evolution Graph Memory (PSGM), an
597	93:evolving heterogeneous graph memory that organizes users, skills, tools, scenarios, and trajectories
598	94:for preference-aligned skill retrieval. Together, these components form a closed loop of preference
599	95:identification, personalized policy optimization, and structured skill accumulation. Our contributions
600	96:are summarized as follows:
601	97:• We formulate personalized Agentic RL for user-conditioned agent tasks, where optimal behavior
602	98:depends on individual preferences.
603	99:• We propose PARPO, an anchor-stabilized and reward-decoupled policy optimization method for
604	100:learning personalized policies under heterogeneous user reward scales.
605	101:• We introduce a preference-disentangled reward model and PSGM to provide reliable personalized
606	102:supervision and preference-aligned skill retrieval.
607	103:• We evaluate our framework on ETAPP [Hao et al., 2025], ETAPP-Hard, and SJAgent (a real-world
608	104:industrial agent training scenario from a large Chinese e-commerce platform), showing gains in
609	105:personalization and procedural quality while maintaining factual and logical quality.
610	106:2
611	--METHOD--
612	316:Method
613	317:To address the challenge of personalized decision-making in user-conditioned tasks, we propose a
614	318:unified Agentic RL framework. As illustrated in Figure 2, the framework operates as a closed loop of
615	319:personalized retrieval, generation, evaluation, and refinement. Given a user query and profile, the
616	320:framework first retrieves relevant historical skills from a graph-based memory to form a personalized
617	321:rollout context. Conditioned on this enriched context, the LLM-based policy interacts with the
618	322:environment to generate decision-making trajectories. These trajectories are then evaluated by a
619	323:dual-reward system: a general task-quality reward and a personalized preference reward. Finally, the
620	324:policy is updated using these decoupled signals, and high-value trajectories are consolidated back
621	325:into memory as reusable skills.
622	326:In the following, we first introduce the core of our framework—the policy optimization algorithm
623	327:(PARPO, §4.1). We then detail the two supporting modules that make this optimization possible: the
624	328:personalized reward model that provides user-conditioned signals (§4.2), and the skill graph memory
625	329:that structures the rollout context (§4.3).
626	330:4.1
627	331:PARPO: Personalized Anchor Reward-Decoupled Policy Optimization
628	332:We now introduce the policy optimizer in our framework. PARPO separates task quality from
629	333:personalized alignment, allowing the policy to improve user-specific behavior without entangling
630	334:it with shared supervision. In implementation, PARPO is instantiated as a dual-track GRPO-style
631	335:advantage estimator built on the personalized reward model in Section 4.2 and the graph memory in
632	336:Section 4.3.
633	337:Theoretical justification.
634	338:Appendix C shows that under heterogeneous user preferences, personal-
635	339:ized optimization is preferable to user-agnostic optimization, while standard GRPO incurs structural
636	340:bias from pooled baselines and normalization. The analysis yields three conclusions. First, under
637	341:heterogeneous user preferences, user-aware optimization is never worse than user-agnostic optimiza-
638	342:tion: when different users prefer different trajectories for the same query, a single average-optimal
639	343:policy necessarily compromises across users. Second, standard GRPO introduces structural bias in
640	344:personalized settings because it uses pooled baselines and pooled normalization statistics. As a result,
641	345:its advantage estimate can deviate from the true user-specific advantage due to both reward-center
642	346:mismatch and reward-scale mismatch, with the dominant error controlled by cross-user preference
643	347:heterogeneity. Third, PARPO reduces this bias by decoupling generic task-quality rewards from
644	348:personalized preference rewards and calibrating the personalized branch with user-specific anchors.
645	349:4
646	350:

648	352:=== PAGE 5 ===
649	353:============================================================
650	354:

655	645:Experimental Setup
656	646:5.1.1
657	647:Baselines
658	648:We compare against prompting, memory, RL, and memory-RL baselines, including REACT, MEM0,
659	649:GRPO, DAPO, GSPO, GIGPO, MEMRL, and SKILLRL. We also report GPT-4o and Claude
660	650:Sonnet 4 as closed-source references. All open-source methods are evaluated under the same model
661	651:scales, task settings, and tool interfaces whenever applicable. We further include a GDPO-style
662	652:variant in the ablation study, which removes PARPO’s user-anchor calibration while keeping the
663	653:same personalized reward and memory components. For baselines in personalized environments, we
664	654:additionally provide the native personalization reward to ensure fair comparison.
665	655:5.1.2
666	656:Benchmarks, Evaluation, and Training Details
667	657:We evaluate on ETAPP and SJAgent. ETAPP is a public benchmark for personal assistant agents,
668	658:covering user behaviors in daily-life scenarios; we further construct a more challenging split, ETAPP-
669	659:Hard. SJAgent is a realistic environment for merchant decision-making and recommendation, built
670	660:from merchant data on a major Chinese e-commerce platform. Environment details are provided in
671	661:Appendix D.2, and the construction pipeline of ETAPP-Hard is given in Appendix D.3.
672	662:For ETAPP, we report Judge, Personal, Proactive, and Procedure. For SJAgent, we report Reward,
673	663:Data Authenticity, Business Logic, Merchant Profile Match, Task Completion, and Market Anal-
674	664:ysis Depth. Metric definitions, official evaluation prompts, and scoring criteria are provided in
675	665:Appendix D.4, and training hyperparameters are listed in Appendix D.5.
676	666:5.2
677	667:Main Results on Personalized Decision-Making Benchmarks
678	668:Table 1 reports results on ETAPP, ETAPP-Hard, and SJAgent. Our method achieves the best overall
679	669:performance under both 4B and 8B settings and outperforms all open-source baselines on most
680	670:metrics. On ETAPP and ETAPP-Hard, it obtains the highest judge scores, with larger gains on
681	671:ETAPP-Hard, indicating stronger robustness in challenging personalized scenarios. It also performs
682	672:best on Personal, Proactive, and Procedure, showing better preference alignment and decision quality.
683	673:On SJAgent, our method again achieves the highest Reward and leads on key dimensions including
684	674:Data Authenticity, Business Logic, Task Completion, and Market Analysis Depth, demonstrating
685	675:strong cross-domain generalization.
686	676:5.3
687	677:Ablation Study
688	678:Table 2 reports ablation results on ETAPP. A1 removes skill memory, and A2 replaces PSGM with
689	679:the original flat skill pipeline. Within PSGM, B1 removes hierarchical communities, B2 replaces
690	680:Leiden with Louvain, B3 disables dynamic graph updates, and B4 replaces dense retrieval with BM25.
691	681:Within reward learning, C1 replaces PARPO with GRPO, C2/C3 remove the base/personalized reward

704	1575:Conclusion and Limitations
705	1576:This work studied personalized Agentic RL for user-conditioned tasks, where optimal behavior
706	1577:depends on user preferences rather than a single correct answer. We proposed a unified framework
707	1578:centered on PARPO, which decouples general-quality and personalized rewards and stabilizes training
708	1579:with user-specific anchors. Experiments on ETAPP, ETAPP-Hard, and SJAgent showed consistent
709	1580:and significant gains in personalization while preserving overall task quality, highlighting the value
710	1581:of training-time personalized optimization for user-centric agents. A key limitation of this work is
711	1582:the scale of the human evaluation: due to annotation cost and limited expert availability, we reported
712	1583:judgments from only 15 experts on 20 randomly sampled examples. Although these results broadly
713	1584:agree with the LLM evaluations, future work should expand the human study to a larger and more
714	1585:diverse pool of annotators and evaluation instances to better assess robustness, generalizability, and
715	1586:real-world validity.

216	--ABSTRACT--
217	10:Abstract
218	11:Following complex instructions with multiple
219	12:explicit constraints remains a fundamental chal-
220	13:lenge for large language models (LLMs). Ex-
221	14:isting alignment methods, such as DPO, opti-
222	15:mize holistic reward signals that often under-
223	16:emphasize strict satisfaction of individual con-
224	17:straints, particularly under out-of-distribution
225	18:or multi-constraint settings.
226	19:In this paper,
227	20:we propose STAIF, a stage-wise optimization
228	21:framework that decouples the alignment of sub-
229	22:jective (soft) constraints from the optimiza-
230	23:tion of objectively verifiable (hard) constraints.
231	24:Stage 1 applies preference optimization with
232	25:multiple negative samples to sharpen the sen-
233	26:sitivity to soft constraints, while Stage 2 ap-
234	27:plies Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable
235	28:Rewards (RLVR) to enforce strict compliance
236	29:with hard constraints. To support this method,
237	30:we construct STAINSTRUCT, a high-quality
238	31:bilingual (English, Chinese) dataset of approx-
239	32:imately 31,000 complex multi-constraint in-
240	33:structions. Extensive analyses validate the de-
241	34:sign of STAIF and show state-of-the-art perfor-
242	35:mance on representative benchmarks against
243	36:strong baselines, as well as genuine generaliza-
244	37:tion. We have released our code and dataset1.

429	1327:Conclusion
430	1328:We propose STAIF, a stage-wise framework that
431	1329:separates soft-constraint alignment from hard-
432	1330:constraint optimization, combining preference
433	1331:learning with multiple negative samples and RL
434	1332:with verifiable rewards. We also construct STAIN-
435	1333:STRUCT, a large-scale bilingual dataset of complex
436	1334:multi-constraint instructions, under an automated
437	1335:complex-constraint data synthesis framework.
438	1336:Our methodology achieve SoTA performance
439	1337:on representative benchmarks with different lan-
440	1338:guages and constraint distributions, demonstrating
441	1339:the efficacy of STAIF and the potential of RL in
442	1340:complex instruction following. In future work, we
443	1341:plan to explore further methodology and data en-

447	--ABSTRACT--
448	1:
449	2:============================================================
450	3:=== PAGE 1 ===
451	4:============================================================
452	5:
453	6:Don’t Mix Rewards, Mix Policies:
454	7:Policy Decomposition and Optimization for
455	8:Multi-Reward RL
456	9:Ruiming Liang1,2,3,∗,‡, Yi Zhong3,4,∗,‡, Yizhen Yuan3, Yinan Zheng3, Tianyi Tan3,
457	10:Tianyue Wang1,2, Haiyun Guo1,�, Jinqiao Wang1, Xianyuan Zhan3,�
458	11:1Fundation Model Research Center, CASIA, 2School of Artificial Intelligence, UCAS, 3Institute for
459	12:AI Industry Research (AIR), Tsinghua University, 4College of Automotive and Energy Engineering
460	13:(CAEE), Tongji University
461	14:∗Equal contribution, �Corresponding authors, ‡Work done during internship at THU-AIR
462	15:Modern large language models (LLMs) are expected not just to answer correctly, but to adapt their
463	16:behavior to different human values and use cases. As a result, multi-reward reinforcement learning (RL)
464	17:has become an increasingly important problem for LLMs, where each reward captures a different aspect
465	18:of desired behavior. However, optimizing with multiple rewards suffers from a more severe alignment
466	19:tax issue, where different optimization objectives can trade off or even conflict with each other, leading
467	20:to unstable and inefficient post-training. In this work, we propose PRISM , a new multi-reward RL
468	21:framework built upon the idea of policy-space decomposition and composition. Instead of compositing
469	22:different rewards, PRISM optimizes a set of standalone positive policies and a global negative
470	23:policy. This alleviates the potential conflict during multi-reward policy optimization, while enabling
471	24:controllability during inference by flexible policy composition. Experiments on scientific reasoning,
472	25:tool-use reasoning, and helpfulness–safety alignment show that PRISM consistently outperforms
473	26:existing multi-reward RL baselines, with extra controllability for inference-time preference control.
474	27:Emails: liangruiming2024@ia.ac.cn, zhanxianyuan@air.tsinghua.edu.cn
475	28:1
476	29:Introduction
477	30:Large language models [2, 19] are widely deployed as general-purpose assistants, making alignment with
478	31:human intent a central concern [4, 13]. Reinforcement learning [35] is among the most effective tools for this
479	32:purpose, optimizing LLMs directly against reward signals that encode human preferences [5, 23]. Yet human
480	33:preferences are rarely captured by a single objective: users expect models to be helpful, safe, and honest at
481	34:the same time [21, 39], and these goals often conflict, so improving one dimension costs another [18, 23, 42].
482	--INTRO END--
483	54:
484	55:multi-reward alignment tax.
485	56:We therefore introduce PRISM , a multi-reward RL algorithm built on a different philosophy: do not mix
486	57:rewards, mix policies. As shown in Figure 1, PRISM learns one standalone positive policy per reward and
487	58:a single global negative policy. Desirable behaviors are reward-specific and deserve dedicated optimization
488	59:directions. In contrast, undesirable behaviors need not be attributed to individual rewards. A single negative
489	60:policy captures the union of all reward-specific failure modes and penalizes them jointly. Each reward drives
490	61:updates mainly through its own positive branch. This design alleviates gradient competition among conflicting
491	62:preferences and mitigates the multi-reward alignment tax.
492	63:For efficiency, all sub-policies share a single language model conditioned on different prefix tokens and are
493	64:composed at sampling time via a weighted sum of logits; the same mixture policy serves both training rollouts
494	65:and inference. The merge weights thus form an explicit, interpretable interface for preference trade-offs,
495	66:adjustable at inference time without retraining.
496	67:Experiments on three multi-reward settings show that PRISM consistently outperforms reward-space baselines.
497	68:On GPQA [30] and ScienceQA [32], it achieves the best overall score on every backbone, surpassing the
498	69:strongest baseline by 17.8, 8.0, and 0.6 points on DeepSeek-R1-1.5B [34], Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-
499	70:3B-Instruct [37].
500	71:On the tool-calling benchmark BFCL-v3 [24] and the helpfulness–safety benchmarks
501	72:Alpaca [36], HH-RLHF [10], and PKU-SafeRLHF [6], it ranks first among all RL methods, and remains more
502	73:robust and controllable as reward complexity grows.
503	74:Our contributions are threefold:
504	75:• We identify the multi-reward alignment tax induced by reward-space composition, and advocate composing
505	76:preferences in policy space instead.
506	77:• We propose PRISM , which decomposes multi-reward RL into per-reward positive policies and a global
507	78:negative policy, realized via prefix-conditioned sub-policies with logit-level composition.
508	79:• Experiments on scientific QA, tool-use reasoning, and helpfulness–safety alignment show consistent gains
509	80:over strong baselines, with training-free inference-time controllability.
510	81:2

520	90:format compliance. The native multi-reward objective is the system of N coupled maximization problems

634	--LIMITATIONS--
635	1696:Limitations
636	1697:There are several limitations in this study. First, PRISM assumes that each reward can be represented by a
637	1698:distinct positive policy. It also assumes that a single negative policy can capture the union of reward-specific
638	1699:failure modes. This design is effective across all our experimental settings, which cover up to three rewards.
639	1700:Validating it at substantially larger reward counts is left for future work. Second, the current policy-space
640	1701:composition relies on manually specified merge weights, and how to automatically adapt these weights to
641	1702:different prompts, users, or deployment contexts remains underexplored. Third, although per-token latency
642	1703:stays that of a single forward pass, mixture decoding requires multiple prefix-conditioned branches, and
643	1704:its memory and FLOPs scale with the number of rewards. Future work can study more adaptive policy
644	1705:composition mechanisms, more expressive negative-policy designs, and more efficient decoding strategies.
645	1706:21
646	--CONCLUSION--
647	1122:Conclusion
648	1123:In this work, we propose PRISM , a policy-space composition framework for multi-reward LLM alignment.
649	1124:Instead of scalarizing heterogeneous rewards into a single optimization signal, PRISM keeps each reward
650	1125:as a separate optimization direction by learning one positive policy per reward. A single global negative
651	1126:policy further captures the union of failure modes. These policies are composed through explicit merge
652	1127:weights, enabling controllable preference trade-offs without retraining. Experiments on scientific reasoning,
653	1128:tool-use reasoning, and helpfulness–safety alignment show that PRISM consistently outperforms reward-space
654	1129:baselines, remains more robust as reward complexity increases, and supports effective inference-time preference
655	1130:control. These results suggest that mixing policies rather than rewards offers a more effective and controllable
656	1131:path toward multi-reward aligned language models.

665	--ABSTRACT--
666	15:Abstract
667	16:Reinforcement learning fine-tuning of large
668	17:language models increasingly adopts multi-
669	18:ple reward dimensions, including verifiable
670	19:rules, task-specific evaluators, and learned re-
671	20:ward models, to provide richer supervision
672	21:across diverse capabilities. These dimensions
673	22:are commonly scalarized with fixed aggrega-
674	23:tion weights. We identify a failure mode in
675	24:which aggregation itself induces reward hack-
676	25:ing: static projection aliases qualitatively differ-
677	26:ent reward profiles into a single scalar, steering
678	27:optimization toward whichever dimensions are
679	28:easiest, densest, or systematically favored by
680	29:the reward signal. Over training, this traps the
681	30:policy in suboptimal profiles and prevents con-
682	31:vergence to better-balanced ones that would
683	32:yield higher task performance. To address this,
684	33:we propose Adaptive Multi-Reward Projection
685	34:(AMRP), a lightweight online method that re-
686	35:allocates aggregation weights using three sig-
687	36:nals—relative shortfall, reward volatility, and
688	37:recent progress—increasing pressure on lag-
689	38:ging, unstable, or stagnant dimensions while
690	39:relieving saturated ones.
691	40:Across structured
692	41:reasoning, citation-grounded generation, and
693	42:open-ended alignment under GRPO, AMRP
694	43:consistently improves reward-profile balance
695	44:and downstream performance over fixed and
696	45:dynamic weighting baselines; it also remains
697	46:effective with GDPO and PPO, supporting
698	47:compatibility across RL algorithms.
699	48:Our
700	--INTRO END--
701	129:across three different multi-reward settings: rule-
702	130:based mathematical reasoning, citation-grounded
703	131:generation with automatic evaluators, and open-
704	132:ended alignment with learned reward-model scores.
705	133:AMRP consistently improves downstream perfor-
706	134:mance and reward-profile dynamics, with partic-
707	135:ularly large gains in mathematical reasoning and
708	136:citation-grounded generation and consistent gains
709	137:in the more correlated open-ended setting. We fur-
710	138:ther show that AMRP composes effectively with
711	139:GDPO and PPO and remains robust across the
712	140:tested hyperparameter ranges.
713	141:Our contributions can be summarized as:
714	142:• We identify reward-profile collapse as a mode
715	143:of aggregation-induced reward hacking in
716	144:multi-reward reinforcement learning, arising
717	145:from profile aliasing and shortcut lock-in.
718	146:• We propose Adaptive Multi-Reward Projec-
719	147:tion, a dynamic aggregation method that
720	148:adapts reward projection online according to
721	149:three signals: relative shortfall, reward volatil-
722	150:ity, and recent progress.
723	151:• We validate AMRP across structured reason-
724	152:ing, citation-grounded generation, and open-
725	153:ended alignment with multiple backbones,
726	154:showing consistent downstream gains and
727	155:compatibility with GRPO, GDPO, and PPO.

82	196:i-th constraint; in realistic scenarios |C| is rarely

233	--ABSTRACT--
234	1:
235	2:============================================================
