238	5:
239	6:CM-DPO: Constraint-Margin Direct Preference
240	7:Optimization for LLM Planning
241	8:Rabimba Karanjai1, Qun Gu1, Hemanth Hegadehalli Madhavarao1, Wenhuan Sun1, Xiaojiao Yu1,
242	9:Suryabhan Singh Hada1, Libin N. George1, Uma Kona1, Richard Williamson1, Linsey Pang1, Prakhar
243	10:Mehrotra1
244	11:1PayPal AI Lab
245	12:rkaranjai@paypal.com
246	13:Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) treats all constraint violations equally: a $1 budget overshoot
247	14:and a $1,000 overshoot induce the same training signal. It is also susceptible to length and style
248	15:bias when preference pairs come from different model families. We introduce Constraint-Margin
249	16:DPO (CM-DPO), which replaces DPO’s binary preference signal with a continuous margin derived
250	17:from a deterministic symbolic verifier and scaled by violation severity. Hard and soft constraints are
251	18:separated through a lexicographic objective, ensuring hard constraints are never traded off against
252	19:preferences. To supply CM-DPO with bias-reduced training pairs, we generate preference data through
253	20:procedurally generated constraint profiles (DCCG) and minimal-edit distillation from a reasoning
254	21:teacher (RT-MED), within a framework we call SynPlan-R. On TravelPlanner, NaturalPlan, and
255	22:out-of-distribution PlanBench, an 8B model fine-tuned with CM-DPO achieves 89.2% pass rate and
256	23:93.4% solve rate, matching multi-agent systems at 13× lower latency while outperforming GPT-4o on
257	24:unseen Blocksworld by 9.2 points.
258	25:Date October 2026
259	26:1
260	27:Introduction
261	28:The deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) is increasingly shifting from open-ended conversa-
262	29:tional generation toward agentic workflows that require precise, long-horizon planning under complex con-
263	30:straints Valmeekam et al. (2023); Xie et al. (2024). Real-world planning queries are rarely governed by a single
264	31:homogeneous rule set; instead, they combine hard functional constraints, such as budget ceilings, temporal
265	32:non-overlap, and capacity limits, that must be satisfied without exception, with soft user preferences, such
266	33:as preferred carriers, dining cuisines, and proximity to landmarks, that should be optimized but may be
267	34:relaxed. A user requesting “a weekend trip under $500 that avoids red-eye flights, preferably with boutique
268	--INTRO END--
269	36:preference. Standard LLMs often conflate these two categories, producing plans that are semantically fluent
270	37:but either violate hard constraints or unnecessarily sacrifice soft-constraint preferences Xie et al. (2024).
271	38:We characterize this failure landscape as a Planning Trilemma among three constraints:
272	39:• Accuracy: strict, verifiable satisfaction of all hard constraints and best-effort adherence to soft preferences.
273	40:• Efficiency: sub-second, single-pass inference compatible with real-time deployment.
274	41:• Controllability: responsiveness to dynamic, per-query constraint profiles without retraining.
275	42:Existing methods typically satisfy at most two of these three criteria. We propose a unified data-synthesis
276	43:and alignment framework with the following contributions:
277	44:1. Dynamic Contextual Constraint Graphs (DCCG): A formal representation that decomposes planning problems
278	45:into parameterized hard and soft constraint profiles over procedurally generated knowledge bases (synthetic
279	46:flight and hotel databases with randomized prices and schedules). DCCG reduces the risk of domain
280	47:memorization and encourages the model to learn transferable combinatorial reasoning (§3).
281	48:1
282	49:arXiv:2610.09219v1  [cs.AI]  6 Oct 2026
283	50:
284	51:============================================================
285	52:=== PAGE 2 ===
286	53:============================================================
287	54:
288	55:2. Reasoning-TraceMinimal-EditDistillation(RT-MED): A teacher–student synthesis pipeline in which a reasoning
289	56:model (DeepSeek-R1, o3-mini) corrects a flawed student draft through the minimum necessary semantic
290	57:edits, isolating the logical “gradient” from stylistic noise and mitigating the length bias inherent in full-rewrite
291	58:distillation (§4).
292	59:3. Constraint-Margin Preference Optimization (CM-DPO): An extension of DPO that injects a continuous
293	60:penalty margin into the preference loss, scaled by the deterministic severity of hard-constraint violations
294	61:computed by a symbolic verifier. Soft-constraint adherence is incorporated as a lexicographic secondary
295	62:objective, ensuring that hard constraints are never traded off against preference satisfaction (§5).

369	--LIMITATIONS--
370	745:Limitations
371	746:The method depends on a symbolic verifier, so extending it to open-world environments where constraints
372	747:cannot be checked deterministically remains an open problem. Budget violations account for the largest
373	748:share of TravelPlanner errors (36.8%), suggesting that implicit arithmetic remains a bottleneck for longer
374	749:plans. Preliminary experiments with Qwen3-8B in thinking mode suggest that reasoning-enabled base models
375	750:further reduce budget violations under SynPlan-R; however, we exclude these results to avoid confounding
376	751:comparisons between thinking and non-thinking inference regimes. Teacher-guided data synthesis incurs
377	752:nontrivial cost (approximately $320 for 15K pairs), so larger-scale deployment may require more efficient
378	753:self-play strategies. Finally, we have not tested whether the same gains transfer to substantially smaller or
379	754:larger model scales.
380	755:9
381	756:Conclusion
382	757:We introduced Constraint-Margin DPO (CM-DPO), a preference-optimization objective that replaces DPO’s
383	758:binary signal with a continuous, verifier-derived margin scaled by hard-constraint violation severity, together
384	759:with a lexicographic secondary objective for soft preferences. To supply CM-DPO with bias-reduced training
385	760:pairs, we developed DCCG for procedural constraint-profile generation and RT-MED for minimal-edit
386	761:distillation from a reasoning teacher. Experiments on TravelPlanner, NaturalPlan, and out-of-distribution
387	762:PlanBench show that the resulting 8B model approaches multi-agent accuracy at a fraction of the latency,
388	763:and that severity-aware preference optimization transfers to unseen planning domains.

395	##### library/02_objective_factorization/2610.19525_RewardHackingVerifiableIF/2610.19525_RewardHackingVerifiableIF_fulltext.txt  (1448 lines)
396	--ABSTRACT--
397	16:ABSTRACT
398	17:Verifiable instruction-following benchmarks emphasize output-constraint satisfac-
399	18:tion but can overlook whether responses meaningfully answer the underlying re-
400	19:quest, creating an evaluation blind spot. We show that frontier models can re-
401	20:ceive full credit for responses with little substantive answer content. Using the
402	21:same verifier-based criterion as a training reward can induce reward hacking, as
403	22:publicly released checkpoints exhibit higher constraint satisfaction but lower re-
404	23:sponse quality after reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. To address
405	24:this reward hacking, we introduce CALIF, a lightweight method that augments
406	25:verifier rewards with a calibrated likelihood-based bonus to preserve response
407	26:quality. CALIF evaluates response likelihood under the request alone using the
408	27:existing frozen reference policy, requiring no additional judge or learned reward
409	28:model. Across models ranging from 1.7B to 8B in reasoning and non-reasoning
410	29:modes, CALIF improves constraint satisfaction on IFBench while maintaining
411	30:response quality near or above pre-RL levels. It also outperforms correspond-
412	31:ing base policies in 40 of 45 model–metric comparisons across three rubric-based
413	32:instruction-following benchmarks, demonstrating gains beyond training verifiers.
414	33:1
415	34:INTRODUCTION
416	35:Instruction following is central to the practical use of large language models (LLMs), enabling them
417	36:to translate user intent into desired outputs (Ouyang et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023; Chung et al.,
418	37:2024). In real-world applications, a user input typically comprises a request, which specifies the
419	38:task to be performed, and one or more constraints, which define the conditions the response must
420	39:satisfy (Jiang et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2024; He et al., 2024; 2026). Successful instruction following
421	40:therefore requires both high Response Quality by providing a substantive answer to the request
422	41:and high Constraint Satisfaction by adhering to the stated constraints. However, achieving both
423	42:objectives consistently remains challenging even for highly capable models (Zhang et al., 2025).
424	43:Evaluating instruction following for open-ended user inputs heavily relies on human assessment or
425	44:LLM judgments, which can be costly, subjective, and sensitive to the choice of evaluator (Zheng
426	45:et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024; Thakur et al., 2025). Verifiable instruction-following
427	46:(VIF) benchmarks (Zhou et al., 2023; He et al., 2024) address these evaluation challenges by fo-
428	47:cusing on requirements that can be checked programmatically. IFBench (Pyatkin et al., 2025), for
429	48:example, appends output constraints to a request and measures Constraint Satisfaction using pro-
430	49:grammatic verifiers, enabling scalable and reproducible evaluation without relying on LLM judges.
431	--INTRO END--

450	218:achieves a high Response Quality score of 9.33 when given the request alone, but its constrained
451	219:response includes exactly five numbers as required while scoring only 2.00 in Response Quality.
452	220:RLVR, which indicates that CALIF learns to satisfy constraints with substantially less degradation
453	221:in its answers to the request. Importantly, these gains generalize to three rubric-based instruction-
454	222:following benchmarks, where CALIF outperforms baselines in 40 of 45 model–metric comparisons,
455	223:versus only 14 of 45 for IF-RLVR. These results demonstrate that CALIF’s reference-calibrated
456	224:reward provides an effective signal for mitigating reward hacking in IF-RLVR without any additional
457	225:models or explicit supervision. CALIF thus brings the scalability of verifiable rewards to the full
458	226:objective of instruction following: satisfying constraints while adequately answering the request.

551	--ABSTRACT--
552	13:Abstract
553	14:Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve an agent’s task capability while reinforcing
554	15:violations of explicitly stated contextual requirements, even when reward accurately
555	16:measures useful work. We study this reward-driven misalignment through verifiable
556	17:reward–context conflicts, where compliant completion is feasible but executable violations
557	18:earn more reward than every compliant strategy.
558	19:Encoding these conflicts in task
559	20:dynamics supports scalable environment construction and compliance feedback from
560	21:execution histories. In resource and reporting workflows, task optimization increases real
561	22:productivity through unauthorized resource use or raises reported scores while actual
562	23:work declines. We observe both amplification of existing violations and the emergence of
563	24:violations on tasks where none were observed before training. Controlled changes in the
564	25:training distribution show that minority conflict exposure can still lead to widespread
565	26:shortcut acquisition, reaching 97.9% certified profitable violations on an API task under
566	27:a 25% conflict mixture after 128 updates. The same contextual checks supply a simple
567	28:binary penalty that supports joint capability and compliance gains and partially mitigates
568	29:acquired violations. Learned safety adapts to expanded authorization and transfers across
569	30:mechanisms into workflows with evolving evidence and approval requirements. On 32
570	31:unseen changing-evidence tasks, resource-trained safety increases safe completion from
571	32:53.1% to 89.1% relative to task-only training, while both policies achieve full real work.
572	33:These results connect a verifiable account of reward-driven misalignment with scalable
573	34:task construction and safety learning that remains useful under changing execution
574	35:requirements.
575	36:1
576	37:Introduction
577	38:Capable and reliable language-model agents are increasingly expected to repair software, schedule resources,
578	39:and complete complex workflows over long horizons while following human requirements. To develop these
579	40:capabilities, reinforcement learning (RL) commonly uses task reward based on the quality or amount of
580	41:work accomplished at the end of an episode, providing a direct, scalable training signal across diverse
581	42:tasks [1–3]. However, whether the work meets human expectations also depends on the context in which
582	43:it is carried out [4]. This context includes user intent, interaction history, and specific constraints such as
583	44:authorization or organizational rules, which determine which actions are appropriate and which constraints
584	45:apply [5–7]. Following these contextual requirements becomes more challenging as execution horizons
585	46:grow [8]. Agents must continue to respect resource permissions and preserve evaluation requirements
586	--INTRO END--
587	1184:occur. It is also how we assess mitigation. Early work on agent-assisted monitoring and investigation
588	1185:offers a way to share this work with models [21]. Our methodological commitment is to make the
589	1186:resulting evidence verifiable. An opaque LLM-judge verdict can leave it unclear which action violated
590	1187:which requirement, and why. Fixed work requirements, observable state changes, historical checks, and
591	1188:executable counterexamples give a reviewer evidence they can inspect and correct.
592	1189:Contextual safety is a trainable direction. A shaped terminal reward combines task performance with
593	1190:a history-based violation penalty. Training on this scalar feedback supports useful compliance under
594	1191:changed authorization, extending to workflows with evolving evidence and approval requirements. In
595	1192:environments with feasible compliant completion and a verified reward–context conflict, this objective
596	1193:creates pressure to anticipate and respect requirements during productive execution without prescribing a
597	1194:step-by-step safety strategy. These results motivate the conjecture that contextual safety awareness can
598	1195:be learned and inherited as part of task competence.
599	1196:This form of RL-induced misalignment can arise without an attacker: ordinary task feedback can reinforce
600	1197:violations even when requirements are given, while the policy does more genuine work.
601	1198:Reasoning
602	1199:over explicit safety specifications [22] and attack and defense methods [10] address different problem
603	1200:formulations. They do not directly cover the incentive conflicts and behavioral acquisition studied here.
604	1201:We see learning from verifiable contextual consequences as a distinct direction for safety training. Because
605	1202:real requirements cannot be exhaustively listed, the policy would need to apply context beyond the
606	1203:particular rules seen in training. Verifiable environments make that hypothesis testable as capability
607	1204:training scales.

618	392:same contextual requirements supports useful, transferable compliance. RQ1. What does task reward
619	393:optimization learn when profitable shortcuts are available despite explicitly stated contextual requirements?
620	394:RQ2. Can context-dependent feedback train useful safety behavior, both from Base and after shortcut
621	395:acquisition? RQ3. How far do capability, shortcut behavior, and contextual safety generalize?

698	1239:Conclusion
699	1240:The experiments support our premise that contextual safety is a learnable part of task execution. Encoding
700	1241:requirements in the dynamics makes reward–context conflicts reproducible and turns their consequences
701	1242:into training feedback. Mechanisms establish compliant feasibility and a rewarding opportunity beyond
702	1243:the contextual boundary; LLM setters realize diverse tasks while independent work and history checks
703	1244:preserve the distinction between score, capability, and compliance. The experiments expose two routes
704	1245:to reward improvement: additional real work through unauthorized resources, and higher reported
705	1246:scores despite degraded work. The shortcut interpretation connects these incentive conflicts to verifiable
706	1247:construction and intervention. Controlled changes in conflict prevalence and training exposure reveal
707	1248:substantial shortcut acquisition even when conflicts occupy a minority of training data. Verified feedback
708	1249:supports joint capability and compliance gains, partially mitigates acquired violations, and transfers
709	1250:authorization-sensitive behavior across new contexts. Cross-task cases show that both boundary-crossing
710	1251:behavior and learned protection can reach excluded workflows; Validation-to-Allocation transfer provides
711	1252:a concrete protection example with useful work retained. Together, these findings support a data-driven
712	1253:route to safety training in which agents learn contextual compliance from the same task interactions used
713	1254:to develop capability. The construction provides a scalable task distribution and verifiable signals for this

906	--ABSTRACT--
907	14:Abstract
908	15:LLM agents that execute multi-step tool calls must satisfy two objectives simul-
909	16:taneously: completing the user’s task (utility) and conforming to domain policies
910	17:and correctness constraints (safety). These objectives are in tension – blocking an
911	18:unsafe action prevents a violation but can leave the agent stranded with no prin-
912	19:cipled way to recover. Existing approaches sacrifice one objective for the other.
913	20:We introduce SOTERIA, a framework that reconciles safety and utility through
914	21:verified hierarchical planning and runtime enforcement of specifications. Before
915	22:execution, the agent generates a structured plan that is formally verified against
916	23:the specifications prior to any tool invocation. During execution, the verified plan
917	24:serves dual roles: it ensures that the agent takes specification-conformant trajec-
918	25:tories and provides guidance when unsafe actions are blocked. Across multiple
919	26:benchmarks covering a diverse range of tool-use tasks, SOTERIA achieves 1.7
920	27:times the average task success rate of the best baselines, with no violations of
921	28:policy specifications, demonstrating that safety and utility need not be traded off.
922	29:1
923	30:Introduction
924	31:LLM agents are increasingly deployed for complex, multi-step tasks — from software engineer-
925	32:ing [Jimenez et al., 2024] and scientific discovery [Novikov et al., 2025] to customer service [Su
926	33:et al., 2025] and enterprise automation [Zhou et al., 2023] — that require orchestrating many tool
927	34:calls whose real-world effects are difficult or impossible to reverse. In these domains, correctness
928	35:is not optional: an airline agent that cancels a reservation without verifying the passenger’s eligibil-
929	36:ity violates a policy specification; a retail agent that processes a return without first retrieving the
930	37:order details by passing fabricated data to downstream tools violates a tool data-flow specification.
931	38:Domain policies and tool contracts define what constitutes correct behavior of an agent, and the
932	39:challenge is ensuring agents satisfy these specifications without sacrificing utility.
933	40:Existing approaches to ensuring conformance rely on runtime guardrails, which take two forms.
934	41:LLM-based guardrails deploy a secondary model to judge each proposed action before it executes
935	42:[Rebedea et al., 2023, Gu et al., 2025]. They are easy to deploy but probabilistic, offering no
936	43:formal safety guarantees. Specification-based monitors provide stronger guarantees by checking
937	44:preconditions, postconditions, or trajectory invariants at runtime [Wang et al., 2025, Kamath et al.,
938	45:2025, Bhardwaj, 2026], but offer no verified recovery plan when a call is blocked. Recovering during
939	46:execution can degrade utility, especially when earlier actions have left the agent in a non-recoverable
940	47:state. Our key insight is that agents can achieve safety without sacrificing utility by constructing a
941	--INTRO END--

954	952:closes the gap entirely: both models reach 100% conformance with zero violations, and success
955	953:equals raw utility (60% GPT, 62% Gemini) because no utility is lost to violations.
956	954:4.3
957	955:Ablation on Sub-plans
958	956:To answer (RQ3), we compare two configurations on τ 2-Airline (GPT-5.4-mini, 8 retries): the full
959	957:system with a sub-plan library and a variant where the planner must produce a single monolithic
960	958:plan at each planning turn. Sub-plans reduce the median plan size from 11 states to 8 (Figure 6a,
961	959:top), since complex sub-tasks are encapsulated in pre-verified fragments rather than replicated. This
962	960:simplification nearly doubles the number of verified plans (65 of 68 planning turns vs. 38 of 60), with
963	961:48.5% verifying on the first attempt vs. 23.3% without sub-plans (Figure 6b). The dominant failure
964	962:mode shifts accordingly: without sub-plans, specification failures persist across retries because they
965	963:require plan redesign; with sub-plans, residual failures are parse and compile errors that the retry
966	964:loop can address with syntactic fixes. These results validate the modular verification design (§2.4):
967	965:factoring policies into independently verified sub-plans reduces the planner’s burden and transforms
968	966:failures into incrementally fixable ones, enabling 95.6% of plans to verify within the retry budget.

1062	--CONCLUSION--
1063	1003:Conclusion
1064	1004:We presented SOTERIA, a framework that enables verification and runtime enforcement of plans for
1065	1005:LLM-based agentic systems. By representing plans as guarded transition systems with hierarchical
1066	1006:sub-plans, SOTERIA formally verifies LLM-generated plans against policy specifications, covering
1067	1007:temporal, relational, and value-flow constraints, before any tool is invoked. At runtime, the veri-
1068	1008:fied plan guides the executor, while the SpecMonitor blocks specification violations and the plan
1069	1009:provides recovery guidance. Our evaluation shows that SOTERIA achieves 100% conformance with
1070	1010:zero specification violations across all models, while improving task success by 4.7–43.9 percentage
1071	1011:points over the best baseline.
1072	1012:Limitations and future work. First, SOTERIA requires a set of formalized specifications as inputs,
1073	1013:which are currently obtained through a semi-automated workflow that combines LLM-based auto-
1074	1014:formalization with manual validation. In future work we aim to investigate how auto-formalization
1075	1015:(e.g., An et al. [2026]) could help reduce this manual effort. Second, SOTERIA’s plan verification
1076	1016:assumes that tool contracts faithfully model tool behavior and postconditions are satisfied at run-
1077	1017:time. Furthermore, SOTERIA leverages automated theorem provers Leino [2010], De Moura and
1078	1018:Bjørner [2008] that support limited first-order theories and may not complete verification in prac-

2	--ABSTRACT--
3	30:ABSTRACT
4	31:Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly expected to tackle complex tasks, driven
5	32:by their expanding applications and users’ growing proficiency in crafting sophisticated
6	33:prompts. However, as the number of explicitly stated requirements increases (particularly
7	34:more than 10 constraints), LLMs often struggle to accurately follow such complex instruc-
8	35:tions, which limits their applicability in complex real-world scenarios. To the best of our
9	36:knowledge, existing datasets do not exceed 10 constraints per instance. To address this chal-
10	37:lenge, we propose RECAST, an efficient and scalable framework for synthesizing datasets
11	38:where each example incorporates far more constraints than those in existing benchmarks,
12	39:aiming to challenge and extend the boundaries of models’ ability to follow complex in-
13	40:structions. These constraints are extracted from real-world prompt-response pairs to ensure
14	41:practical relevance. Using this framework, we construct RECAST-30K, a large-scale, high-
15	42:quality dataset comprising 30k instances spanning 19 constraint types. Experimental results
16	43:demonstrate that models fine-tuned on RECAST-30K substantially improve in following
17	44:complex instructions while maintaining their general capabilities without degradation.
18	45:Moreover, RECAST enables automatic verification of constraint satisfaction via rule-based
19	46:validators for quantitative constraints and LLM-based validators for qualitative ones, the
20	47:verifiability provided by RECAST enables the design of reward functions for reinforcement
21	48:learning, which further boosts model performance on complex and challenging tasks. Code
22	49:and data are available at https://github.com/Thekey756/RECAST.

118	1518:MAIN RESULTS
119	1519:4.2.1
120	1520:EVALUATION ON RECAST-TEST
121	1521:Table 1 presents comprehensive results from our multi-level constraint satisfaction benchmark. Analysis of these findings
122	1522:reveals three results:
123	1523:Performance Degradation with Increasing Constraint Complexity. Across all models, performance consistently
124	1524:declines from Level 1 to Level 4, underscoring the difficulty of satisfying multiple constraints simultaneously. Rule-based
125	1525:constraints prove more challenging than model-based ones. Gemini-2.5-Pro shows the best performance with a 39.75%
126	1526:average satisfaction rate. Overall, complex instruction following remains difficult for current LLMs, highlighting the need
127	1527:for further advancement.
128	1528:Effectiveness of RECAST-30K for Instruction Following. Models fine-tuned on RECAST-30K demonstrate substantial
129	1529:improvements in constraint satisfaction capabilities. The RECAST-30K-SFT variant achieves a 31.25% average
130	1530:satisfaction rate on Qwen-2.5-7B, significantly outperforming both instruction-tuned models and alternative fine-tuning
131	1531:approaches. This enhancement underscores the effectiveness of our constraint-focused dataset in developing robust
132	1532:instruction-following capabilities, particularly for navigating complex, multi-constraint scenarios.
133	1533:Performance Enhancement Through RLVC Optimization. The application of RLVC further enhances model perfor-
134	1534:mance across all difficulty levels. RECAST-30K-RLVC variants consistently outperform their SFT counterparts, achieving
135	1535:a 32.33% average satisfaction rate on Qwen-2.5-7B. This improvement is particularly pronounced in higher difficulty
136	1536:levels (Levels 3-4), where constraint interactions become more complex. These gains confirm that our constraint-specific
137	1537:reinforcement learning approach effectively optimizes for simultaneous satisfaction of multiple requirements, addressing
138	1538:a key challenge in practical complex instruction following.
139	1539:These results clearly demonstrate that specialized fine-tuning approaches—particularly our RECAST-30K dataset
140	1540:and RLVC optimization framework—significantly enhance LLMs’ capability to satisfy multiple complex constraints
141	1541:simultaneously. This improvement addresses a critical gap in current instruction-following systems and enables more
142	1542:reliable performance in constraint-rich applications.
143	1543:Comparison with Divide-Verify-Refine (DVR). We further compare our models with the inference-time instruction-
144	1544:following enhancement method Divide-Verify-Refine (DVR) (Zhang et al., 2025) on RECAST-Test. Since DVR in its
145	1545:original form only leverages rule-based verifiers, we report the Rule-based Constraint Satisfaction Rate (RSR) for a fair
146	1546:comparison. As shown in Table 2, applying DVR at inference time on top of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-
147	1547:Instruct leads to substantially lower RSR than our RECAST-30K-SFT models, which consistently achieve higher RSR
148	--CONCLUSION--
149	1822:CONCLUSION
150	1823:We present RECAST, a scalable, low-cost framework for constructing complex instruction-following datasets through
151	1824:systematic mining and verification of rule- and model-based constraints. Using this, we release RECAST-30K, enabling
152	1825:smaller models (e.g., Llama3.1-8B) to outperform larger instruct-tuned models. Leveraging constraint verifiability, we
153	1826:propose RLVC, a reinforcement learning method using fine-grained, constraint-specific rewards to enhance performance.
154	1827:Experiments show RECAST-trained models excel on our hierarchical benchmark, generalize to IFEVAL and FollowBench,
155	1828:and remain competitive on general tasks (GPQA, MUSR). RECAST advances automated data construction by offering
156	1829:scalable, verifiable supervision, improving constraint diversity, complexity, and quality, and providing practical resources
157	1830:for more controllable LLMs, and advancing their real-world applications.

167	--ABSTRACT--
168	12:ABSTRACT
169	13:Agentic language models operate in a fundamentally different safety regime than
170	14:chat models: they must plan, call tools, and execute long-horizon actions where a
171	15:single misstep, such as accessing files or entering credentials, can cause irreversible
172	16:harm. Existing alignment methods, largely optimized for static generation and
173	17:task completion, break down in these settings due to sequential decision-making,
174	18:adversarial tool feedback, and overconfident intermediate reasoning. We introduce
175	19:MOSAIC, a post-training framework that aligns agents for safe multi-step tool use
176	20:by making safety decisions explicit and learnable. MOSAIC structures inference as
177	21:a plan, check, then act or refuse loop, with explicit safety reasoning and refusal as
178	22:first-class actions. To train without trajectory-level labels, we use preference-based
179	23:reinforcement learning with pairwise trajectory comparisons, which captures safety
180	24:distinctions often missed by scalar rewards. We evaluate MOSAIC zero-shot across
181	25:three model families, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-4B-Thinking, and Phi-4, and across
182	26:out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning harmful tasks, prompt injection, benign
183	27:tool use, and cross-domain privacy leakage. MOSAIC reduces harmful behavior by
184	28:up to 50%, increases harmful-task refusal by over 20% on injection attacks, cuts
185	29:privacy leakage, and preserves or improves benign task performance, demonstrating
186	30:robust generalization across models, domains, and agentic settings.

207	753:Figure 4: Judge agreement over training.
208	754:Ablation 2: Pointwise Scalar vs. Pairwise Preference Rewards.
209	755:Replacing pairwise trajectory
210	756:preferences with a pointwise (scalar) reward model leads to systematically weaker safety alignment.
211	757:As shown in Table 5, scalar-reward training (row2) reduces harmful-task refusal on AgentHarm from
212	758:0.87 to 0.79 and increases non-refusal harm from 0.52 to 0.61, indicating substantially less safe
213	759:behavior even when the agent acts. Benign utility also degrades, with non-refusal score dropping from
214	760:0.61 to 0.54. On Agent Security Bench, scalar rewards exhibit higher prompt-injection vulnerability,
215	761:increasing DPI ASR from 0.42 to 0.51 and IPI ASR from 0.33 to 0.44, alongside weaker refusal
216	762:under attack (Appendix H has detailed results).
217	763:These failures arise because scalar rewards collapse sequential safety decisions into a single score and
218	764:cannot reliably distinguish trajectories that reach similar end states but differ in when unsafe actions
219	765:occur (e.g., early refusal versus late abort after unsafe progress). In contrast, pairwise preference
220	766:rewards explicitly encode relative safety ordering between trajectories, prioritizing early refusal and
221	767:avoidance of irreversible actions. This yields consistently higher refusal reliability, lower harm, and
222	768:stronger robustness to both direct and indirect prompt injection.
223	769:Pairwise judgment stabilizes over training. Figure 5 shows the agreement rate of the preference-
224	770:based LLM judge during training. Agreement, defined as the fraction of comparisons with consistent
225	771:ordering, increases steadily across all models, indicating that trajectory distributions become more
226	772:consistent and that the judge converges toward a stable safety decision boundary.
227	773:Key Ablation Insight: Pairwise Rewards Are Essential
228	774:Pointwise rewards miss sequential safety distinctions; pairwise preferences are required for early refusal and
229	775:safe behavior.
230	776:5
231	--EXP SETUP--
232	313:EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
233	314:3.1
234	315:TRAINING DATA: AGENT-SAFETYBENCH
235	316:We train agentic policies on the Agent-SafetyBench dataset (Zhang et al., 2024), which is designed to
236	317:elicit safety-critical decision-making in tool-using agents. The benchmark contains explicitly harmful
237	318:tasks, benign tasks, and tasks that admit both safe and unsafe execution strategies, enabling models to
238	319:learn calibrated, context-dependent behavior rather than relying on surface cues or task labels.
239	320:Task Structure and Attack Surfaces. Agent Safety Bench (Zhang et al., 2024) comprises 349
240	321:interaction environments and approximately 2,000 task instances spanning 8 safety risk categories
241	322:and 10 common agent failure modes. Tasks include both single- and multi-step interactions, with and
242	323:without tool use, and explicitly model realistic attack surfaces via prompt injection. These include
243	324:direct injections embedded in the user prompt and indirect injections introduced through adversarial
244	325:tool responses or environment state (see Appendix B.2 for more details).
245	326:Execution-Aware Supervision. A key feature of the dataset is that task correctness depends on
246	327:how the agent executes intermediate steps—interpreting tool outputs, assessing risk, and deciding
247	328:whether to act or refuse—rather than on task completion alone. This structure supports supervision
248	329:over execution quality instead of outcome-only.
249	330:Pairwise Safety Preferences. Training supervision is provided via an LLM-as-judge framework
250	331:(Section 2.2.1). Rather than assigning absolute safety labels, we derive pairwise preferences by
251	332:comparing two trajectories for the same task and selecting the safer outcome. These pairwise
252	333:judgments serve as reinforcement learning signals, enabling data-efficient optimization without
253	334:step-level annotations or ground-truth safety labels.

285	453:RESULTS: FRONTIER MODELS ARE STRONG, BUT REQUIRE EXPLICIT SAFETY
286	454:SCAFFOLDING.
287	455:Table 1 shows that even frontier-scale proprietary models such as GPT-4o and GPT-5 do not exhibit
288	456:reliable agentic safety in the absence of explicit safety scaffolding. When deployed without safety
289	457:reasoning and a refusal mechanism, both models never refuse harmful requests and exhibit severe
290	458:safety failures, including high harmful-task scores and susceptibility to prompt injection, for example
291	459:GPT-4o achieves a harm score of 0.31 and a DPI ASR of 0.76. Introducing MOSAIC by explicitly
292	460:separating safety-aware reasoning and enabling refusal as a first-class action fundamentally changes

299	467:agent behavior. Harmful-task refusal increases from 0% to over 90% for both models, harmful scores
300	468:drop by more than 75% for GPT-4o from 0.31 to 0.07, and robustness improves substantially for
301	469:both direct and indirect prompt injection attacks. Importantly, these gains do not degrade task utility.
302	470:Benign-task completion remains high, with CR = 0.93 for GPT-4o and CR = 0.99 for GPT-5. Together,
303	471:these results indicate that safe agentic behavior in frontier models is not an emergent property of
304	472:scale alone, but is induced through explicit safety reasoning and refusal mechanisms.
305	473:Key Result: Frontier Models Need Safety Guardrails
306	474:Without safety reasoning and refusal, GPT-4o and GPT-5 fail on agentic safety; MOSAIC raises harmful-task
307	475:refusal above 90%, cuts harm by over 75%, and preserves benign performance.
308	476:4.2
309	477:RESULTS: OPEN-SOURCE MODELS
310	478:We evaluate MOSAIC across three open-weight agentic models, examining safety, execution reliabil-
311	479:ity, and task utility in multi-step tool use. Explicit, trainable safety decisions consistently reshape
312	480:agent behavior, with model-specific effects driven by baseline biases.
313	--CONCLUSION--
314	809:CONCLUSION
315	810:We show that agentic safety requires explicit control over when models act, verify, or abstain, espe-
316	811:cially in multi-step tool use where failures are sequential and irreversible. MOSAIC demonstrates that
317	812:making safety reasoning and refusal first-class, learnable decisions leads to consistent improvements
318	813:across model families, task types, and domains, including out-of-distribution privacy settings. Our
319	814:results suggest that agentic alignment is not primarily a function of scale, but of structured inference
320	815:and training signals that reflect temporal safety decisions. More broadly, MOSAIC points toward
321	816:a principled path for building reliable agents by integrating modular reasoning, preference-based
322	817:learning, and explicit abstention into the agent’s core decision loop rather than treating safety as an
323	818:external filter.
324	819:REFERENCES

326	821:Michael Harrison, Russell J Hewett, Mojan Javaheripi, Piero Kauffmann, et al. Phi-4 technical
327	822:report. arXiv preprint arXiv:2412.08905, 2024a.
328	823:Marah Abdin, Sam Ade Jacobs, Ammar Ahmad Awan, et al. Phi-3 technical report: A highly capable
329	824:language model locally on your phone. arXiv preprint arXiv:2404.14219, 2024b.

332	--ABSTRACT--
333	14:Abstract
334	15:Training tool-calling agents requires large-scale trajectory data with verifiable la-
335	16:bels, yet existing approaches either synthesize environments that diverge from real
336	17:API behavior or generate tasks without ground-truth outcomes for verification. We
337	18:present FIREFLY, a pipeline for generating verified tool-call data from real-world
338	19:MCP servers. Our key insight is to invert the standard synthesis pipeline: rather
339	20:than generating tasks and hoping they are solvable, we first let a strong LLM ex-
340	21:plore real APIs along graph-guided DAG structures, then synthesize tasks back-
341	22:ward from observed outcomes, guaranteeing label correctness by construction. To
342	23:handle the scale of real-world tool spaces (∼1,000 tools), we build a pairwise
343	24:tool graph and sample sub-DAGs to focus exploration on semantically coherent
344	25:workflows. To address environment drift in live APIs, we construct a retrieval-
345	26:augmented simulator that caches all exploration results and replays them dur-
346	27:ing training and evaluation, enabling reproducible RL without live server access.
347	28:Applying this pipeline yields 5,144 verified tasks spanning 240 servers and 993
348	29:tools. A 4B-parameter model trained with GRPO on FIREFLY matches Claude
349	30:Sonnet 4.6 on our held-out test set and shows improvements on multiple tool-
350	31:calling benchmarks including Tau2-Bench, MCPMark, and MCP-Atlas. Code
351	32:is available at https://github.com/leoleoasd/firefly-neurips-2026/,
352	33:and data and model are available at http://firefly.hailab.io/.
353	34:1
354	35:Introduction
355	36:Tool-calling agents interact with external APIs to complete user intents, and they have become a
356	37:central paradigm for building AI systems that can act in real environments [19, 33, 2, 25]. However,
357	38:training such agents requires many tasks with correct intermediate tool calls and verifiable final
358	39:outcomes. Even data-efficient reinforcement learning recipes consume thousands of such tasks,
359	40:for example 2.4k training samples for a search agent [10], whereas recent agent benchmarks each
360	41:offer only tens to hundreds, such as 50 to 115 tasks per domain in Tau2-Bench [2], 127 tasks in
361	42:MCPMark [28], and 500 public tasks in MCP-Atlas [1]. Human annotation could close this gap,
362	43:but it is expensive, domain-specific, and difficult to scale to the long tail of real APIs [33, 14, 4, 6,
363	44:5]. Synthetic pipelines scale more easily, although each existing design gives up either realism or
364	45:verifiability. When they rely on purely simulated environments, an LLM invents tool responses that
365	46:often diverge from real API behavior [9]. When they instead generate a user task first and then ask
366	47:an LLM to produce a trajectory over real tools [21, 16, 31], the trajectory may be infeasible and the
367	--INTRO END--
368	181:
369	182:outside the cached trajectories are unlikely to be necessary for the correct solution and should not
370	183:be rewarded (Sec. 7 quantifies the resulting truncation risk). As a result, FIREFLY keeps tool re-
371	184:sponses grounded in real API execution while providing the reproducibility and scalability required
372	185:for simulator-based online RL.
373	186:Putting these ideas together, FIREFLY follows a three-stage pipeline. First, it collects and filters
374	187:real MCP servers, constructs a pairwise tool-compatibility graph, and performs graph-guided ex-
375	188:ploration to obtain executable tool-call DAGs. Second, it synthesizes natural-language tasks by
376	189:back-chaining from observed tool outputs and validates the resulting task-trajectory pairs for verifi-
377	190:ability, specificity, realism, and difficulty. Third, it builds a retrieval-augmented simulator from the
378	191:cached exploration traces and uses it as the environment for simulator-based online RL training and
379	192:for evaluation. Applying this pipeline yields 5,144 verified tasks and 9,749 trajectories spanning 240
380	193:servers and 993 tools. Training a 4B-parameter model with GRPO [20] and dynamic filtering [34]
381	194:on FIREFLY improves pass@1 on the FIREFLY held-out test set from 28.1% to 41.5%, matching
382	195:Claude Sonnet 4.6 under the same evaluation protocol. The resulting model also transfers to public
383	196:tool-calling benchmarks, improving all evaluated Tau2-Bench domains [33, 2], MCP-Atlas [1], and
384	197:MCPMark [28] tasks.
385	198:Our contributions are threefold:
386	199:• We introduce FIREFLY, a large-scale verified tool-calling dataset grounded in real MCP
387	200:servers, together with a retrieval-augmented simulator that enables reproducible training
388	201:and evaluation without live servers3.
389	202:• We propose a scalable data-generation framework that combines graph-guided exploration
390	203:with back-chaining task synthesis, making it possible to construct verified trajectories
391	204:across hundreds of heterogeneous real-world API servers.
392	205:• We empirically show that RL training on FIREFLY substantially improves a 4B model on
393	206:in-distribution verified MCP tasks and transfers to out-of-distribution tool-calling bench-
394	207:marks such as Tau2-Bench [33, 2], MCP-Atlas, and MCPMark.
395	208:2
396	--METHOD--
397	268:Method
398	269:Our pipeline constructs verifiable tool-use data in three phases: server collection (Sec. 3.1), task
399	270:synthesis (Sec. 3.2), and trajectory generation during evaluation and rollout (Sec. 3.3).
400	271:3.1
401	272:Server Collection
402	273:3.1.1
403	274:Scraping
404	275:We collect MCP servers from the Smithery registry4 using broad listing queries, prefix enumeration,
405	276:and domain-specific keyword searches. After deduplication and metadata fetching (tool definitions,
406	277:input schemas, connection configurations), we obtain approximately 3,000 unique servers, of which
407	278:roughly 900 expose at least one tool.
408	279:3.1.2
409	280:Filtering
410	281:Many scraped servers are unsuitable for verified data construction. We screen each server against
411	282:four criteria using an LLM evaluator: Statelessness (no session memory or cross-call state), No
412	283:user authentication (no OAuth, credentials, or user-owned keys), Schema clarity (explicit JSON
413	284:typing and parameter descriptions), and Non-triviality (no echo or diagnostic-only tools). A server
414	285:must meet all four. We spot-check a subset for alignment. 240 servers with 993 tools remain.
415	286:3.1.3
416	287:Tool Graph
417	288:The tool graph is the mechanism that makes multi-step tasks possible in FIREFLY. In an early
418	289:pilot without the graph, the exploring LLM sampled tools at random across the full tool space, so
419	290:successive calls were semantically unconnected and the output of one call was never usable as the
420	291:input of the next. As a result, essentially all tasks synthesized in that pilot collapsed to single-step
421	292:lookups. To obtain tool chains in which earlier outputs feed later inputs, we build a directed tool
422	293:4https://smithery.ai/
423	294:4
424	295:

427	298:============================================================
428	299:
429	300:graph G = (T , E) over all retained tools across all servers. Each node represents a tool and each
430	301:edge indicates that the source tool can be chained with the destination tool: the output of tool ti can
431	302:be transformed into or used as input to tool tj. Since schema-level type matching alone is too coarse
432	303:(e.g., two string fields may be semantically unrelated), we use an LLM to judge each candidate
433	304:pair based on tool descriptions and schemas, assigning a confidence level (high, medium, or low)
434	305:to each positive edge. The resulting graph contains approximately 83K directed edges (average
435	306:88 successors per tool), of which 64K are medium-or-higher confidence. The graph includes both
436	307:intra-server and cross-server edges.
437	--EXP SETUP--
438	479:Experiments
439	480:We evaluate whether training on FIREFLY improves tool-calling ability. We fine-tune a model using
440	481:reinforcement learning and evaluate on both our held-out test set and public benchmarks.

519	--LIMITATIONS--
520	701:Limitations
521	702:Model scale.
522	703:Due to computational constraints, we only train and evaluate a 4B-parameter model.
523	704:While the results demonstrate clear gains from FIREFLY’s verifiable supervision, larger models are
524	705:likely to benefit even more: the modest gap between pass@1 and pass@16 (41.5% vs. 57.0%)
525	706:suggests that the 4B model lacks the capacity to solve many harder multi-step tasks regardless of
526	707:sampling budget. Scaling to larger models (e.g., 30B+ parameters) would likely raise both the
527	708:pass@1 ceiling and the pass@16 coverage, as larger models can internalize more diverse solution
528	709:strategies from the training trajectories.
529	710:Single-turn interaction.
530	711:All tasks in FIREFLY follow a single-turn format: the user issues one
531	712:request and the agent completes it through multi-step tool calls. Real-world tool-use scenarios often
532	713:involve multi-turn conversations where the user provides clarifications, changes requirements, or
533	714:builds on previous results. Extending the pipeline to generate and validate multi-turn dialogues with
534	715:interleaved user messages is an important direction for future work.
535	716:Conservative simulator errors.
536	717:The simulator returns a tool error for calls that differ semantically
537	718:from every cached call, so an agent that finds a valid path outside the explored trajectories during
538	719:RL receives an error for that path, which may narrow the policy toward explored paths. To bound
539	720:this truncation risk, we classified every evaluation tool call as an exact, minor, or major deviation
540	721:from the nearest cached call and related the classes to task success. In successful trajectories, about
541	722:24% of calls deviate from the cached ground-truth path (13.8% with major and 10.4% with minor
542	723:deviations) and still lead to full reward, so alternative paths can pass through the simulator. In failed
543	724:trajectories, 66.8% of calls deviate majorly, so the errors fall mostly on semantically wrong calls,

545	##### library/03_paired_benchmark/2606.21140_MatchingMatters/2606.21140_MatchingMatters_fulltext.txt  (2145 lines)
546	--ABSTRACT--
547	11:Abstract
548	12:Rapid advances in large language models have improved the
549	13:task-solving capabilities of command-line-interface (CLI)-
550	14:based agents, whose CLIs determine how models invoke
551	15:tools, maintain interaction history, and recover from failures.
552	16:Consequently, effective matching between CLIs and LLMs
553	17:has become essential. However, existing agent benchmarks
554	18:largely emphasize success rate while overlooking practical
555	19:objectives such as cost and efficiency, as well as the se-
556	20:lection of LM–CLI combinations, all of which are critical
557	21:in real-world deployment. We therefore introduce AGENT-
558	22:METER, a quality–efficiency benchmark with a new met-
559	23:ric, the AgentMeter Score (AMS), that jointly characterizes
560	24:task quality, budget sensitivity, and resource-intensive zero-
561	25:reward execution, enabling a more complete assessment of
562	26:deployed LM–CLI pairs.
563	27:Furthermore, collected task de-
564	28:scriptions may inadvertently favor LM–CLI pairs that are par-
565	29:ticularly compatible with their wording and structure, causing
566	30:evaluation results to reflect description-specific advantages
567	31:rather than general task-solving capability. We therefore pro-
568	32:pose AGENTMETER-OPT, a trajectory-grounded optimiza-
569	33:tion framework that constructs pair-adapted, task-preserving
570	34:description variants to build a fairer evaluation set across
571	35:LM–CLI pairs. Extensive experiments show that no CLI is
572	36:universally optimal across language models and that task suc-
573	37:cess, execution cost, and AMS identify different competitive
574	38:configurations. Results on AGENTMETER-OPT further re-
575	39:veal that task-preserving description changes affect LM–CLI
576	40:pairs unevenly and can alter their relative ordering across
577	41:valid description conditions. Together, AGENTMETER and
578	42:AGENTMETER-OPT provide a practical foundation for fair
579	43:and deployment-relevant evaluation of command-line agents.
580	44:Introduction
581	--INTRO END--

610	--METHOD--
611	337:Methodology
612	338:Problem Formulation
613	339:We treat the pairing of a language model and a command-
614	340:line interface as an LM–CLI configuration, denoted by π.
615	341:Each task i is specified by its objective, input artifacts and
616	342:their roles, required outputs, execution environment, evalu-
617	343:ator, and success criterion. Together, these elements define
618	344:the task semantics. Given a public task, executing config-
619	345:uration π on task i produces a trajectory τi(π), an evalu-
620	346:ator reward Ri(π) ∈[0, 1], and a billable execution cost
621	347:Ci(π) ≥0.
622	348:AgentMeter Score
623	349:We first collect the dataset as AgentMeter, which evaluates
624	350:each LM–CLI pair under the original description of every
625	351:task. Then, we propose AgentMeter Score (AMS), which
626	352:measures not only how much task quality a configuration
627	353:achieves, but also how efficiently it achieves that quality
628	354:and how much it spends on zero-reward executions. AMS
629	355:combines three complementary components: Task Qual-
630	356:ity (TQ), cost-aware Area Under the Budget–Quality Curve
631	357:(AUBQC), and Expensive Failure Rate (EFR).
632	358:Because execution costs are meaningful only relative to
633	359:task demand, AMS first estimates the observed effort of each
634	360:task from a fixed reference set of LM–CLI configurations,
635	361:denoted by Πref. Throughout this subsection, τi(π), Ri(π),
636	362:and Ci(π) denote the trajectory, reward, and cost obtained
637	363:by configuration π on task i under its collected public de-
638	364:scription. Let Tok(τ) and Step(τ) denote the token usage
639	365:and number of execution steps recorded in trajectory τ, re-
640	366:spectively. We define the observed-effort index of task i as
641	367:ei = q

652	832:Experiments
653	833:Datasets
654	834:The Full Benchmark contains 80 executable command-line
655	835:tasks from SkillsBench, Terminal-Bench, and DA-Code (Li
656	836:et al. 2026; Merrill et al. 2026; Huang et al. 2024). It pro-
657	837:vides the reference task distribution used for effort and cost
658	838:calibration. The 30-task Core Subset preserves coverage of
659	839:the source benchmarks and observed-effort strata while sup-
660	840:porting the complete 7×4 LM–CLI grid, yielding 840 pair–
661	841:task runs. We assess its fidelity using the 16 configurations
662	842:with complete Full-Benchmark coverage, comprising 1,280
663	843:Full-Benchmark pair–task runs in total.
664	844:For AGENTMETER-OPT, we use a fixed 16-task subset
665	845:spanning 5 Easy, 7 Medium, and 4 Hard tasks to study how
666	846:task-preserving description variants affect LM–CLI perfor-
667	847:mance and ranking.
668	848:Implementation Details
669	849:Models and interfaces.
670	850:We evaluate seven language
671	851:models:
672	852:Qwen3.6-Plus,
673	853:DeepSeek-V4-Pro,
674	854:GLM-5.1,
675	855:MiniMax-M2.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.3-Codex, and
676	856:Gemini 3.5 Flash (Alibaba Cloud 2026; DeepSeek 2026;
677	857:Z.AI 2026; MiniMax 2026; Anthropic 2026b; OpenAI
678	858:2026b; Google 2026). Each model is paired with Claude
679	859:Code, Codex CLI, Kimi Code CLI, and Qwen Code (An-
680	860:thropic 2026a; OpenAI 2026a; Moonshot AI 2026; Qwen
681	861:Team 2026a). Exact provider model IDs, snapshots, infer-
682	862:ence settings, CLI releases or commits, and evaluation dates
683	863:are reported in the supplementary material.
684	864:Evaluation protocol. AMS is the primary metric. We ad-
685	865:ditionally report pass count, tokens per successful task, and
686	866:USD per successful task. We set α = 0.6. Within each Full-
687	867:Benchmark effort stratum, the billable-cost budget grid is
688	868:calibrated at the 20th, 40th, 60th, 80th, and 90th percentiles
689	869:of positive-reward reference executions.
690	870:The expensive-
691	871:failure threshold is the 90th percentile of zero-reward ex-
692	872:ecution cost in the same stratum. All calibration choices,
693	873:including the reference configurations, effort strata, budget
694	874:grids, failure thresholds, and pricing rules, are fixed in ad-
695	875:vance and shared across all evaluated configurations. Un-
696	876:less otherwise stated, 95% confidence intervals use 10,000
697	877:task-level paired bootstrap resamples.
698	878:Description construction.
699	879:We use four LM–CLI pairs:
700	880:Qwen3.6-Plus/Kimi Code CLI, Qwen3.6-Plus/Codex CLI,
701	881:DeepSeek-V4-Pro/Kimi Code CLI, and GLM-5.1/Qwen
702	--LIMITATIONS--
703	1985:Limitations
704	1986:The reported rankings are conditional on the selected tasks,
705	1987:calibration reference, pricing configuration, and execution
706	1988:harness. The Core–Full audit supports Core as an efficient
707	1989:approximation within the studied benchmark pool, while the
708	1990:16-task, four-pair AGENTMETER-OPT experiment is a con-
709	1991:trolled diagnostic rather than an exhaustive estimate over
710	1992:all models, interfaces, and domains. The tested sensitiv-
711	1993:ity settings preserve the leading configuration but do not
712	1994:cover every possible quality–cost objective. The preserva-
713	1995:tion gate rejects explicit changes to public task semantics but
714	1996:cannot formally prove natural-language equivalence. Task-
715	1997:level bootstrap intervals quantify variation over tasks, and
716	1998:reported USD values exclude local infrastructure costs.

728	1202:Conclusion
729	1203:We introduced AGENTMETER to evaluate complete LM–
730	1204:CLI configurations using AMS, which combines graded task
731	1205:quality, quality under calibrated cost budgets, and costly
732	1206:zero-reward failures. Experiments show that pass rate, ex-
733	1207:ecution cost, and AMS identify different leading configura-
734	1208:tions, and that no CLI is consistently best across language
735	1209:models. AGENTMETER-OPT further shows that measured
736	1210:performance and ranking can depend on the collected task
737	1211:formulation.

739	1213:dependence on any formulation, while generic public-only
740	1214:rewriting does not explain the main gains.

746	--ABSTRACT--
747	10:Abstract
748	11:Language models can reach the right normative verdict for
749	12:the wrong reason. We introduce NormWorlds-CF, a solver-
750	13:verified environment for counterfactual normative reasoning
751	14:in executable rule worlds. Its deterministic solver produces
752	15:final answers, proof and falsification certificates, argument
753	16:statuses, support sets, and paired-world change labels, en-
754	17:abling supervision and evaluation without LLM judges. The
755	18:benchmark contains staged SFT diagnostics and a compact
756	19:paired-world task with 270 root families and 1080 canonical-
757	20:to-variant pairs. The SFT diagnostics show that final-answer
758	21:supervision can saturate verdict accuracy without inducing
759	22:falsification competence: answer-only SFT reaches perfect
760	23:answer accuracy but scores zero on joint falsification cer-
761	24:tificates, while full-mix training with targeted replay reaches
762	25:strong all-task accuracy (0.99). For the structured-change task,
763	26:we introduce metamorphic-relation GRPO (MR-GRPO), a
764	27:class-conditioned reward for GRPO that gives partial credit
765	28:for relation families and solver-visible change fields. In
766	29:matched Qwen3-1.7B continuation experiments, MR-GRPO
767	30:improves held-out relation accuracy and relation-family cor-
768	31:rectness, and reduces wrong-family error, compared to sparse
769	32:and answer-only GRPO. In Qwen3-4B three-seed validation,
770	33:sparse reward preserves coarse relation labels best, answer-
771	34:only reward improves answer-change but weakens relation-
772	35:family structure, and MR-GRPO leads on answer-, support-,
773	36:and status-change fields as well as class-conditioned MR and
774	37:change-presence. These results show that verified counterfac-
775	38:tual structure can shape post-training beyond final answers,
776	39:while exact full change-record generation, invariant subtype
777	40:recognition, and out-of-distribution (OOD) transfer remain
778	41:open problems.
779	42:1

792	796:Interventions, partial credit, and attribution
793	797:Root-level
794	798:MR pairs are interventions, not generic augmentations: sur-
795	799:face/distractor edits should leave certificates fixed, while sup-
796	800:port/priority edits should change them in solver-specified
797	801:ways. Compact change records are a practical RL inter-

799	803:port_delta with priority_delta is wrong on subtype yet
800	804:right on the invariant/change boundary; class-conditioned
801	805:partial credit follows that diagnostic hierarchy, whereas
802	806:sparse exactness ignores it and often starves GRPO. Refusing
803	807:LLM judges keeps reward design an experimental variable,

806	810:uation by asking whether verified structure can be taught

817	532:reward geometry reappear when change fields are more ex-
818	533:pressible? Which failures remain?

820	535:an LLM judge. We treat relation, relation-family, wrong-

4	13:High-quality tool-use data is critical for train-
5	14:ing language models to interact effectively with
6	15:external tools. However, existing synthetic ap-
7	16:proaches typically follow a generate-then-filter
8	17:paradigm with static post-hoc verification, of-
9	18:ten yielding inefficient data with imbalanced
10	19:feature distributions. We propose ToolLoop, a
11	20:closed-loop framework that decomposes syn-
12	21:thesis into three progressive stages: (1) sam-
13	22:pling function name combinations as ground
14	23:truth; (2) backward derivation of user queries;
15	24:and (3) forward derivation of tool calls. At
16	25:each stage, dynamic self-feedback iteratively
17	26:guides the model toward high-quality genera-
18	27:tion, realizing a transition from generate-then-
19	28:filter to generate-verify-refine. On the Berkeley
20	29:Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL), a 4B pa-
21	30:rameter model trained with our 11K synthetic
22	31:examples achieves 86.40% accuracy in non-
23	32:reasoning mode, while an Isolate variant that re-
24	33:moves BFCL-overlapping candidate functions
25	34:still reaches 86.07%. Cross-benchmark evalua-
26	35:tion on ACEBench further demonstrates strong
27	36:generalization, with 72.1% overall accuracy us-
28	37:ing only 18.3% of baseline training data.

192	1143:we cannot verify whether our synthesized data ad-

233	--ABSTRACT--
234	35:Abstract
235	36:For repository-grounded coding agents, a functionally correct patch is not necessarily an acceptable one:
236	37:developers also constrain how the task must be carried out—modification scope, workflow order, validation,
237	38:tool use, and reporting. This capability, which we call engineering constraint following, remains largely
238	39:invisible to current evaluations. We introduce ANCHOR (Assessing Naturalistic Constraint Hierarchies
239	40:and Ordering in Repository-Grounded Agentic Coding), a benchmark built on naturalistic, multilingual
240	41:repository tasks spanning eight language groups. ANCHOR combines (i) a hierarchical taxonomy of
241	42:10 categories and 78 leaf types distilled from real developer interactions, (ii) an automated pipeline that
242	43:instantiates task-grounded atomic constraints and composes them into typed AND/THEN/PRIORITY relations,
243	44:and (iii) a trajectory-grounded evaluation framework that checks both the code diff and the execution
244	45:trajectory with rule-based and LLM judges. Across 19 agent configurations spanning 2 scaffolds and 10
245	46:foundation models on 358 tasks, the strongest measured system, Claude Opus 4.8 under Cline, reaches
246	47:70.1% atomic compliance and 63.7% relation compliance, while 19.0% of tasks pass every scored checklist
247	48:item under the strict all-item FCCR criterion. A five-engineer audit of constraints from 50 instances
248	49:reports 94% feasibility, 94% repository consistency, and 96% realism. In the primary paired set (14
249	50:configurations), the mean signed change in task completion after adding constraints is +0.7 percentage
250	51:points; individual changes vary in both directions. These results distinguish functional success from
251	52:constraint compliance, with failures concentrated in workflow ordering, tool-use discipline, and reporting,
252	53:and substantial interactions between models and scaffolds.
253	54:Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Yone-01/ANCHOR
254	55:Code: https://github.com/bupterlxp/ANCHOR
255	56:1
256	57:Introduction
257	58:Software engineering tasks are rarely unconstrained objectives. Developers ask agents not only to fix the bug, but also
258	59:to preserve APIs, reproduce before patching, run specific tests, avoid prohibited tools, and report what was actually
259	60:executed. For coding agents, success is therefore not merely to solve the task, but to solve it under explicit engineering
260	61:constraints.
261	62:We argue that this is not simply generic instruction following with code context. In repository-grounded agentic
262	63:coding, many requirements are trajectory-grounded: they constrain tool use, workflow order, validation, and reporting

355	1130:than GPT-5.4 under Cline (12.0%). Nevertheless, 81.0% of tasks still fail at least one checklist item. Completion and
356	1131:FCCR are different marginal rates, not a measured joint success rate; their 24.6-point difference lower-bounds the share

422	##### library/03_paired_benchmark/2610.26359_DiscoveryProbabilityGraph/2610.26359_DiscoveryProbabilityGraph_fulltext.txt  (2151 lines)
423	--ABSTRACT--
424	15:ABSTRACT
425	16:Embodied agents are increasingly capable of perceiving, planning, and acting au-
426	17:tonomously in dynamic environments, demonstrating strong performance on com-
427	18:plex cooperative tasks. Recent advances typically assume that cooperative tasks
428	19:are known in advance. In real-world applications, however, hidden-cooperation
429	20:tasks are more common: the need for cooperation only becomes apparent after
430	21:an agent observes and interacts with task-related targets. In this paper, we first
431	22:present HiddenCoop, a benchmark for effectively evaluating agent cooperation in
432	23:hidden-cooperation tasks. We further propose Discovery-Probability Graph Plan-
433	24:ning (DPGP), a method for enabling effective agent cooperation in such tasks.
434	25:At the core of DPGP is a discovery-probability graph that encodes the probabil-
435	26:ity distribution over the number and locations of task-related targets, facilitating
436	27:effective and efficient information exchange among agents. A search algorithm
437	28:is then used to derive action plans that minimize expected costs. Experiments
438	29:show that DPGP achieves cooperative-task success rates of 99.3% on C-WAH
439	30:and 58.3% on TDW-MAT, surpassing all compared baselines, while also reducing
440	31:overall embodied execution time and substantially lowering LLM token usage.
441	32:Our code is available at https://github.com/hnu-vis/DPGP.
442	33:1
443	34:INTRODUCTION
444	35:Embodied agents show a steadily increasing capacity to perceive and interact with their environ-
445	36:ments in human-like ways, while autonomously handling planning, decision-making, and action ex-
446	37:ecution (ichter et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023). These advances have generated considerable interest
447	38:in such agents, particularly for tasks requiring cooperative execution in dynamic environments (Seo
448	39:et al., 2026). Consider two household agents rearranging a home: each may search different rooms
449	40:and transport objects individually, yet through interaction they discover that some objects require
450	41:both agents. Such tasks, whose collaborative requirements must be discovered rather than specified
451	42:in advance, pose a significant challenge to agent cooperation planning: the agents must share newly
452	43:acquired evidence, coordinate a rendezvous, and revise the allocation of the remaining work.
453	44:To tackle the challenges in agent cooperation planning, many methods have been proposed (Zhang
454	45:et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025; Zu et al., 2025; Seo et al., 2025; Jain et al., 2020; Kang et al., 2026).
455	46:Early studies have primarily focused on Cooperation-Optional Tasks (Figure 1(a)), in which each
456	47:task can be handled independently by a single agent, but involving multiple agents can further im-
457	48:prove results through parallel exploration and task allocation (Zhang et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2025;
458	--INTRO END--
459	93:from multiple agents and this need is known in advance. (c) Hidden-Cooperation Tasks, where the
460	94:need for cooperation only becomes apparent after an agent interacts with task-related targets.
461	95:common: the need to cooperate only becomes apparent after an agent observes or interacts with task-
462	96:related targets. In such tasks, the agents must first explore the environment to establish situational
463	97:awareness (Figure 1①); then interact with task-related targets to identify those requiring coopera-
464	98:tion (Figure 1②); next exchange the information gathered and align plans with others (Figure 1③);
465	99:finally execute jointly the hidden-cooperation tasks (Figure 1④). This complex process reveals a
466	100:critical yet underexplored problem: how to evaluate and enable effective agent cooperation in
467	101:hidden-cooperation tasks when cooperation requirements must be discovered by the agents?
468	102:In this paper, we introduce HiddenCoop, a benchmark for evaluating agent cooperation in hidden-
469	103:cooperation tasks, and Discovery-Probability Graph Planning (DPGP), a method for enabling effec-
470	104:tive agent cooperation in such tasks. HiddenCoop is built on C-WAH and TDW-MAT (Zhang et al.,
471	105:2024) and includes both ordinary and cooperative household tasks. Cooperative tasks can only be
472	106:completed by two agents, a requirement that remains unknown to the agents until they attempt them.
473	107:To model the uncertainty during discovering and completing these cooperative tasks, DPGP builds
474	108:its core around a discovery-probability graph. This graph encodes, for a given cooperative task, the
475	109:probability distribution over the number of task-related targets and their locations. As discoveries
476	110:unfold, the graph is updated dynamically and shared among the agents, enabling precise informa-
477	111:tion sharing and efficient transmission. Based on this graph, a search algorithm is applied to find the
478	112:action plans that minimize the expected costs. Experiments show that DPGP achieves cooperative-
479	113:task success rates of 99.3% on C-WAH and 58.3% on TDW-MAT, exceeding all compared baselines.
480	114:It also achieves lower overall embodied execution time and substantially lower LLM token usage
481	115:compared to baselines. In summary, our contributions are threefold:
482	116:• A new benchmark, HiddenCoop, for evaluating agent cooperation in hidden-cooperation tasks.
483	117:• A Discovery-Probability Graph Planning method for enabling effective agent cooperation in
484	118:hidden-cooperation tasks.
485	119:• A series of experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness and efficiency of our method.
486	120:2

491	179:using only its history of local observations and actions, execution feedback, and messages delivered
492	180:to it. The action and communication rules are public, but complete object locations and unconfirmed
493	181:cooperation requirements are not provided.
494	182:For task-relevant category c, we distinguish its requirement from agent i’s confirmed knowledge:

501	189:instances of a category; unknown denotes unconfirmed knowledge, not a third object type.

579	--RESULTS--
580	747:MAIN RESULTS
581	748:Table 1 shows that DPGP delivers the best overall and cooperative-task performance in both environ-
582	749:ments, achieving the highest Task SR, lowest EET, and highest TGC-AUC. Its overall success rates
583	750:reach 99.7% on C-WAH and 64.6% on TDW-MAT, while cooperative-task success reaches 99.3%
584	751:and 58.3%, respectively. Across all methods, cooperative tasks reduce success and delay goal com-
585	752:pletion, reflecting the combined burden of discovering cooperation requirements and executing joint
586	753:actions. DPGP is least affected by this transition, exhibiting the smallest ordinary-to-cooperative
587	754:drops in Task SR and TGC-AUC, together with the smallest increase in EET, in both environments.
588	755:The framework also requires substantially fewer LLM tokens, averaging only 7.16k and 1.41k per
589	756:evaluated episode on C-WAH and TDW-MAT, respectively.
590	757:Figure 3 complements the main table by examining two effects of the execution budget. First,
591	758:failed episodes can consume the available budget, making average EET sensitive to the chosen
592	759:cutoff. Panel (a) therefore compares the same 264 C-WAH records completed successfully by all five
593	760:methods within the 600 s collection budget. On this common-success intersection, DPGP reduces
594	761:EET by 20.2% relative to the fastest baseline, PCE, demonstrating an efficiency advantage without
595	762:failed-episode termination times. Second, panel (b) evaluates all C-WAH records across 100–600 s
596	763:cutoffs, placing the main table’s 200 s result in a broader budget range. DPGP maintains the highest
597	764:or tied-highest success rate throughout; at 150 s, it achieves 95.0% versus 75.7% for the strongest
598	765:baseline. The advantage is therefore not confined to the selected cutoff, while convergence at larger
599	766:budgets explains why final success alone can obscure execution-efficiency differences.

610	--CONCLUSION--
611	846:CONCLUSION
612	847:We introduced HiddenCoop to study multi-agent exploration and execution with interaction-revealed
613	848:cooperation requirements.
614	849:Our framework, DPGP, combines confirmed facts with resource-
615	850:discovery beliefs to evaluate exploration and transport jointly under execution constraints. Experi-
616	851:ments on C-WAH and TDW-MAT show strong cooperative-task performance, improved execution
617	852:efficiency and goal progress, and substantially lower LLM token usage. Common-success and ex-
618	853:ecution trajectory analyses further distinguish execution efficiency from final task success. These
619	854:findings support evaluating potential discoveries together with their downstream execution costs
620	855:when coordinating partially observable tasks. Future work will investigate larger, heterogeneous
621	856:teams and more complex cooperation requirements.

630	69:ABSTRACT
631	70:Reusable Web-agent verification requires a rule to follow chang-
632	71:ing requirements and support subsequent execution. We introduce
633	72:AgentProofBench, which connects paired tests of a frozen accep-
634	73:tance rule to execution from identical saved openings. The resource
635	74:spans 97 tasks, 79 families, and four Web services. Experiments with
636	75:DeepSeek Flash/Pro establish two linked measurements. Across 48
637	76:families, complete-panel and decision-replay tests retain 82/96 Flash
638	77:and 79/96 Pro source programs; paired reuse–rebuild BA intervals
639	78:are [−5.47, 1.57] and [−10.16, 0.00] percentage points. Across 22
640	79:execution families, deployment-state panel correctness separates
641	80:program assignments whose two saved openings are both delivered
642	81:correctly: 32/33 assignments with error-free panels, versus 1/11
643	82:with panel errors. All reference-defined program-gate regressions
644	83:and withheld deliveries occur in the latter group. Neutral continua-
645	84:tion attains the highest correct delivery under the tested generic
646	85:feedback, providing a concrete baseline for measuring the value
647	86:added by a gate. Released instructions, states, programs, reference
648	87:∗Corresponding author. jening@cs.cmu.edu.
649	88:rules, and trajectories connect each test failure to its execution con-
650	89:sequences. AgentProofBench makes reusable verification assessable
651	90:at both the requirement and policy levels.
652	91:KEYWORDS
653	92:Web agents, reusable verifiers, verifier generation, initial-state gen-
654	93:eralization, execution-based evaluation
655	94:1
656	95:INTRODUCTION
657	96:Reusable acceptance checks can make Web-agent operation fast and
658	97:inspectable. A program can encode the conditions for completing a
659	98:task, inspect the relevant business state, and issue the same explicit
660	99:checks on subsequent executions. The central challenge is that the
661	100:public instruction can stay fixed while the required work changes.

663	102:or the value that must be preserved comes from the initial state of

669	137:evidence, and a reconstructable business state.
670	138:The benchmark provides three contributions.
671	139:• A paired reuse test that holds the public instruction and
672	140:generated program fixed while changing its required initial-

674	142:cisions measure complementary obligations.

676	144:correctness to matched policy outcomes. The 22-family

679	147:• An executable resource with 97 tasks across four Web ser-
680	148:vices, including versioned reference rules, legal alternatives,
681	149:reconstructable states, programs, and action histories.
682	150:The central empirical result is the connection between tests
683	151:and execution. Programs with error-free deployment-state panels
684	152:correctly deliver both saved openings in 32 of 33 assignments, com-
685	153:pared with one of eleven assignments whose panels contain errors.
686	154:The paired reuse study explains which requirements those panels
687	155:exercise; replay witnesses expose additional errors in three source
688	156:programs. Fixed-instance acceptance and cost profiles then describe
