784	--ABSTRACT--
785	16:ABSTRACT
786	17:Small open language models can call tools, but they do not reason about what a call does: they delete
787	18:without asking, repeat writes, re-read state they already hold, and issue one call per turn where a
788	19:short program would do. We introduce EffectWorld, an executable world of effect-typed tools in
789	20:which every tool declares its effect (pure, read, write or destructive), whether it is idempotent, and
790	21:which resources it reads and writes. These declarations let a replay verifier decide whether a trace is
791	22:effect-safe without labels or judge models, let an executor run tool programs of several dependent
792	23:calls in one turn, and let a compiler-style optimizer turn wasteful traces into verified training signal;
793	24:together they make EffectWorld a benchmark of effect safety and call efficiency. Low-rank adapters
794	25:trained on EffectWorld data deliver large gains: on Qwen3-4B, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) raises
795	26:task success from 53% to 99% in distribution, from 52% to 81% on a held-out split with unseen
796	27:task kinds and distractor tools, and from 74% to 83% on an unseen online-shopping domain, with
797	28:about a third of the output tokens. The gains carry over to three model families, lifting Qwen3-1.7B,
798	29:Phi-4-mini and Falcon3-3B from 4–25% to 69–99% in distribution and by 26 to 55 points on the
799	30:held-out splits. On the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) the adapter matches the
800	31:base model’s live accuracy and raises multi-turn accuracy from 21.9 to 26.6, and a recipe with
801	32:near-miss declines lifts the BFCL average above the base model’s (70.0 against 68.7) while matching
802	33:its irrelevance detection. Along the way we uncover and fix a pitfall that in-domain evaluation alone
803	34:would miss: refusal templates in widely used public tool-use corpora teach a small model not to
804	35:call tools, cutting BFCL non-live accuracy from 88.0 to 31.4, and filtering them restores 84.8. We
805	36:also find that positive examples, not negative ones, carry the learning: suppression and preference
806	37:objectives on the verified negatives add nothing over an SFT-only control, while targeted positives
807	38:move exactly the behaviour they show. Efficiency transfers to unseen tools out of the box; effect
808	39:discipline does so only partly, and EffectWorld makes that remaining gap measurable for future work.
809	40:1
810	41:Introduction
811	42:A tool-calling agent is efficient when it reaches the intended final state with few calls, few turns and few generated
812	43:tokens, and safe when it never takes an irreversible action the user has not approved. Public benchmarks such as the
813	44:Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) mostly score whether a call is well formed (Patil et al., 2024, 2025).
814	45:They say little about whether an agent re-reads data it already has, serialises independent look-ups, or cancels a meeting
815	46:without asking. Tool protocols already annotate tools as read-only, destructive or idempotent (Anthropic, 2024; Model
816	47:Context Protocol contributors, 2025), yet small open models are not trained to act on such annotations, and, as we
817	48:found in our own first adapters, the annotations often never reach the model at all. The idea is older than agents:
818	49:type-and-effect systems let a compiler reason about what a piece of code may read or write (Lucassen and Gifford,
819	--INTRO END--
820	65:labelled negative examples.
821	66:Negative examples for tool agents are usually mined from model failures or produced by ad-hoc perturbation. Ours
822	67:differ in one respect: an efficiency negative is a call the optimizer has shown to be unnecessary, because replaying
823	68:the trace without it reaches the same final state with no new errors. We combine these with rule-based correctness
824	69:and policy negatives and train adapters to suppress the bad action at the exact prefix where it occurs, keeping the
825	70:span-localised recipe of LUNE (Liu et al., 2025), which trains only low-rank adapters (LoRA) on negative examples,
826	71:but replacing its objective with suppression by unlikelihood training (UL; Welleck et al., 2020) or negative preference
827	72:optimisation (NPO; Zhang et al., 2024a), since for an agent the negative target is an action that must not be produced.
828	73:We make five contributions.
829	74:1. EffectWorld, an effect-typed executable tool world with a replay verifier, a scripted user, a training domain
830	75:and two test-only splits: a hard split with unseen task kinds and distractor tools, and an online-shopping
831	76:(commerce) domain whose tools never appear in training (§§3.1–3.4).
832	77:2. Tool programs: a minimal $ref convention that lets one assistant turn express a dependency graph of calls
833	78:inside native tool-call blocks, so existing parsers and benchmarks keep working (§3.2).
834	79:3. A compiler-style trace optimizer with footprint-based legality, and a taxonomy of 19 negative classes derived
835	80:from its diffs, from rule perturbations and from policy checks, each mapped to the BFCL categories it should
836	81:affect (§3.5).
837	82:4. A controlled comparison of two suppression objectives (UL, NPO) against direct preference optimisation

872	482:The commerce domain is an online-shopping assistant. Its state holds a product catalogue with prices and stock, the
873	483:user’s cart, past orders with their delivery status, and saved addresses and payment methods. Its 17 tools search and
874	484:read products, edit the cart, list and read orders, place an order (which pays for it), change an order’s delivery address,
875	485:cancel an order and request a refund. None of them shares a name, an argument or an entity type with the workspace
876	486:tools, and no commerce trajectory is used in training. The 13 task kinds range from look-ups (the price of a product, a
877	487:comparison of two prices, the status of an order) and cart edits, including adding several items with one batch call, to the
878	488:three irreversible actions, buying, cancelling and refunding, each of which must follow a confirmed proposal. In four
879	489:kinds the correct outcome is that nothing irreversible happens: an order that has already shipped cannot be cancelled, a
880	490:product that is missing from the catalogue or out of stock cannot be bought, and one request needs no tool at all.
881	491:We chose a shop for three reasons. Its effects have the same structure as the workspace’s, with reads, reversible writes
882	492:and irreversible actions, so the five policies of the system prompt apply unchanged: a model that has learnt them
883	493:over effects should follow them here, whereas a model that has learnt them over tool names has nothing to go on. Its
884	494:irreversible actions move money, so an unconfirmed call is a failure that needs no argument. And retail is one of the
885	495:domains of widely used agent benchmarks such as τ-bench (Yao et al., 2024), so the behaviour it tests is the one agents
886	496:are deployed for. The commerce split therefore measures transfer: whether what the adapters learn about efficiency and

932	1769:EffectWorld is small: nine task kinds in one training domain, one test-only domain, and template utterances (paraphrases

934	1771:proposal it recognises as one, including a proposal to act on the wrong entity; the verifier counts any proposal the
935	1772:scripted user confirmed as confirmed. A model that asks, is told the entity does not exist, and then proposes a substitute
936	1773:is therefore scored as if it had not asked (Figure 6). Efficiency negatives are only as good as the optimizer’s provenance

948	1785:Conclusion
949	1786:Declaring what tools do makes efficiency and safety checkable properties of a trace. In EffectWorld the declarations
950	1787:drive a replay verifier that decides effect safety without labels or judge models, an optimizer that proves calls unnecessary,

957	--ABSTRACT--
958	16:ABSTRACT
959	17:Tool-using language models are increasingly deployed in conversational settings,
960	18:yet most large-scale tool-use benchmarks focus on isolated requests. We introduce
961	19:ToolTurns, a benchmark of 2,620 problems spanning 1,827 tools and 11,004 API
962	20:endpoints across 47 categories. Each dialogue begins with an intentionally under-
963	21:specified request and continues through two context-dependent follow-ups, testing
964	22:clarification, tool use, and retention of conversational context. We also introduce
965	23:an open-source user simulator that reveals withheld context through dialogue and
966	24:generates follow-up requests, with a checker–fixer pipeline for improving its turns.
967	25:Across nine language models, the best agent resolves 69.6% of individual requests
968	26:but completes only 39.8% of full dialogues. Under this evaluation protocol, every
969	27:evaluated model receives lower success scores on follow-up requests than on the
970	28:initial request, and dialogue-quality rubric scores and task success can rank models
971	29:very differently. Paired turn-level evaluation shows that the checker–fixer reduces
972	30:detected dialogue defects, and blind human evaluation favors the revised turns.
973	31:ToolTurns provides a testbed for evaluating whether agents sustain task success
974	32:across multi-turn dialogue with tools.
975	33:1
976	34:INTRODUCTION
977	35:A tool-using assistant must do more than answer an initial request. A user asking “What games are
978	36:happening this weekend?” may omit the sport or location, then ask follow-up questions about the
979	37:results. The assistant must elicit missing information, use the available APIs, and carry relevant
980	38:context into subsequent requests. These decisions shape the conversation itself: an assistant’s
981	39:clarification or answer changes what the user says next. Evaluating this behavior therefore requires
982	40:following the agent through an interaction, including the requests that arise after its first answer.
983	41:Existing benchmarks capture different aspects of this challenge (Table 1). ToolBench (Qin et al.,
984	42:2024) provides broad API coverage, while ToolDial (Shim et al., 2025) evaluates conversational
985	43:tool-use capabilities from recorded dialogue histories. Interactive benchmarks such as τ-bench
986	44:(Yao et al., 2024) and ToolSandbox (Lu et al., 2025) evaluate agents within stateful application
987	45:environments; τ 2-bench (Barres et al., 2025) further tests coordination when users can also act on the
988	46:environment. We study the combination of broad API coverage and adaptive, end-to-end dialogue
989	47:evaluation: whether agents can clarify underspecified requests and resolve related follow-ups across
990	48:diverse tool sets.
991	49:We introduce ToolTurns, a benchmark of 2,620 initially underspecified problems spanning 1,827
992	--INTRO END--

1003	70:revised message in 63.3% of 120 sampled pairs (Appendix B.2.3, Appendix B.3). We evaluate task
1004	71:completion separately from dialogue quality, reporting both the fraction of requests resolved and the
1005	72:fraction of dialogues in which all three requests succeed.
1006	73:Across nine proprietary and open-weight agent models, our evaluator reports a highest subtask
1007	74:success rate of 69.6% and a highest full-dialogue completion rate of 39.8% (§4). Under the existing
1008	75:evaluation protocol, every evaluated model receives lower success scores on both follow-ups than
1009	76:on the initial request. Task-success rankings also differ from rankings under the dialogue-quality
1010	77:rubric. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating completion throughout a conversation
1011	78:and measuring it directly alongside diagnostic quality scores.
1012	79:Our contributions are:
1013	80:1. ToolTurns, a benchmark combining broad API coverage with adaptive dialogue: 2,620
1014	81:problems with clarification exchanges and follow-up requests evaluated along the agent’s
1015	82:own trajectory.
1016	83:2. A user-simulation pipeline with targeted message revision, evaluated through paired auto-
1017	84:matic measurements and blind human annotation.
1018	85:3. An evaluation of nine agents that characterizes request-level and full-dialogue completion,
1019	86:follow-up performance, and differences between task-success and dialogue-quality rankings.

1021	--METHOD--
1022	237:BENCHMARK DESIGN
1023	238:3.1
1024	239:PROBLEM DESIGN
1025	240:A ToolTurns problem is a triple (qi, Ti, Gi), where qi is the user’s initial natural-language query, Ti
1026	241:is a fixed set of callable tool endpoints and their schemas, and Gi = {(sij, vij)}mi
1027	242:j=1 is the unseen
1028	243:user’s goal, represented as a set of slot–value constraints. Each slot sij corresponds to an argument in
1029	244:a tool schema, and vij is the value that the user has in mind but does not initially specify in qi.
1030	245:The dialogue begins with qi. At each step t, conditioned on the dialogue history and the schemas
1031	246:of Ti, the agent selects an action at ∈A(Ti) that either (1) invokes an endpoint and receives a tool
1032	247:observation ot, (2) sends a message to the user and receives a user response ot, or (3) completes the
1033	248:current request with a final answer yt. In response to a clarification request, the user simulator reveals
1034	249:relevant slot values from Gi.

1063	383:EVALUATION DESIGN
1064	384:We evaluate each generated dialogue along two axes: dialogue quality, measured by a five-aspect
1065	385:LLM-judged rubric, and task success, a per-subtask binary judgment of whether the user’s informa-
1066	386:tion need for that query was fully resolved. Both rely on LLM judges with structured function-calling
1067	387:outputs and a fixed prompt set across conditions.
1068	388:3.4.1
1069	389:DIALOGUE QUALITY RUBRIC
1070	390:The dialogue quality rubric scores each generated dialogue across five aspects, one LLM call per
1071	391:aspect: consistency, factual coherence between the assistant’s claims and tool outputs; relevance,
1072	392:whether assistant turns address the user’s request; efficiency, economy of tool calls and turns; cor-
1073	393:rectness, whether the final answer is factually right with respect to tool evidence; and adaptability,
1074	394:handling of clarifications, corrections, and underspecified inputs. Each aspect is scored on a discrete
1075	395:[0, 1] scale with five levels (0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0) and the judge additionally returns a brief justifica-
1076	396:tion. Aspect scores are combined into a single weighted aggregate (correctness 0.30; consistency,
1077	397:relevance, efficiency 0.20 each; adaptability 0.10). Because scores take only five discrete values,
1078	398:mean differences at the second decimal place correspond to a one-level shift on a small fraction of
1079	399:dialogues, so we do not read small second-decimal gaps as meaningful differences.
1080	400:3.4.2
1081	401:TASK SUCCESS
1082	402:Task success is determined by a hybrid evaluator that applies a deterministic hard-fail gate before
1083	403:invoking an LLM judge. It scores each subtask of the dialogue (the initial query and each follow-up
1084	404:query, §3.2) independently, rather than issuing a single judgment for the dialogue as a whole. The
1085	405:gate handles failure modes that can be identified cheaply and with certainty, so the LLM judge is
1086	406:reserved for cases where the outcome is uncertain.
1087	407:Subtask segmentation. Each dialogue is split into its three main queries (one initial query and
1088	408:num_follow_up_queries = 2 follow-ups), and the gate and LLM judge below are applied separately
1089	409:to each subtask’s slice of the dialogue (its query, turns, tool calls, and tool responses).
1090	410:Deterministic gate. A subtask fails without an LLM call when every substantive tool observation
1091	411:is StableToolBench documentation-placeholder prose, a description of the API rather than live data
1092	412:(for example, “The API call to . .. is designed to provide .. .”), and none of the observations yields
1093	413:data-shaped output such as structured fields, lists, or typed scalars beyond bookkeeping keys like
1094	414:status, success, or code. The gate is rarely decisive: it applies to only 20 of the 70,740 subtasks
1095	415:across the nine agents in §4.1 (0.03%; at most five per agent), placeholder prose appears at all in
1096	416:only 154 (0.2%), and no pooled subtask pass rate in Table 3 moves by more than 0.03 points with or
1097	417:without it, so cache coverage does not account for the failure rates we report.
1098	418:LLM judge. If the gate passes, a single LLM call decides semantic task completion for that
1099	419:subtask via structured function-calling. The judge receives the subtask’s query and its slice of the
1100	420:dialogue (turns, tool calls and their responses, and the assistant’s answer) and must return a boolean
1101	421:task_succeeded with a brief justification. The system prompt instructs the judge to be strict on
1102	422:wrong or missing answers; a subtask passes only if the user’s information need for that query was
1103	423:fully met by the final outcome.
1104	424:Dialogue-level score. A dialogue’s task-success score is the fraction of its subtasks that succeed,
1105	425:success_count / total_subtasks (e.g. 2/3 if the initial query and one of the two follow-ups
1106	426:succeed); a dialogue counts as fully successful only if every subtask succeeds. We report both
1107	427:quantities in §4.1: the pooled subtask pass rate as the headline figure, and the stricter all-subtasks-
1108	428:pass rate alongside it.
1109	429:4
1110	430:EXPERIMENTS
1111	431:We report two experiments: a comparison of nine agent models on dialogue quality and task success
1112	432:(§4.1), and a validation of the simulated user’s turn quality (§4.2).

1121	574:discriminating: requiring all three subtasks of a dialogue to succeed drops every model below 40%,

1123	576:cases out of five. The gap between task success and passing all three highlights the difficulty of
1124	577:ToolTurns. If subtask outcomes within a dialogue were independent, a 69.6% subtask rate would
1125	578:imply a 0.6963 ≈34% all-pass rate; the observed 39.8% is higher, so successes and failures are
1126	579:positively correlated within a dialogue. Either some problems are simply harder, or an agent that
1127	580:establishes the right tool and context early tends to keep succeeding. These two task-success rates

2	--ABSTRACT--
3	24:Abstract
4	25:Reinforcement learning (RL) is central for aligning large lan-
5	26:guage models (LLMs) with complex reasoning, yet the lead-
6	27:ing critic-free algorithm, Group Relative Policy Optimization
7	28:(GRPO), broadcasts a single sequence-level advantage uni-
8	29:formly across long Chain-of-Thought (CoT) generations and
9	30:constrains exploration with an unbounded Kullback-Leibler
10	31:(KL) penalty, which dilutes token-level supervision and in-
11	32:duces gradient instability and mode-seeking conservatism.
12	33:We propose TIDE (Token-level Importance via Deviation
13	34:and Entropy), a critic-free RL framework that reinterprets
14	35:distribution deviation as a guiding signal rather than a rigid
15	36:penalty. TIDE replaces the volatile reverse KL divergence
16	37:with the bounded Hellinger distance, safely quantifying
17	38:token-level exploration without risk of gradient explosion.
18	39:To separate genuine reasoning breakthroughs from confi-
19	40:dent hallucinations, an entropy gating mechanism scales
20	41:this deviation by the policy’s predictive uncertainty, and
21	42:the gated scores redistribute the sequence-level advantage
22	43:across tokens. The resulting updates amplify exploratory
23	44:steps while suppressing low-entropy deviations, without a
24	45:value network and with negligible overhead. Across in-
25	46:domain, held-out, and out-of-domain benchmarks, TIDE out-
26	47:performs strong critic-free baselines: on the Qwen2.5-32B
27	48:backbone it reaches 60.0% and 46.0% Avg@32 accuracy on
28	49:AIME 2024 and AIME 2025, respectively, above competitive
29	50:baselines such as DAPO. Token-level attribution, causal per-
30	51:turbation, and exploration analyses further support the inter-
31	52:pretation that the entropy-gated deviation identifies pivotal
32	53:reasoning steps rather than merely perturbing optimization
33	54:dynamics.

79	##### library/04_credit_assignment/2609.12424_GranularityAdaptiveCredit/2609.12424_GranularityAdaptiveCredit_fulltext.txt  (1792 lines)
80	--ABSTRACT--
81	32:ABSTRACT
82	33:Long-horizon language-model agents trained with reinforcement learning often
83	34:receive sparse outcome rewards that do not reveal which decisions along a tra-
84	35:jectory deserve credit. Episode-level advantages provide coarse trajectory-wide
85	36:credit, while step-level comparisons offer finer resolution with context-dependent
86	37:estimation noise. We propose Granularity-Adaptive Credit Assignment (GACA),
87	38:a critic-free method that adaptively mixes episode- and step-level credit for each
88	39:decision during policy optimization. GACA normalizes the sampled response’s
89	40:mean per-token negative log-likelihood (NLL) within each trajectory and uses the
90	41:resulting criticality score to determine the step-specific mixture. The computation
91	42:reuses rollout log-probabilities without additional training rollouts or model eval-
92	43:uations. Our analysis characterizes optimal score-dependent mixing and derives
93	44:conditions linking expected NLL to a lower bound on the preferred step-level
94	45:weight. Across ALFWorld and WebShop with 1.5B and 7B backbones, GACA
95	46:achieves the highest reported mean success rates among the compared methods,
96	47:while introducing negligible additional computation.
97	48:1
98	49:INTRODUCTION
99	50:Language-model agents act over many steps to complete household tasks, browse web stores, and
100	51:use external tools (Yao et al., 2022b; Shridhar et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2022a). Reinforcement learning
101	52:can improve these agents using task outcomes (Ouyang et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2025), but a sparse
102	53:terminal reward leaves a difficult credit-assignment problem: which decisions should receive the
103	54:learning signal? A trajectory can contain both consequential choices and actions whose alternatives
104	55:would have little effect on the outcome (Arjona-Medina et al., 2019).
105	56:Critic-free methods avoid training a value model by comparing several rollouts of the same task.
106	57:GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) computes an episode-level relative advantage and broadcasts it to every
107	58:action. GiGPO (Feng et al., 2026) adds local resolution by grouping steps with the same anchor
108	59:observation and comparing their continuation returns. Its fixed combination of episode- and step-
109	60:level signals leaves a further question: should every decision rely on these two credit estimates in
110	61:the same proportion?
111	62:The two granularities offer a decision-dependent estimation trade-off. Episode credit spreads the
112	63:outcome over all decisions, while step credit separates local continuations using finite, context-
113	64:dependent comparison groups.
114	65:We propose Granularity-Adaptive Credit Assignment (GACA),
115	--INTRO END--
116	69:ity score that measures how surprising the response is relative to other responses in that interaction.
117	70:1
118	71:arXiv:2609.12424v2  [cs.LG]  4 Oct 2026
119	72:
120	73:============================================================
121	74:=== PAGE 2 ===
122	75:============================================================
123	76:
124	77:Preprint
125	78:A bounded mapping converts this score into a step-specific mixing weight, placing more weight
126	79:on step-level credit at higher scores. These computations reuse quantities already available for the
127	80:policy update, requiring no additional model or training rollouts.
128	81:Our analysis characterizes how a score-dependent mixture balances the errors of the two credit
129	82:estimates. It then identifies conditions under which greater variation in action values favors step-
130	83:level credit and expected NLL provides a lower bound on that variation. These results motivate
131	84:increasing the weight of local credit with the NLL-based score.
132	85:GACA complements methods that refine the step estimator, including history-consistent grouping
133	86:in HGPO (He et al., 2026), behavior-aware grouping in BiPACE (Wang et al., 2026a), and progress-
134	87:conditioned credit in ProGPO (Yang et al., 2026). Uncertainty-based modulation in AEM and
135	88:STARE rescales an existing advantage (Zhao et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026); GACA uses uncer-
136	89:tainty to control the relative contribution of two credit granularities. Appendix A discusses these
137	90:connections.
138	91:Our evaluation covers ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-Instruct at 1.5B and 7B scales. On
139	92:ALFWorld 1.5B, matched ablations compare GACA with five fixed mixtures and within-trajectory
140	93:random score assignment. Adaptive mixing reaches 96.88% success, compared with 93.05% for the
141	94:best tested fixed mixture and 88.54% for random assignment. These comparisons examine both the
142	95:choice of mixing weights and their assignment to individual decisions.

236	--CONCLUSION--
237	674:CONCLUSION
238	675:GACA uses rollout NLL to adapt the mixture of episode- and step-level credit during policy opti-
239	676:mization, without additional training rollouts or model evaluations. Conditional risk analysis char-
240	677:acterizes score-dependent mixing and conditions favoring finer credit. Across ALFWorld and Web-
241	678:Shop with two backbone sizes, GACA achieves the highest reported mean success rates among
242	679:the compared methods. In matched ALFWorld ablations, GACA improves over the tested fixed
243	680:weights and within-trajectory random assignment. Together, these results support step-dependent
244	681:credit mixing as a practical design choice for critic-free agent training.

254	##### library/04_credit_assignment/2610.00838_SHARPO/2610.00838_SHARPO_fulltext.txt  (903 lines)
255	--ABSTRACT--
256	17:Abstract
257	18:Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) trains a large language model (LLM) to act
258	19:over long, multi-step interactions. However, a single localized error can cause
259	20:task failure, while trajectory-level rewards provide limited guidance for assigning
260	21:credit to individual decisions. To address this limitation, we introduce Segment-
261	22:level Hindsight Advantage Reweighting for Policy Optimization (SHARPO), a
262	23:credit-assignment mechanism that refines Group Relative Policy Optimization
263	24:(GRPO) at the level of environment-facing segments. Inspired by the existing
264	25:on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) method, SHARPO computes teacher–student
265	26:log-probability gaps within each segment and uses the resulting signal to compute
266	27:a bounded multiplier on the GRPO advantage. This multiplier is shared by all
267	28:tokens within the segment, allowing credit to vary across different segments. With
268	29:Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, SHARPO outperforms existing baselines on the ALFWorld
269	30:and WebShop benchmarks, including GRPO, SDAR, RLSD, and StepOPSD.
270	31:1
271	32:Introduction
272	33:Post-training plays a key role in adapting large language models (LLMs) to specific tasks and
273	34:improving their performance in interactive environments [Ouyang et al., 2022, Jin et al., 2025].
274	35:Reinforcement learning (RL) supports this adaptation by optimizing agent behavior using feedback
275	36:from task outcomes. When these outcomes can be automatically verified, their correctness provides
276	37:a direct reward signal for training, as demonstrated in mathematical reasoning and search-based
277	38:question answering [Guo et al., 2025a, Jin et al., 2025]. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)
278	39:offers an efficient approach to learning from such rewards without training a separate value network
279	40:[Shao et al., 2024]. For each task, GRPO samples a group of rollouts and normalizes their rewards
280	41:within the group to estimate advantages. Under outcome supervision, each rollout receives a single
281	42:advantage that is shared by all of its generated tokens.
282	43:In multi-turn interactions, however, an agent must make a sequence of decisions before receiving
283	44:feedback on the final outcome. In this case, the rewards are sparse and are available only at the end
284	45:of an episode, hence they provide little direct information about the contribution of each intermediate
285	46:step to that outcome. For example, a shopping agent may find a suitable product but select an incorrect
286	47:option before completing the purchase. If the resulting trajectory receives a negative advantage,
287	48:both the useful search and the mistaken selection inherit the same negative coefficient. The shared
288	49:advantage therefore does not distinguish actions that helped accomplish the task from those that led
289	50:to failure. This motivates us to design a credit-assignment mechanism in RL that uses finer-grained
290	--INTRO END--
291	116:feedback within selected interaction segments and assigns a shared advantage weight to each segment.
292	117:Compared to StepOPSD [Zhang et al., 2026], which retains token-specific weights within selected
293	118:action-centered spans, SHARPO aggregates the feedback within each segment before determining its
294	119:weight. Favorable and unfavorable evidence across a substep is therefore considered jointly, allowing
295	120:the credit adjustment to reflect the teacher’s overall support for the complete decision.
296	121:We evaluate SHARPO on ALFWorld and WebShop using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. As shown in Figure 1,
297	122:SHARPO achieves higher final validation success rates than baselines on both benchmarks at both
298	123:parameter configurations. To summarize, our main contributions are threefold:
299	124:• We propose SHARPO, a segment-level credit-assignment method that uses successful peer
300	125:rollouts to guide the weighting of intermediate decisions in GRPO. By aggregating self-
301	126:distillation feedback over meaningful interaction segments, it supplements sparse outcome
302	127:supervision without requiring an external teacher or additional environment rollouts.
303	128:2
304	129:
305	130:============================================================
306	131:=== PAGE 3 ===
307	132:============================================================
308	133:
309	134:• We provide a theoretical explanation of why this self-distillation feedback is useful in our
310	135:method and how it supports finer-grained credit assignment.
311	136:• We demonstrate that SHARPO outperforms GRPO, RLSD, SDAR, and StepOPSD on both
312	137:ALFWorld and WebShop. Analyses of subtask success rates and product-matching quality
313	138:further characterize these gains.
314	139:2
315	140:Method
316	141:We first review GRPO and OPSD in Section 2.1 and then present SHARPO in Section 2.2. Section 2.3
317	142:provides a theoretical analysis of our segment-level credit assignment.
318	143:2.1
319	--METHOD--
320	140:Method
321	141:We first review GRPO and OPSD in Section 2.1 and then present SHARPO in Section 2.2. Section 2.3
322	142:provides a theoretical analysis of our segment-level credit assignment.
323	143:2.1
324	144:Preliminaries: GRPO and OPSD
325	145:We consider an LLM agent initialized from a pretrained model, with trainable parameters θ. Its
326	146:autoregressive policy πθ defines a probability distribution over the next token given the available
327	147:context. Starting from a task prompt x, the agent generates responses and receives observations
328	148:from the environment after executing actions. Together, these responses and observations form an
329	149:interaction trajectory τ. Let yℓdenote the ℓ-th token generated by the agent across τ, and let T be the
330	150:total number of such tokens. Each token is sampled as yℓ∼πθ(· | cℓ), where cℓcontains the prompt
331	151:x, previously generated tokens, and environment observations available before yℓ. At the end of the
332	152:episode, a verifier assigns r(τ) = 1 if the task succeeds and 0 otherwise. We use RL post-training
333	153:methods to update the policy parameters θ so as to maximize the expected terminal reward.
334	154:Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).
335	155:GRPO [Shao et al., 2024] samples G trajectories

360	--EXP SETUP--
361	383:Experiments
362	384:We conduct experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop to demonstrate the effectiveness of SHARPO
363	385:through comparisons with existing RL baselines.
364	386:3.1
365	387:Setup
366	388:We fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [Yang et al., 2024] on two interactive benchmarks, ALFWorld
367	389:[Shridhar et al., 2021] and WebShop [Yao et al., 2022]. ALFWorld covers six families of household
368	390:tasks. WebShop requires agents to search for and purchase products that satisfy user requests. Both
369	391:environments use binary terminal success rewards for training.
370	392:All methods share the same backbone, prompts, environments, reward function, optimizer, rollout
371	393:settings, and evaluation protocol. We train each configuration for 200 optimization steps with 16
372	394:tasks per batch, a learning rate of 5 × 10−7, and a KL coefficient of βKL = 0.01. For SHARPO, we
373	395:set α = 0.2, ρmin = 0.25, and ρmax = 4. We evaluate two mixing weights, λ ∈{0.2, 0.05}, each
374	396:held fixed throughout training.
375	397:Our primary metric is the final validation success rate at step 200, evaluated on 128 held-out tasks. We
376	398:report the mean and sample standard deviation over three independent runs. To examine performance
377	399:in more detail, we also report subtask success rates by ALFWorld task family and the continuous task
378	400:score in WebShop, which measures how well the purchased product matches the request.
379	401:We compare our SHARPO with GRPO [Shao et al., 2024], which assigns a single outcome-derived
380	402:advantage to all generated tokens within each trajectory. We also consider baselines that combine RL

411	--RESULTS--
412	466:Main results
413	467:Table 1 reports the overall comparison. SHARPO achieves the highest mean final validation success
414	468:rate on both benchmarks at both tested mixing weights. Relative to GRPO, the gains are 13.80–14.32
415	469:percentage points on ALFWorld and 8.85–9.11 points on WebShop. Compared with StepOPSD
416	470:at the corresponding reported λ values, SHARPO gains 6.77 points on ALFWorld at both settings
417	471:and 5.99–7.55 points on WebShop. These results support the effectiveness of using segment-level
418	472:self-distillation feedback to refine GRPO credit assignment.
419	473:The improvements persist across both tested mixing weights. Although λ = 0.2 and λ = 0.05 differ
420	474:by a factor of four, their mean success rates differ by only 0.52 percentage points on ALFWorld
421	475:and 0.26 points on WebShop. Across the three independent runs, SHARPO has lower variability
422	476:than GRPO on ALFWorld, with standard deviations of 2.82 and 1.19 points compared with 7.83.
423	477:On WebShop, its standard deviations of 1.19 and 1.35 points are comparable to GRPO’s 1.19. The
424	478:higher mean success rates therefore accompany lower run-to-run variability on ALFWorld and similar
425	479:variability on WebShop.
426	480:3.3
427	481:Fine-grained analysis
428	482:Subtask performance.
429	483:Table 2 shows that SHARPO performs strongly across the six ALFWorld
430	484:task families. At both tested mixing weights λ = 0.2 and λ = 0.05, it outperforms all evaluated
431	485:baselines on Pick, Clean, Cool, and Pick2, and remains within 0.30 percentage points of the best
432	486:baseline on Look. These broad gains persist across the two mixing weights, which differ by a factor
433	487:of four.
434	488:The improvements extend to complicated tasks such as Heat, Cool, and Pick2, which requires
435	489:object-state changes or the handling of multiple objects. On Pick2, SHARPO exceeds the strongest
436	490:baseline by 7.02 and 10.10 percentage points at λ = 0.2 and 0.05, respectively. On Cool, λ = 0.2
437	491:improves over the strongest baseline by 6.89 percentage points. On Heat, λ = 0.05 exceeds SDAR,
438	492:the strongest baseline for this task, by 6.67 percentage points. These tasks require several coordinated
439	493:decisions, and a final failure can follow both useful intermediate actions and local mistakes. The gains
440	494:are consistent with the motivation for segment-level credit assignment, which uses successful-peer
441	495:feedback to differentiate the training weights of intermediate decisions.
442	--CONCLUSION--
443	655:Conclusion
444	656:In long-horizon tasks, RL agents often receive rewards only when an episode ends. These sparse
445	657:rewards provide little direct feedback on which intermediate decisions helped or harmed task com-
446	658:pletion. SHARPO addresses this credit-assignment problem through successful-peer hindsight. It
447	659:aggregates teacher–student log-probability gaps within complete interaction segments before assign-
448	660:ing each segment a shared, bounded advantage weight, providing differentiated feedback without a
449	661:learned critic.
450	662:Our analysis explains how the hindsight correction aligns with local decision value under an ideal
451	663:success-conditioned reference. On ALFWorld and WebShop, SHARPO achieves higher mean final
452	664:success than the baselines at both tested mixing weights. These results support supplementing sparse
453	665:outcome supervision with segment-level hindsight feedback for long-horizon agent learning.
454	666:References
455	667:Long Ouyang, Jeffrey Wu, Xu Jiang, Diogo Almeida, Carroll Wainwright, Pamela Mishkin, Chong
456	668:Zhang, Sandhini Agarwal, Katarina Slama, Alex Ray, et al. Training language models to follow
457	669:instructions with human feedback. Advances in neural information processing systems, 35:27730–
458	670:27744, 2022.

460	##### library/04_credit_assignment/2610.29292_ContrastiveAttributionTopology/2610.29292_ContrastiveAttributionTopology_fulltext.txt  (1306 lines)
461	--ABSTRACT--
462	14:Abstract
463	15:An LLM multi-agent system (MAS) is only as good as the agents it chooses to trust:
464	16:its accuracy and cost hinge on its topology, meaning which agents are included
465	17:and how they communicate. A single task score, however, does not reveal which
466	18:agents help or hinder performance. We propose Contrastive Attribution Topology
467	19:Search (CATS), which searches for compact teams within a fixed supergraph of
468	20:specialized agents. An LLM attributer compares execution traces across candidate
469	21:topologies and assigns credit to individual agents. CATS uses these credits to update
470	22:supergraph edges while progressively pruning weak edges and agents, yielding a
471	23:small team for deployment. With small open-weight models and matched candidate
472	24:evaluations, CATS improves mean accuracy on BigCodeBench by 5.3 percentage
473	25:points over score-only heuristic search while using 54% fewer deployment tokens.
474	26:On MBPP, CATS matches the strongest baselines with fewer tokens than the
475	27:other searches. In a HotpotQA prompt-poisoning stress test, CATS excludes all
476	28:adversarially prompted agents in all three runs, whereas random search retains some
477	29:at comparable accuracy. Per-agent credit thus supports both team optimization and
478	30:the pruning of potentially harmful agents.
479	31:1
480	32:Introduction
481	33:LLM-based multi-agent systems split work across specialized agents, for example one that writes
482	34:code and another that tests it. Such collaboration can improve small models [9, 10], but more agents
483	35:and messages mean more tokens. Building a good system therefore requires choosing which agents
484	36:to include and how they communicate, that is, the topology. Since the best topology depends on the
485	37:task, manual design is difficult [5, 6], which motivates automated search over candidate teams.
486	38:Task scores, however, evaluate the team as a whole: a correct solution may contain unnecessary work,
487	39:and a failed one may include useful contributions. Scores alone thus say little about which agents to
488	40:keep. Can feedback on individual agents guide the search for compact, effective teams?
489	41:We introduce Contrastive Attribution Topology Search (CATS), an offline meta-agent that assembles
490	42:teams from a fixed agent pool. Starting from a supergraph of candidate links, CATS evaluates
491	43:sampled teams on target-domain tasks. An LLM compares their transcripts and assigns each agent
492	44:signed credit. CATS then updates link probabilities, prunes weak links and unreachable agents, and
493	45:selects one fixed team for deployment. Agent models, prompts, roles, and tools never change.
494	46:Our contributions are: (i) contrastive per-agent credit to guide team construction (Figure 1), (ii) higher
495	47:mean accuracy and lower deployment token use than score-only search on two coding benchmarks
496	--INTRO END--

506	454:A meta-agent that assembles teams must also decline
507	455:to delegate to agents it should not trust. To probe
508	456:this failure mode, we construct a poisoned variant
509	457:of HotpotQA [12], a third domain distinct from the
510	458:coding tasks above. Its supergraph contains six ad-
511	459:versarially prompted agents and four honest agents.
512	460:The attacks include plan misdirection, fabricated
513	461:evidence, citation spoofing, instruction hijacking,
514	462:late answer overwrites, and exact-match sabotage
515	463:(Table 3). The search receives no adversarial super-
516	464:vision: it observes only task scores and transcripts,
517	465:and is never told which agents are poisoned. Table 2
518	466:shows why task score alone is insufficient to assess
519	467:delegation: comparable scores can mask different levels of poisoned-agent recruitment. CATS retains
520	468:no poisoned agents across all three seeds. Random search retains two on average. Score-only search’s
521	469:teams are cheap but inaccurate: 1, 2, and 5 agents, one with four poisoned. CATS instead removes
522	470:their incoming edges, making them unreachable (Figure 3). Exclusion is therefore a byproduct of the
523	471:optimization signal, not a separate security filter.

525	--METHOD--
526	284:Method
527	285:CATS repeatedly samples teams from a supergraph, credits each agent, and prunes weak edges.
528	286:Supergraph. We search for an optimized multi-agent topology as a subgraph of a hand-crafted
529	287:complete directed acyclic graph specialized to a chosen problem domain (Figure 1). Its nodes are
530	288:agents and its edges denote direct communication (and thereby the scheduling order). Agents are
531	289:specialized via system prompts, optional reasoning, and tool sets. We hand-craft them using domain
532	290:knowledge (automating this is left to future work). Each edge e carries a logit θe with sampling
533	291:probability αe = σ(θe), initialized to a common α0. Following DARTS [7], we relax the discrete
534	292:edge choices to these continuous parameters but replace gradient descent with heuristic credit-based
535	293:updates derived from contrastive attribution.
536	294:Sampling. At each step, we sample K topologies by independently drawing e ∼Bernoulli(αe),
537	295:rejecting graphs with nodes unreachable from the source. Since agents share an environment, not
538	296:every agent needs a downstream consumer: edges are optional communication channels. We evaluate
539	297:each candidate on N tasks, obtaining scores sk,q. Candidates, tasks, and often agents run in parallel.
540	298:Attribution. An LLM attributer assigns each participating agent i in candidate k on task q a credit
541	299:ck,q,i ∈[−1, 1] (harmful to helpful) by comparing candidate rollouts on the same task. The attributer
542	300:sees task scores, length-capped agent outputs, tool calls, and the final artifact state (e.g., the coding
543	301:environment), and runs in parallel across tasks.
544	302:Update. Credits are normalized into per-agent advantages Ak,i = |Qk,i|−1 �
545	303:q∈Qk,i(ck,q,i −bq),
546	304:where Qk,i holds the tasks with a credit for i in k and bq is the mean credit over participating agents and
547	305:candidates for task q. Each edge (u, v) fired in candidate k is updated by θuv ←θuv +ηAk,v. Unfired
548	306:non-source edges into an active agent v receive a smaller secondary update θuv ←θuv + ηρAk,v.
549	307:After each step we prune weak edges whose probability has fallen below the fraction δ of its initial
550	308:value (the pruning fraction), E ←{e ∈E : αe ≥δα0}, and remove nodes that are no longer
551	309:reachable from the source. This shrinks |E| and thus |V |, reducing the per-step cost.
552	310:Selection. After T steps we return the best final candidate G⋆= arg maxk 1
553	311:N

556	314:step-T candidates, which are sampled under the accumulated priors. Ties are broken in favor of fewer
557	315:agents and then the earlier candidate. As an ablation, we also evaluate the pruned supergraph Gp,

617	--LIMITATIONS--
618	483:Limitations, Responsible Use, and Conclusion
619	484:Evaluating a single model family across three domains and three seeds limits what we can conclude
620	485:about broader transfer and variance, while high baseline scores on MBPP leave little headroom for
621	486:accuracy gains. Moreover, although pruning yields sparse coding teams, this may reflect coordination
622	487:via the shared environment rather than a general lack of need for direct communication. Finally, we
623	488:only track token cost without optimizing it, making Pareto search over score and cost, as done for
624	489:prompts by Büssing et al. [2], a natural next step.
625	490:Attribution credits have not been validated against human judgments. Credit–success correlation
626	491:(Table 9) is only a consistency check, since the attributer sees system_score. The score-only
627	492:baseline was not separately tuned and does not isolate which component of CATS accounts for the
628	493:difference. Credit is node-level, propagated equally to all incoming fired edges. A comparison with
629	494:Graph-GRPO’s statistical edge-level credit remains future work [3].
630	495:CATS turns a hand-crafted supergraph into a small fixed team. It improved the balance between
631	496:performance and efficiency on BigCodeBench, reduced unnecessary complexity on the easier MBPP,
632	497:and excluded poisoned agents that task scores alone could not detect. In all three domains it matched
633	498:or beat score-only heuristic search on score, deployment-token use, or both. This supports attribution
634	499:for team optimization and the pruning of potentially harmful agents, not a security guarantee.
635	500:Responsible-use statement.
636	501:Selecting a topology determines which agents gain access to tools and
637	502:task context. Our stress test shows that attribution can exclude fixed adversarial prompts, but this
638	503:does not establish deployment safety. An adaptive adversary could act beyond the capped transcript
639	504:window or exploit the unverified LLM attributer directly. Tool and data permissions must therefore
640	505:remain outside the optimizer.

645	15:ABSTRACT
646	16:Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed software engineering (SE), ex-
647	17:hibiting exceptional abilities in various coding tasks. Although recent advance-
648	18:ments have led to the development of autonomous software agents using LLMs
649	19:for end-to-end development tasks, these systems are often tailored to specific SE
650	20:tasks. We present HYPERAGENT , a novel generalist multi-agent system that ad-
651	21:dresses a broad spectrum of SE tasks across multiple programming languages by
652	22:emulating the workflows of human developers. HYPERAGENT consists of four
653	23:specialized agents—Planner, Navigator, Code Editor, and Executor—capable of
654	24:managing the full lifecycle of SE tasks, from initial planning to final verifica-
655	25:tion. HYPERAGENT achieves state-of-the-art results on diverse SE tasks, includ-
656	26:ing GitHub issue resolution on the well-known SWE-Bench benchmark, surpass-
657	27:ing strong baselines. Additionally, HYPERAGENT excels in repository-level code
658	28:generation (RepoExec) and fault localization and program repair (Defects4J), fre-
659	29:quently outperforming SOTA baselines.
660	30:GitHub: https://github.com/FSoft-AI4Code/HyperAgent
661	31:1
662	32:INTRODUCTION
663	33:In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in as-
664	34:sisting with various coding tasks, ranging from code generation and completion to bug fixing and
665	35:refactoring. These models have transformed the way developers interact with code, providing pow-
666	36:erful tools that can understand and generate human-like code snippets with impressive accuracy.
667	37:However, as software engineering tasks grow in complexity, there is an emerging need for more
668	38:sophisticated solutions that can handle the intricacies of real-world software development.
669	39:Software agents built on LLMs have emerged as a promising solution to automate complex software
670	40:engineering tasks, leveraging the advanced reasoning and generative abilities of LLMs. These agents
671	41:can handle tasks such as code generation, bug localization, and orchestrating multi-step development
672	42:processes. However, most current agents are limited in scope, typically focused on a specific SE
673	43:task, such as resolving GitHub issues (Jimenez et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Arora et al., 2024;
674	44:Xia et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024a; Yang et al., 2024) using benchmarks like SWE-bench (Jimenez
675	45:et al., 2023), or tackling competitive code generation tasks like APPS (Hendrycks et al., 2021),
676	46:HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021a), and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021). Other agents (Qian et al., 2024;
677	47:Hong et al., 2023; Nguyen et al., 2024) focus on generating complex software based on requirements.
678	48:While these specialized agents excel in their domains, their claim of addressing general software

832	891:CONCLUSION
833	892:In this paper, we introduced HYPERAGENT , a generalist multi-agent system designed to address a
834	893:wide range of software engineering tasks. By closely mimicking typical software engineering work-
835	894:flows, HYPERAGENT incorporates stages for analysis, planning, feature localization, code editing,
836	895:and execution/verification. Our extensive evaluations across diverse benchmarks, including GitHub
837	896:issue resolution, code generation at repository-level scale, and fault localization and program repair,
838	897:demonstrate that HYPERAGENT not only matches but often exceeds the performance of specialized
839	898:systems. The success of HYPERAGENT highlights the potential of generalist approaches in soft-
840	899:ware engineering, offering a versatile tool that can adapt to various tasks with minimal configuration
841	900:changes. Its design emphasizes generalizability, efficiency, and scalability, making it well-suited for
842	901:real-world software development scenarios where tasks can vary significantly in complexity and
843	902:scope.

849	##### library/05_review_queue/2510.10611_HyperAgent-Hypergraph/2510.10611_HyperAgent-Hypergraph_fulltext.txt  (1428 lines)
850	--ABSTRACT--
851	41:ABSTRACT
852	42:Recent advances in large language model-powered multi-agent sys-
853	43:tems have demonstrated remarkable collective intelligence through
854	44:effective communication. However, existing approaches face two
855	45:primary challenges: (i) Ineffective group collaboration modeling, as
856	46:they rely on pairwise edge representations in graph structures, lim-
857	47:iting their ability to capture relationships among multiple agents;
858	48:and (ii) Limited task-adaptiveness in communication topology de-
859	49:sign, leading to excessive communication cost for simple tasks
860	50:and insufficient coordination for complex scenarios. These issues
861	51:restrict the scalability and practical deployment of adaptive col-
862	52:laboration frameworks. To address these challenges, we propose
863	53:HyperAgent, a hypergraph-based framework that optimizes com-
864	54:munication topologies and effectively captures group collaboration
865	55:patterns using direct hyperedge representations. Unlike edge-based
866	56:approaches, HyperAgent uses hyperedges to link multiple agents
867	57:within the same subtask and employs hypergraph convolutional
868	58:layers to achieve one-step information aggregation in collabora-
869	59:tion groups. Additionally, it incorporates a variational autoencoder
870	60:framework with sparsity regularization to dynamically adjust hy-
871	61:pergraph topologies based on task complexity. Experiments high-
872	62:light the superiority of HyperAgent in both performance and effi-
873	63:ciency. For instance, on GSM8K, HyperAgent achieves 95.07% accu-
874	64:racy while reducing token consumption by 25.33%, demonstrating
875	65:the potential of hypergraph-based optimization for multi-agent
876	66:communication.
877	67:∗Corresponding author.
878	68:This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution Inter-
879	69:national 4.0 License.
880	70:Proc. of the 25th International Conference on Autonomous Agents and Multiagent Systems
881	71:(AAMAS 2026), C. Amato, L. Dennis, V. Mascardi, J. Thangarajah (eds.), May 25 – 29,
882	72:2026, Paphos, Cyprus. © 2026 International Foundation for Autonomous Agents and
883	73:Multiagent Systems (www.ifaamas.org). https://doi.org/10.65109/
884	74:KEYWORDS
885	--INTRO END--
886	196:• We observe that pairwise graph representations fail to cap-
887	197:ture multi-agent collaboration effectively. Existing methods
888	198:force a tradeoff between sparse topologies, which fragment
889	199:coordination, and dense topologies, which increase commu-
890	200:nication overhead.
891	201:• We propose HyperAgent, a hypergraph-based framework
892	202:that uses hyperedges to represent group collaboration units.
893	203:This representation enables direct synchronization within
894	204:teams through unified node-edge-node transformations.
895	205:• We develop a variational hypergraph autoencoder for task-
896	206:adaptive topology generation. It encodes agent features and
897	207:task semantics into latent representations and generates
898	208:sparse hypergraphs, adjusting complexity according to task
899	209:difficulty.
900	210:• Extensive experiments demonstrate HyperAgent outperforms
901	211:state-of-the-art methods, achieving 88.50% accuracy on MMLU
902	212:and 92.90% pass@1 on HumanEval, with up to 25.33% re-
903	213:duction in communication token consumption.
904	214:
905	215:============================================================
906	216:=== PAGE 3 ===
907	217:============================================================
908	218:
909	219:Figure 2: The HyperAgent pipeline. We encode agents and tasks into a hypergraph, then apply a variational autoencoder
910	220:with sparsity regularization to generate task-adaptive communication topologies. Agents interact through hyperedge-based
911	221:collaboration for multiple rounds. The VAE is trained via policy gradients to maximize task performance while minimizing
912	222:communication overhead.
913	223:2
914	--METHOD--
915	280:Problem Formulation
916	281:We model the multi-agent system as a hypergraph H = (V, E, W).
917	282:The node set V = {𝑣1, . . . , 𝑣𝑁} represents 𝑁agents in the system.
918	283:Each node 𝑣𝑖∈V corresponds to an agent, formalized as:
919	284:𝑣𝑖= {Base𝑖, Role𝑖, State𝑖, Plugin𝑖}
920	285:(1)
921	286:Each agent 𝑣𝑖is composed of four key elements: (1) Base𝑖, the
922	287:language model instance powering 𝑣𝑖; (2) Role𝑖, the agent’s pre-
923	288:assigned role or function; (3) State𝑖, representing the agent’s accu-
924	289:mulated knowledge and interaction history; and (4) Plugin𝑖, a set of
925	290:external tools available to 𝑣𝑖, such as web searchers, code compilers,
926	291:or file readers. The hyperedge set E contains collaboration units.
927	292:Each hyperedge 𝑒∈E connects multiple agents participating in
928	293:the same subtask. The weight matrix W ∈R| E|×| E| assigns impor-
929	294:tance scores to different collaboration units. We set W = I|E|×|E|
930	295:by default, treating all collaboration units equally.
931	296:
932	297:============================================================
933	298:=== PAGE 4 ===
934	299:============================================================
935	300:

1008	1142:In this work, we propose HyperAgent, a hypergraph-based multi-
1009	1143:agent communication framework that connects agents sharing
1010	1144:subtasks via hyperedges for efficient single-step information ag-

1025	--ABSTRACT--
1026	17:Abstract
1027	18:Agentic tool use has gained traction with the rise of agentic tool calling, yet
1028	19:most existing work overlooks the complexity of multi-turn tool interactions. We
1029	20:introduce OrchDAG, a synthetic data generation pipeline that models tool execution
1030	21:as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) with controllable complexity. Using this dataset,
1031	22:we benchmark model performance and propose a graph-based reward to enhance
1032	23:RLVR training. Experiments show that the dataset presents a challenging but
1033	24:solvable benchmark, and the proposed reward is effective when combined with
1034	25:GRPO-style algorithms, highlighting the importance of leveraging topological
1035	26:structure and data complexity in multi-turn tool use.
1036	27:1
1037	28:INTRODUCTION
1038	29:Large Language Models (LLMs) ([3, 5, 6, 26, 36]) have been at the forefront of advancing artificial
1039	30:intelligence, marking significant breakthroughs in diverse fields. The planning capabilities of LLMs,
1040	31:particularly their ability to use tools ([33, 34]), enable them not only to execute commands and
1041	32:perform web searches but also to enhance their advanced mathematical reasoning abilities. LLM
1042	33:Compiler [12] and its subsequent work ([7, 8]) propose constructing tooling usage as a directed acyclic
1043	34:graph (DAG) to enable the parallel execution of independent tools, thereby improving tool-calling
1044	35:efficiency. CodeAct [28] and CodePlan [29] propose leveraging the generation of pseudo-Python code
1045	36:to outline high-level reasoning processes for complex multi-step reasoning tasks, where each tool
1046	37:usage is represented as a function call within the code. ReWOO [30] proposes a modular framework
1047	38:that decouples the reasoning process from the external observations of each tool usage, thereby
1048	39:reducing token consumption and improving efficiency. [15] clusters the provided tools into groups
1049	40:of toolkits, plans at the toolkit level, and replans by selecting tools within the same toolkit if error
1050	41:comes out. [17] proposes a method called Predictive-Decoding, which leverages Model Predictive
1051	42:Control from the optimal control field to mitigate early errors in planning and promote non-myopic
1052	43:planning, thereby enhancing overall accuracy. ReasonFlux [31] proposes a framework in which the
1053	44:LLM reasons over template fields, executes tools based on the templates, and employs reinforcement
1054	45:learning to improve planning accuracy using an action completion reward.
1055	46:In the agentic setting, LLMs are evolving beyond purely textual reasoning toward dynamic agents
1056	47:capable of planning, tool use, and multi-step (also multi-turn) execution. The introduction of Group
1057	48:Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [22] further inspired the development of Reinforcement
1058	49:Learning with Verifiable Reward (RLVR) for agentic tool use, driven by its efficiency. The xLAM
1059	50:∗Work is done during internship in Amazon. Equal contribution.
1060	--INTRO END--
1061	106:the plan list after topological sorting, T is the set of available tools, and D is the collection of
1062	107:descriptions for all available tools. At each step t, the LLM generates an intermediate reasoning
1063	108:output rt ∼ρθ(rt | T , D, x, p, O1, . . . , Ot−1) and executes the plan step Pt to obtain the observation
1064	109:Ot. The final response is then generated as R ∼ρθ(R | T , D, x, p, O1, . . . , On).
1065	110:In later turns, a user may issue an irrelevant query requiring a completely new tool execution graph, or
1066	111:a dependent query that builds on partial outputs from earlier tool executions or responses. Additionally,
1067	112:some tools may return errors (e.g., timeouts), requiring unfinished execution paths from prior queries
1068	113:to be rescheduled.

1075	120:2.2
1076	121:Tool Execution as DAG
1077	122:Given a plan p generated by the LLM, we represent it as a directed graph G = (V, E), where
1078	123:V = (v1, . . . , vn) is the set of nodes and E = (e1, . . . , em) is the set of edges. The node v1
1079	124:corresponds to the user query, and vn represents the final node that aggregates observations and
1080	125:returns the response. The intermediate nodes v2, . . . , vn−1 correspond to tool calls, each associated
1081	126:with an attribute that stores its tool payload in JSON format. An edge ei ∈E denotes a dependency
1082	127:between two tools, where an output key from the source tool serves as an input key to the target tool.
1083	128:We represent the tool graph as an ordered list of tasks in a JSON-like text style. Each task contains
1084	129:four fields : task_id, toolname, payload, and dependencies. A task can be associated with
1085	130:multiple dependencies. A task can be expressed as {task_id: task_4, toolname: name, payload:
1086	131:{param1: val1, param2: $2.outputkey1, param3: $3.outputkey4}, dependencies: [task_2,
1087	132:task_3]}.
1088	133:3
1089	--METHOD--
1090	134:METHODOLOGY
1091	135:In real-world domains, API specifications and orchestrations are often considerably more complex,
1092	136:making it challenging for LLMs pretrained on general public data to generate accurate and reliable
1093	137:plans for diverse user queries. Drawing inspiration from LLMCompiler [12, 8], for queries involving
1094	138:complex tool interactions, it is advantageous to first construct a tool execution DAG. This DAG serves
1095	139:as a blueprint for executing tools sequentially or in parallel, with subsequent replanning guided by
1096	140:both the execution results of the current DAG and any new user queries in later turns.
1097	141:3.1
1098	142:OrchDAG – Synthetic Data Generation Pipeline for Multi-Turn Tool Use
1099	143:As discussed in Section 1, the design of the data generation pipeline follows several key principles to
1100	144:better reflect real-world tool-use scenarios: (1) the complexity of the tool execution DAG for each
1101	145:synthetic user query should be controllable through pipeline hyperparameters, (2) the system prompt
1102	146:provided to the LLM must include irrelevant tools (both schema and description) so that the model
1103	147:learns to identify and select only the relevant ones, (3) the output payload of each tool should contain
1104	148:multiple fields, typically four or five, and (4) at least one key output field from a tool should serve as
1105	149:an input to another tool, but with a different field name, to capture schema misalignment commonly
1106	150:observed in practice.
1107	151:Moreover, in multi-turn settings, the data should capture scenarios where certain nodes in the tool
1108	152:execution DAG fail. When the user issues a follow-up query, the corresponding DAG in the dataset
1109	153:should exclude nodes that have already been executed in the previous turn, while reusing their
1110	154:available results whenever applicable. In light of these requirements, we develop a graph-based data
1111	155:generation pipeline implemented with LangGraph 2, accompanied by a set of validation functions to
1112	156:ensure the quality of the generated data points.
1113	157:As shown in Figure 1, the data generation pipeline begins by collecting real high-quality tools
1114	158:from existing benchmarks, Specifically, we leverage APIGEN [16] and TOOLACE [14]. To ensure
1115	159:sufficient complexity, we retain only examples where the final answer involves more than two distinct
1116	160:functions represented in JSON format. Notably, we extract tools directly from the answers rather than
1117	161:from the system-prompt tool lists. This design choice eliminates the need for additional categorization
1118	162:or clustering steps, which could introduce unnecessary uncertainty, while naturally yielding a smaller
1119	163:and more coherent set of related tools. After filtering, APIGEN contributes 2,542 data points and
1120	164:TOOLACE contributes 1,005.
1121	165:For each data point, suppose it contains four real tools; these are placed as the first layer of the tool
1122	166:execution DAG. Based on the hyperparameters of the DAG (height and width), we then randomly
1123	167:sample a topological order to obtain a DAG template (see Figure 1). According to this template,
1124	168:we synthesize the tools for each node layer by layer under the following conditions: (1) each input
1125	169:key must depend on an output key from one of its parent nodes in the DAG, and (2) the field names
1126	170:should not remain identical across instances but instead vary randomly. After populating the DAG
1127	171:template, we obtain the tool execution DAG, which is then used to prompt the LLM to generate
1128	172:the corresponding user query, conditioned on the DAG and a few-shot set of examples. Finally, we
1129	173:2https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/

1158	331:Task Difficulty
1159	332:We investigate two central questions: (1) Given the designed difficulty of our synthetic data, is the
1160	333:dataset solvable in principle? A dataset that cannot be solved even by advanced closed-source models
1161	334:such as Claude 4 or GPT-4o would lack practical utility. (2) If it is solvable, does the dataset offer a
1162	335:sufficient level of challenge to meaningfully evaluate model performance? To begin with, we evaluate
1163	336:several closed-source and open-source models by providing them with the system prompt defined in
1164	337:Section 3.1, and measure whether they can correctly predict the DAG by analyzing tool dependencies.
1165	338:In the multi-turn setting, models must generate the DAG by considering both the available tools and
1166	339:the observations from previous turns. We use Accuracy (pass@1) to evaluate performance, as our
1167	340:focus here is on assessing the task difficulty introduced by the dataset.

1181	--CONCLUSION--
1182	546:CONCLUSION
1183	547:In summary, we introduce OrchDAG, a synthetic multi-turn data generation pipeline that models
1184	548:tool execution as DAGs with controllable complexity. Leveraging this dataset, we evaluate model
1185	549:performance and propose a graph-based reward to enhance RLVR training. Extensive experiments
1186	550:validate the effectiveness of our approach, underscoring the importance of exploiting the topological
1187	551:structure of tool execution graphs and managing data complexity in multi-turn tool use.

1200	--ABSTRACT--
1201	1:
1202	2:============================================================
1203	3:=== PAGE 1 ===
1204	4:============================================================
1205	5:
1206	6:HyperAgents
1207	7:Jenny Zhang1,2†, Bingchen Zhao3†, Wannan Yang4†, Jakob Foerster6
1208	8:Jeff Clune1,2,5, Minqi Jiang‡, Sam Devlin7, Tatiana Shavrina6
1209	9:1University of British Columbia, 2Vector Institute, 3University of Edinburgh
1210	10:4New York University, 5Canada CIFAR AI Chair, 6FAIR at Meta, 7Meta Superintelligence Labs
1211	11:†Work done during internship at Meta, ‡Work done at Meta
1212	12:Self-improving AI systems aim to reduce reliance on human engineering by learning to improve
1213	13:their own learning and problem-solving processes. Existing approaches to recursive self-improvement
1214	14:typically rely on fixed, handcrafted meta-level mechanisms, which fundamentally limit how fast such
1215	15:systems can improve. The Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM) (Zhang et al., 2025b) demonstrates that
1216	16:open-ended self-improvement is achievable in coding. Starting from a single coding agent, the DGM
1217	17:repeatedly generates and evaluates self-modified variants, forming a growing archive of stepping stones
1218	18:for future improvement. Because both evaluation and self-modification are coding tasks, gains in
1219	19:coding ability can translate into gains in self-improvement ability. However, this alignment does
1220	20:not generally hold beyond coding domains. We introduce hyperagents, self-referential agents that
1221	21:integrate a task agent (which solves the target task) and a meta agent (which modifies itself and the
1222	22:task agent) into a single editable program. Crucially, the meta-level modification procedure is itself
1223	23:editable, enabling metacognitive self-modification, improving not only task-solving behavior, but also
1224	24:the mechanism that generates future improvements. We instantiate this framework by extending DGM
1225	25:to create DGM-Hyperagents (DGM-H). By allowing the improvement procedure to evolve, the DGM-H
1226	26:eliminates the assumption of domain-specific alignment between task performance and self-modification
1227	27:skill, and can potentially support self-accelerating progress on any computable task. Across diverse
1228	28:domains (coding, paper review, robotics reward design, and Olympiad-level math-solution grading),
1229	29:the DGM-H improves performance over time and outperforms baselines without self-improvement or
1230	30:open-ended exploration, as well as prior self-improving systems like DGM. We further show that the
1231	31:DGM-H improves the process by which it generates new agents (e.g., persistent memory, performance
1232	32:tracking), and that these meta-level improvements transfer across domains and accumulate across
1233	33:runs. All experiments were conducted with safety precautions (e.g., sandboxing, human oversight).
1234	34:We discuss what safety entails in this setting and the broader implications of self-improving systems.
1235	--INTRO END--
1236	92:achieves gains comparable to the most established prior self-improving algorithm (the Darwin Gödel Machine,
1237	93:Zhang et al., 2025b), despite not being handcrafted for coding. Beyond coding, the DGM-H substantially
1238	94:improves performance on paper review (Zhao et al., 2026) and robotics reward design (Genesis, 2024), with
1239	95:gains transferring to held-out test tasks and significantly outperforming prior self-improving algorithms,
1240	96:which struggle outside coding unless customized. Ablations without self-improvement or without open-ended
1241	97:exploration show little to no progress, highlighting the necessity of each component (Section 5.1). Crucially,
1242	98:the DGM-H learns transferable mechanisms on how to self-improve (e.g., persistent memory, performance
1243	99:tracking) that systematically improve its ability to generate better task or meta agents over time. As a
1244	100:result, meta-level improvements learned by the DGM-H transfer across domains. Specifically, hyperagents
1245	101:optimized in one setting (i.e., paper review and robotics tasks) remain significantly effective at generating
1246	102:improved task agents in a different domain (i.e., Olympiad-level math grading), and an ablation shows that
1247	103:the transferred meta agent, rather than the transferred task agent, accounts for nearly all of this benefit
1248	104:(Section 5.2). We further show that self-improvements learned by the DGM-H in one setting can compound
1249	105:with continued self-improvement in another setting (Section 5.3). We note that these results are obtained in
1250	106:finite benchmark settings with fixed task distributions, frozen closed FMs, fixed evaluation protocols, and (in
1251	107:the main experiments) fixed parent selection. They demonstrate useful task-level and meta-level improvements
1252	108:and their transfer across domains; they do not yet establish unbounded or self-accelerating improvement,
1253	109:which we view as the long-term motivation that DGM-H contributes to (Section 7). We discuss the safety
1254	110:implications of such open-ended self-improving systems and outline practical considerations for responsible
1255	111:deployment in Section 6. Overall, hyperagents open up the possibility of improving their ability to improve

1306	331:Experiment Setup
1307	332:The DGM-H is initialized with a single hyperagent built around a frozen FM (Brown et al., 2020) with
1308	333:external tool-use capabilities (Schick et al., 2023). The FM autonomously invokes tools as needed at each
1309	334:step. This initial hyperagent is equipped with two tools: a bash tool for executing shell commands, and a
1310	335:specialized tool for inspecting and modifying files. In the initial hyperagent, the task agent receives the task
1311	336:inputs and outputs the response from a single FM call. The meta agent receives the location of the agent’s
1312	337:repository, the location of previous evaluation results, and the number of remaining experiment iterations
1313	338:(the experiment budget is a hyperparameter), and is tasked with modifying any part of the given codebase
1314	339:(Appendix A.1). We deliberately keep the implementation of the initial hyperagent (i.e., both the task agent
1315	340:5
1316	341:
1317	342:============================================================
1318	343:=== PAGE 6 ===
1319	344:============================================================
1320	345:
1321	346:and the meta agent) simple, allowing for a broad search space and avoiding prematurely constraining the range
1322	347:of possible improvements. Appendix D.1 details the FMs and the hyperparameters used in each experiment,
1323	348:while Appendix D.2 reports the corresponding cost estimates.
1324	349:4.1
1325	350:Baselines
1326	351:We compare the Darwin Gödel Machine with Hyperagents (DGM-H) against a set of baselines designed
1327	352:to isolate the contributions of self-improving meta agents, open-ended exploration, and metacognitive self-
1328	353:modification (i.e., hyperagents) (Appendix B). DGM-H without self-improving meta agents (DGM-H w/o
1329	354:self-improve) fixes the meta agent modifying other hyperagents to the initial meta agent for the entire
1330	355:run. While the system can still generate and evaluate new hyperagents, the procedures used to propose
1331	356:and apply modifications are not themselves modifiable. This baseline replicates the approach of (ADAS,
1332	357:Hu et al., 2025) in this setting. It tests whether performance gains arise solely from task-level optimization
1333	358:under a fixed meta-level mechanism, or from improvements in the self-improvement process itself. DGM-H
1334	359:without open-ended exploration (DGM-H w/o open-ended exploration) removes the archive of previously
1335	360:generated hyperagents. Instead of retaining previous variants as stepping stones for future exploration, each
1336	361:newly generated hyperagent replaces its predecessor. After generating a new hyperagent, it is evaluated and
1337	362:automatically becomes the next selected parent. This baseline isolates the role of open-ended, population-based
1338	363:search. Comparing against this baseline tests whether sustained improvement requires accumulating and
1339	364:reusing diverse intermediate solutions.
1340	365:We also compare against the original implementation of the Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM) (Zhang et al.,
1341	366:2025b). The DGM relies on a handcrafted, fixed mechanism to generate self-improvement instructions.
1342	367:Because this instruction-generation mechanism is designed specifically for coding benchmarks and is not
1343	368:modifiable, the DGM’s self-improvement capacity in other domains is limited (Section 2). To provide a stronger
1344	369:comparison, we manually customize the DGM’s instruction-generation mechanism for the target domains
1345	370:(DGM-custom) (Appendix B). This baseline measures how much the DGM relies on human engineering to
1346	371:remain competitive across domains. Comparing the DGM-H against this baseline tests whether automated
1347	372:metacognitive self-modification can outperform human-designed self-improvement mechanisms. Additionally,
1348	373:we compare against static solutions that have been handcrafted for each domain in prior work.
1349	374:4.2
1350	375:Domains
1351	376:We evaluate our method and baselines across diverse domains (i.e., coding, paper review, robotics reward
1352	377:design, and Olympiad-level math grading) (Appendix C). To reduce computational cost, for each domain we
1353	378:first evaluate agents on a small subset of the training tasks to estimate overall effectiveness. Only agents that
1354	379:demonstrate sufficient performance are subsequently evaluated on the remaining training tasks. Agents that
1355	380:do not are treated as having zero performance on unevaluated tasks. Domain-specific evaluation protocols are
1356	--RESULTS--
1357	440:Results
1358	441:For each experiment, we run each method 5 times. We report medians with 95% bootstrap confidence
1359	442:intervals computed from 1,000 resamples, using the notation median (CI: lower – upper). In line plots, lines
1360	443:show median performance and shaded regions indicate the confidence intervals (Figures 2 to 4). Bar plots
1361	444:report median performance on held-out test sets, with error bars indicating confidence intervals (Figures 2
1362	445:to 4). Statistical significance is assessed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Overall, the DGM-H exhibits
1363	446:general self-improvement at both the task and meta levels. Improvements to the task agent transfer to
1364	447:held-out test tasks within each domain, exceeding open-sourced static baselines (Section 5.1). Meta-level
1365	448:improvements transfer across domains, enabling hyperagents to significantly improve their ability to generate
1366	449:better task agents in previously unseen domains (Section 5.2). Self-improvements learned in one DGM-H run
1367	450:can potentially accelerate learning in subsequent runs and continue to compound as further self-modifications
1368	451:are applied (Section 5.3). All experiment logs are open-sourced in our codebase.
